cards.a: An assistant presses firmly downward and sideways on the mother's lower abdomen just above the pubic bone, pushing the baby's trapped shoulder under the bone. It is done together with the McRoberts manoeuvre, because the two together resolve most cases without needing the clinician's hand inside the vagina.
cards.q: What is suprapubic pressure and how does it help in shoulder dystocia?

cards.a: Internal manoeuvres: the Wood's screw, rotating the baby's shoulders by pressing on the back of the anterior shoulder, or delivering the posterior arm by reaching in, flexing the arm, and sweeping it across the baby's chest. These free the shoulders from inside the pelvis and are the next step when external manoeuvres have not worked.
cards.q: If McRoberts and suprapubic pressure fail, what is the next manoeuvre for shoulder dystocia?

cards.a: Do not pull hard on the baby's head (excessive traction) and do not push down on the top of the uterus (fundal pressure), because both increase the risk of stretching the brachial plexus nerves in the baby's neck and shoulder. The shoulders must be freed by manoeuvres, not by force, and an episiotomy does not fix the problem either, though it may give room for internal manoeuvres.
cards.q: What should NOT be done during shoulder dystocia?

cards.a: Brachial plexus injury, usually Erb's palsy, which weakens the arm because the nerves between the neck and shoulder were stretched when the shoulder was stuck. Most cases recover within months, but some leave permanent weakness, and the risk is higher when excessive traction is applied or the dystocia lasts longer.
cards.q: What is the most common complication of shoulder dystocia for the baby?

cards.a: Postpartum haemorrhage, because the prolonged, difficult delivery often leads to uterine atony, and severe perineal tears are also common. After the baby is delivered, the mother needs active management of the third stage and careful inspection for tears, because bleeding can be heavy and rapid.
cards.q: What is the most common maternal complication of shoulder dystocia?

cards.a: Breech is when the baby's buttocks or feet come first instead of the head, occurring in about 3 to 4 percent of term pregnancies. It matters because the baby's head is the largest part and comes last, so it can get stuck, and the cord can prolapse when the waters break, making vaginal delivery riskier.
cards.q: What is breech presentation?

cards.a: ECV is turning a breech baby to head-down by pressing on the mother's abdomen with the hands, usually around 36 to 37 weeks. It is offered to avoid a caesarean, because a successful version allows a normal vaginal delivery; it works in about half of cases and is done in hospital with monitoring, in case the baby becomes distressed and needs an urgent caesarean.
cards.q: What is external cephalic version (ECV) and when is it offered?

cards.a: ECV should not be done with placenta praevia, a scarred uterus that is unsafe for labour, ruptured membranes, fetal distress, or a multiple pregnancy with the first baby breech. In these situations turning the baby would be unsafe or pointless, because vaginal delivery is already not the plan.
cards.q: What are the contraindications to external cephalic version?

cards.a: Planned caesarean section is the recommended route for a term frank breech baby, because trials showed fewer deaths and serious injuries for the baby compared with planned vaginal breech delivery. Vaginal breech is only considered in selected cases with an experienced operator, a small baby, and a frank breech with a favourable pelvis.
cards.q: A woman at 37 weeks has a frank breech baby and ECV has failed. What is the recommended mode of delivery?

cards.a: Frank breech is buttocks first with the legs straight up in front of the face; complete breech is buttocks first with the legs crossed; footling breech is one or both feet first. Footling breech is the most dangerous for vaginal delivery, because a foot can slip through the cervix and the cord can prolapse, so it is always delivered by caesarean.
cards.q: What is the difference between frank, complete, and footling breech?

cards.a: Do not pull on the baby's body or legs, and let the baby deliver on its own until the umbilicus appears, because pulling down can extend the baby's head and cause it to get stuck. The head must be kept flexed, and the aftercoming head is delivered with the Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit manoeuvre, with the baby's body supported and the head flexed.
cards.q: During a vaginal breech delivery, what is the most important rule?

cards.a: It is the technique for delivering the aftercoming head in a breech birth: the baby's body rests on the clinician's forearm, one finger is placed in the baby's mouth to keep the head flexed, and the other hand presses on the baby's head from above through the abdomen. Keeping the head flexed lets the smallest diameter pass through the pelvis, which is why it is safer than pulling.
cards.q: What is the Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit manoeuvre?

cards.a: Head entrapment, where the baby's body is born but the head, the largest part, gets stuck in the pelvis or a cervix that has not fully dilated. The baby cannot breathe and the cord is compressed, so the head must be delivered within minutes, which is why breech vaginal delivery is only attempted with an experienced team.
cards.q: What is the main risk to the baby in a vaginal breech delivery?

cards.a: Chorionicity is whether the twins share one placenta (monochorionic) or have two (dichorionic), and it determines the risks: monochorionic twins can develop twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome, where blood flows unevenly between them through shared vessels. Dichorionic twins do not share vessels and have a much lower risk, so chorionicity is determined by ultrasound in the first trimester.
cards.q: Why is chorionicity important in a twin pregnancy?

cards.a: In monochorionic twins, blood vessels connect the two babies' circulations, and blood flows from one twin (the donor, who becomes small and has little fluid) to the other (the recipient, who becomes large and has too much fluid). It is a serious complication that needs referral to a specialist centre, where laser treatment can seal the connecting vessels.
cards.q: What is twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome?

cards.a: Around 37 to 38 weeks, because after that the risk of stillbirth rises and the babies gain little from staying in. Dichorionic twins are delivered earlier than singletons, and induction or planned caesarean is arranged at that gestation rather than waiting for labour to start on its own.
cards.q: What is the recommended timing of delivery for uncomplicated dichorionic twins?

cards.a: Around 36 to 37 weeks, earlier than dichorionic twins, because monochorionic twins carry a higher risk of stillbirth from shared-placenta complications. They are monitored more closely with frequent ultrasounds and delivered before the risk of staying pregnant outweighs the benefit.
cards.q: What is the recommended timing of delivery for uncomplicated monochorionic twins?

cards.a: Vaginal delivery is possible when the first twin is head-down, both babies are growing well, there is no other reason for caesarean, and the hospital can do an emergency caesarean for the second twin. The second twin is delivered soon after the first, often with help such as breaking the waters or an internal version, because a long delay risks distress.
cards.q: When can twins be delivered vaginally?

cards.a: The second twin is at risk of distress, cord prolapse, or a change in position after the first baby is born, because the uterus suddenly empties and the placenta may start to separate. That is why the second twin is monitored continuously and delivered promptly, usually within 15 to 30 minutes of the first.
cards.q: What is the main risk for the second twin during a vaginal twin delivery?

cards.a: Vaginal delivery of the first twin is possible, and the second twin can then be turned to head-down or breech by internal version and delivered vaginally, or delivered by caesarean if it cannot be turned. The plan depends on the operator's experience and the second baby's condition, and the mother should be counselled that a caesarean for the second twin is possible.
cards.q: A woman pregnant with twins has one baby head-down and the second transverse. What is the delivery plan?

cards.a: The uterus is stretched more than with one baby, which triggers contractions earlier, and multiple pregnancies also have higher rates of pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, and growth problems. That is why women with twins are monitored more closely and given steroids for fetal lung maturity if preterm delivery looks likely.
cards.q: Why are multiple pregnancies at higher risk of preterm labour?

cards.a: Arrest of dilatation is when the cervix stops dilating for 4 hours despite adequate contractions, or for 6 hours with inadequate contractions, in the active phase of labour (from 6 cm onwards). It is diagnosed only after enough time has passed, because labour can be slow without being arrested, and the cause must be found before deciding on caesarean.
cards.q: What is arrest of dilatation in labour?

cards.a: Arrest of descent is when the baby's head does not descend for 3 hours in a first-time mother with an epidural (2 hours without one), or 2 hours in a woman who has delivered before with an epidural (1 hour without). It suggests the head is too big for the pelvis or malpositioned, and the options are operative vaginal delivery if the head is low or caesarean if it is not.
cards.q: What is arrest of descent in the second stage of labour?

cards.a: Protraction means labour is progressing but too slowly, for example dilating less than 1 cm per hour in the active phase, while arrest means progress has stopped completely for a defined time. Protraction is often fixed by augmentation, whereas arrest usually needs a search for obstruction and often ends in operative delivery or caesarean.
cards.q: What is the difference between protraction and arrest disorders of labour?

cards.a: CPD is when the baby's head is too large to fit through the mother's pelvis, so labour cannot progress no matter how strong the contractions are. It is diagnosed when labour arrests despite adequate contractions with a well-positioned head, and the treatment is caesarean, because stronger contractions against a pelvis that is too small risk uterine rupture.
cards.q: What is cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD)?

cards.a: Occiput posterior is when the baby's head faces the mother's front, so the back of the head is against her back, instead of facing her back. It causes a longer, more painful labour with severe back pain, slower dilatation, and a higher chance of operative delivery, because the head presents a larger diameter to the pelvis.
cards.q: What is occiput posterior position and why does it slow labour?

cards.a: Encourage the mother to change position, especially onto her hands and knees or her side, which can help the baby rotate to face the back. If the head stays posterior and the second stage is prolonged, a vacuum or forceps delivery, or a manual rotation by the clinician, may be needed, and caesarean is used if the head does not descend.
cards.q: How is an occiput posterior position managed in labour?

cards.a: Transverse lie is when the baby lies sideways across the uterus, with the shoulder presenting, so no part of the baby can pass through the cervix. It cannot be delivered vaginally and carries a high risk of cord prolapse if the waters break, so the delivery is by caesarean section.
cards.q: What is a transverse lie and how is it delivered?

cards.a: Obstructed labour is when the baby cannot pass through the birth canal despite strong contractions, usually from cephalopelvic disproportion or malpresentation. The most dangerous complication is uterine rupture, because the uterus keeps contracting against an obstruction until it tears, so obstructed labour needs urgent recognition and caesarean before rupture occurs.
cards.q: What is obstructed labour and what is the most dangerous complication?

cards.a: An epidural delivers local anaesthetic through a small tube into the space around the spinal cord, numbing the lower body and providing the most effective pain relief in labour. It does not affect the baby's consciousness, it can be topped up for a caesarean if needed, and it is the preferred option when a long labour or an operative delivery is expected.
cards.q: What is the role of an epidural in labour analgesia?

cards.a: A drop in the mother's blood pressure, because the anaesthetic blocks the nerves that keep blood vessels constricted. It is prevented and treated with intravenous fluids before the epidural and by turning the mother to her left side; if the pressure stays low, a vasopressor such as ephedrine is given, because low pressure reduces blood flow to the baby.
cards.q: What is the most common side effect of an epidural and how is it managed?

cards.a: An epidural slightly prolongs the second stage, by about 15 to 30 minutes on average, because it reduces the urge to push and weakens the pelvic floor muscles. It does not increase the caesarean rate when given correctly, so the small delay is acceptable given the pain relief it provides.
cards.q: Does an epidural prolong labour?

cards.a: A post-dural puncture headache happens when the needle accidentally pierces the dura and spinal fluid leaks, causing a severe headache that is worse when sitting or standing and better lying flat, usually starting 1 to 2 days after delivery. It is treated with rest, fluids, and caffeine, and if it persists, a blood patch, where the woman's own blood is injected to seal the leak.
cards.q: What is a spinal headache after an epidural and how is it recognised?

cards.a: Pregnancy slows stomach emptying, so a woman in labour is assumed to have a full stomach, and general anaesthesia removes the reflexes that protect the airway, so stomach contents can be inhaled into the lungs (aspiration). That is why women in labour are kept nil by mouth when a caesarean is possible, and why a spinal or epidural is preferred over general anaesthesia whenever possible.
cards.q: Why is a full stomach a concern when a woman in labour needs general anaesthesia?

cards.a: It combines a single spinal injection for immediate, strong pain relief with an epidural catheter left in place for ongoing relief. It works faster than an epidural alone, which is useful when a woman is in severe pain, but it can cause a sudden drop in blood pressure and itching, so the mother and baby need close monitoring after it is given.
cards.q: What is combined spinal-epidural analgesia in labour?

cards.a: Alternatives include inhaled nitrous oxide (gas and air), opioid injections such as pethidine, warm water or a birthing pool, breathing techniques, and continuous support from a midwife or doula. None is as effective as an epidural, and opioids can make the baby sleepy at birth and reduce heart rate variability, so the choice depends on the woman's wishes and the stage of labour.
cards.q: What are the alternatives to an epidural for labour pain?

cards.a: A nuchal cord is when the umbilical cord is wrapped around the baby's neck, which happens in about a quarter of births. It usually causes no problem and the cord is simply slipped over the head after delivery, or the baby is delivered through the loop; it only needs action if the cord is tight and compresses the vessels, causing the heart rate to drop.
cards.q: What is a nuchal cord and does it always need intervention?

cards.a: Cord prolapse is when the umbilical cord slips down through the cervix in front of the baby, and it is an emergency because the cord is squeezed between the baby and the pelvis every time the uterus contracts, cutting off the baby's oxygen. It most often happens when the waters break with a baby that is not engaged, a breech baby, or a transverse lie.
cards.q: What is cord prolapse and why is it an emergency?

cards.a: Call for help, keep the presenting part lifted off the cord by holding the baby's head up with a hand in the vagina, put the mother in the knee-chest position or on her side with her hips raised, give oxygen, stop oxytocin, and deliver immediately by caesarean. The hand stays in place until the baby is delivered, because the cord must not be compressed.
cards.q: What is the immediate management of cord prolapse?

cards.a: Vasa praevia is when fetal blood vessels run across the cervix in front of the baby, unprotected by the cord or placenta, so they tear when the waters break and the baby bleeds rapidly. It is diagnosed by ultrasound with colour Doppler, which shows vessels over the cervix, and the delivery is by planned caesarean before labour starts, because a vaginal birth would be fatal for the baby.
cards.q: What is a vasa praevia and how is it diagnosed?

cards.a: Active management means giving oxytocin as the baby's shoulder is born, clamping and cutting the cord early, and delivering the placenta with gentle controlled cord traction. It reduces postpartum haemorrhage, which is the leading cause of maternal death worldwide, because oxytocin contracts the uterus and closes the blood vessels where the placenta was attached.
cards.q: What is active management of the third stage of labour?

cards.a: Uterine atony, meaning the uterus fails to contract after the placenta is delivered, leaving the blood vessels at the placental site wide open. It is treated with uterine massage, oxytocin, and other drugs that contract the uterus, because a uterus that does not contract cannot stop its own bleeding.
cards.q: What is the most common cause of postpartum haemorrhage?

cards.a: A retained placenta is when the placenta has not been delivered 30 minutes after the baby is born with active management, or 60 minutes with expectant management. It needs manual removal in theatre under anaesthesia, because a retained placenta prevents the uterus from contracting and causes heavy bleeding.
cards.q: What is a retained placenta and when is it diagnosed?

cards.a: First give oxytocin and try controlled cord traction, and if the placenta is still retained, remove it manually under anaesthesia in theatre. After removal, check that the placenta is complete, because a missing piece left inside the uterus will keep bleeding and cause infection, and may need an ultrasound or curettage to remove.
cards.q: What is the management of a retained placenta?

cards.a: The delivered placenta is inspected carefully: a missing cotyledon, a torn membrane, or a ragged edge suggests tissue is still in the uterus. If tissue is suspected, the uterus is explored and the tissue removed, because retained tissue causes ongoing bleeding and infection, and it can prevent the uterus from contracting.
cards.q: How is a missing placental lobe or retained placental tissue recognised?

cards.a: Fetal scalp stimulation is gently rubbing or pinching the baby's scalp during a vaginal examination, and a positive response is an acceleration of the heart rate of at least 15 beats per minute lasting 15 seconds. An acceleration means the baby is well oxygenated and not acidotic at that moment, so it is a reassuring bedside test when the tracing is unclear.
cards.q: What is fetal scalp stimulation and what does a positive response mean?

cards.a: A tiny sample of blood is taken from the baby's scalp to measure its pH and lactate, and it is used when the heart rate tracing is abnormal and the team needs to know whether the baby is truly acidotic before deciding on delivery. A normal pH means labour can continue safely; a low pH means the baby is acidotic and needs to be delivered promptly.
cards.q: What is fetal blood sampling (scalp blood sampling) and when is it used?

cards.a: A scalp pH below 7.20 indicates acidosis and means the baby should be delivered urgently, while a pH above 7.25 is normal and labour can continue. Values between 7.20 and 7.25 are borderline and the sample should be repeated after 30 minutes, because a single borderline result does not by itself prove the baby is in danger.
cards.q: What pH value on fetal blood sampling indicates acidosis and needs urgent delivery?
What is a failed induction of labour and what is the management?
cards.a: Failed induction is when labour does not start after a full course of ripening and oxytocin, usually defined as no regular contractions and no cervical change after at least 12 to 18 hours of oxytocin once the membranes are ruptured. The next step is to rest the mother, reassess the cervix and the baby, and either try again the next day or proceed to caesarean, because continuing oxytocin indefinitely without progress increases infection and fetal distress without benefit.

cards.q: What is the risk of giving oxytocin in a large volume of plain intravenous fluid over many hours?
cards.a: Oxytocin is structurally similar to vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone), so it makes the body retain water, and large volumes of fluid over many hours can dilute the blood sodium and cause water intoxication, with headache, confusion, and seizures. This is prevented by giving oxytocin in a concentrated solution with restricted fluids and by monitoring fluid balance, especially during a long induction.

cards.q: What is precipitate labour and what are its risks?
cards.a: Precipitate labour is a very fast labour lasting less than 3 hours from the start of regular contractions to delivery, usually because the contractions are very strong and the pelvis is roomy. The risks are perineal tears for the mother from the rapid delivery and bruising or intracranial bleeding for the baby, so the baby should be delivered in a controlled way and the mother and baby checked carefully afterwards, and future pregnancies should be planned to deliver in hospital early.

cards.q: The waters break and the fluid is thick green meconium. What is the next best step in labour?
cards.a: Continue to monitor the baby closely with continuous fetal heart rate monitoring, because meconium-stained fluid means the baby may have passed stool from stress and is at risk of meconium aspiration if it gasps at birth. Routine suctioning of the baby's mouth and nose before the shoulders are delivered is no longer done, and the neonatal team should be present at delivery, because the baby may need help clearing its airway and breathing.

cards.q: What is amnioinfusion and when is it used in labour?
cards.a: Amnioinfusion is infusing sterile saline into the uterus through a catheter to replace lost amniotic fluid, and it is used for recurrent variable decelerations caused by cord compression when there is little fluid around the baby. The extra fluid cushions the cord so it is not squeezed during contractions, which often improves the heart rate tracing and can avoid a caesarean.

cards.q: What is a prolonged latent phase of labour and how is it managed?
cards.a: The latent phase is the early, slow part of labour before the cervix reaches 6 cm, and it is prolonged if it lasts more than 20 hours in a first-time mother or 14 hours in a woman who has delivered before. It is usually managed with rest, hydration, and pain relief, often with a sedative so the mother can sleep, because most women then go into active labour on their own, and a caesarean should not be done for a slow latent phase alone.

topic: Prenatal Care & Medical Disorders in Pregnancy

cards.a: Every 4 weeks until 28 weeks, every 2 weeks from 28 to 36 weeks, then weekly until delivery. More frequent visits are needed with complications such as hypertension, diabetes, or twins, because problems develop faster late in pregnancy and need closer monitoring.
cards.q: What is the standard schedule for routine prenatal visits in an uncomplicated pregnancy?

cards.a: First-trimester ultrasound using crown-rump length is the most accurate dating method, ideally done before 14 weeks. Last menstrual period dating is unreliable when cycles are irregular or the date is uncertain, so early ultrasound sets the due date used for all later decisions.
cards.q: What is the most accurate way to date a pregnancy, and when is it done?

cards.a: Order an ultrasound for fetal growth assessment. Fundal height in centimetres should roughly equal gestational age in weeks after 20 weeks, and a measurement more than 2 to 3 cm below expected suggests fetal growth restriction, which needs ultrasound confirmation rather than reassurance.
cards.q: A woman at 24 weeks has a fundal height of 20 cm. What is the next best step?

cards.a: Order an ultrasound to assess fetal size and amniotic fluid. A fundal height more than 2 to 3 cm above expected suggests a large baby, twins, or too much fluid (polyhydramnios), and ultrasound distinguishes these causes.
cards.q: A woman at 32 weeks has a fundal height of 37 cm. What should be done?

cards.a: First-time mothers usually feel movement around 18 to 20 weeks, and mothers who have been pregnant before around 16 to 18 weeks. Decreased movement at 32 weeks needs same-day evaluation with a nonstress test and ultrasound, because it can be the first sign of fetal compromise.
cards.q: When should a pregnant woman first feel fetal movement, and what is the next step if she reports decreased movement at 32 weeks?

cards.a: Blood pressure, weight, urine protein, fundal height, fetal heart rate, and symptoms such as headache, visual changes, vaginal bleeding, or leaking fluid. These catch preeclampsia, growth problems, and preterm labour early, when intervention still helps.
cards.q: What is checked at every prenatal visit regardless of gestational age?

cards.a: Blood type and antibody screen, complete blood count, rubella immunity, HIV, syphilis screen, hepatitis B surface antigen, and urine culture. These are done at the first visit because each one changes management: for example, Rh-negative status needs anti-D, and asymptomatic bacteriuria needs treatment to prevent kidney infection and preterm birth.
cards.q: What is the routine first prenatal laboratory panel?

cards.a: To detect asymptomatic bacteriuria, which is present without symptoms in pregnancy. It must be treated with antibiotics because untreated bacteriuria progresses to kidney infection (pyelonephritis) in up to 30 percent of pregnant women and increases the risk of preterm birth.
cards.q: What is the purpose of the routine urine culture at the first prenatal visit?

cards.a: Between 24 and 28 weeks. If the 1-hour 50-gram screen is abnormal, the next step is the diagnostic 3-hour 100-gram oral glucose tolerance test. Screening at this time catches diabetes that develops as placental hormones increase insulin resistance in the second half of pregnancy.
cards.q: When is the glucose challenge test for gestational diabetes done, and what is the next step if it is abnormal?

cards.a: Establish dating by ultrasound, check blood pressure and urine protein, blood type and antibody screen, HIV and syphilis testing, and assess fetal growth and wellbeing. Late presentation means screening tests were missed, so the priority is to catch the conditions that still change management before delivery.
cards.q: A pregnant woman has no prenatal care and presents at 34 weeks. What is the priority?

cards.a: Nuchal translucency ultrasound plus blood tests for pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A) and free beta-hCG, done at 11 to 14 weeks. Together they estimate the risk of Down syndrome and trisomy 18, and a high-risk result needs counselling and an offer of diagnostic testing.
cards.q: What does first-trimester combined screening include, and when is it done?

cards.a: A blood test measuring alpha-fetoprotein, hCG, unconjugated estriol, and inhibin A, done at 15 to 20 weeks. It screens for Down syndrome, trisomy 18, and neural tube defects. It is used when first-trimester screening was missed or as a second-trimester option.
cards.q: What is the quad screen, and when is it performed?

cards.a: Order a detailed ultrasound to look for a neural tube defect such as spina bifida or anencephaly, and check the dating. High alpha-fetoprotein means fetal proteins are leaking into the mother's blood, most often from an open neural tube defect, and ultrasound confirms the diagnosis.
cards.q: A quad screen shows a very high alpha-fetoprotein level. What is the next best step?

cards.a: A blood test that analyses fetal DNA circulating in the mother's blood, done from 10 weeks onwards. It is the most sensitive screening test for Down syndrome, trisomy 18, and trisomy 13, but it is still a screening test, so a positive result must be confirmed with amniocentesis before any decision is made.
cards.q: What is noninvasive prenatal testing (NIPT), and when can it be done?

cards.a: Offer screening with NIPT or combined first-trimester screening, and explain that screening estimates risk while only amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling give a definite diagnosis. Advanced maternal age raises the risk of chromosomal abnormalities, but diagnostic testing is offered, not forced, because it carries a small risk of miscarriage.
cards.q: A 38-year-old pregnant woman asks about Down syndrome screening. What is the best counselling point?

cards.a: At 18 to 22 weeks. It examines the fetal brain, spine, heart, kidneys, limbs, and placenta, checks the number of fetuses, and measures growth. This is the best time to detect major structural abnormalities while there is still time for counselling, referral, and delivery planning.
cards.q: When is the anatomy ultrasound performed, and what does it assess?

cards.a: A screening test estimates risk and can be positive in a healthy fetus, while a diagnostic test such as amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling gives a definite answer by testing fetal cells. A positive screen therefore needs diagnostic testing or further evaluation, never a decision based on the screen alone.
cards.q: What is the difference between a screening test and a diagnostic test in prenatal care?

cards.a: At 10 to 13 weeks, sampling placental tissue. Its main risk is miscarriage, about 1 in 200 or less, and it cannot detect neural tube defects, which is why amniocentesis at 15 to 20 weeks is preferred when a neural tube defect is the concern.
cards.q: When is chorionic villus sampling done, and what is its main risk?

cards.a: At 15 to 20 weeks, sampling amniotic fluid. It can measure alpha-fetoprotein to detect open neural tube defects, and it diagnoses chromosomal abnormalities. Its miscarriage risk is about 1 in 300 to 500.
cards.q: When is amniocentesis done, and what can it diagnose that chorionic villus sampling cannot?

cards.a: Cystic fibrosis carrier screening is offered to all women, and haemoglobinopathy screening (for sickle cell disease and thalassaemia) is offered based on ancestry. If the mother is a carrier, the partner should be tested, because the baby is at risk only if both parents carry the gene.
cards.q: Which carrier screening tests are routinely offered to all pregnant women?

cards.a: Test the partner. If both are carriers, the baby has a 1 in 4 chance of cystic fibrosis, and the couple should be offered genetic counselling and prenatal diagnosis with amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling.
cards.q: A pregnant woman has a positive cystic fibrosis carrier screen. What is the next step?

cards.a: 400 to 800 micrograms daily, starting at least 1 month before conception and continuing through the first 12 weeks. Folic acid prevents neural tube defects, and the neural tube closes by day 28 of pregnancy, before most women know they are pregnant, so it must be started before conception.
cards.q: What dose of folic acid should a woman take before conception, and why?

cards.a: 4 milligrams daily, starting at least 1 month before conception and continuing through the first 12 weeks. A previous affected child raises the recurrence risk substantially, and the high dose reduces that risk, so the standard 400-microgram dose is not enough.
cards.q: A woman had a previous child with a neural tube defect. What folic acid dose does she need in her next pregnancy?

cards.a: Women with a previous child with a neural tube defect, women taking antiepileptic drugs such as valproate or carbamazepine, and women with pregestational diabetes. All of these raise the risk of neural tube defects, so the higher dose is used to bring the risk down.
cards.q: Which women need high-dose folic acid (4 mg) before pregnancy?

cards.a: Folic acid is the most important supplement. Vitamin A in high doses (retinol) should be avoided because it is teratogenic and causes birth defects, so pregnant women should not take extra vitamin A supplements or acne doses of retinoids.
cards.q: What prenatal vitamin is most important, and which vitamin should be avoided in high doses during pregnancy?

cards.a: Pregnancy increases iron needs for the growing blood volume and the fetus, so a daily prenatal vitamin with iron is routine. Extra iron is needed when haemoglobin falls below 11 g/dL in the first or third trimester, or below 10.5 g/dL in the second trimester, which defines anaemia in pregnancy.
cards.q: Why is iron added to prenatal vitamins, and when is extra iron needed?

cards.a: The 1-hour 50-gram oral glucose challenge test at 24 to 28 weeks, abnormal if the glucose is 130 to 140 mg/dL or higher depending on the cutoff used. An abnormal screen is not a diagnosis; it triggers the 3-hour diagnostic test.
cards.q: What is the screening test for gestational diabetes, and at what glucose level is it abnormal?

cards.a: Two or more abnormal values on the 100-gram test: fasting 95 mg/dL or higher, 1-hour 180 or higher, 2-hour 155 or higher, or 3-hour 140 or higher. Two abnormal values confirm the diagnosis; one abnormal value means repeat testing.
cards.q: What are the diagnostic criteria for gestational diabetes on the 3-hour glucose tolerance test?

cards.a: Diet, exercise, and blood glucose monitoring. Most women achieve control with lifestyle alone, and medication is added only if fasting glucose stays above 95 mg/dL or 2-hour post-meal glucose stays above 120 mg/dL, because uncontrolled glucose causes a large baby and birth complications.
cards.q: What is the first-line management of gestational diabetes?

cards.a: Start insulin. Insulin is the preferred drug in pregnancy because it does not cross the placenta, so it controls the mother's glucose without directly exposing the fetus. Glyburide and metformin are alternatives, but insulin is first-line.
cards.q: A woman with gestational diabetes has fasting glucose of 110 mg/dL despite diet and exercise. What is the next step?

cards.a: Insulin does not cross the placenta, so it treats the mother's high glucose without exposing the fetus to the drug. Oral agents such as glyburide and metformin cross the placenta to some degree, so they are used only when insulin is refused or not feasible.
cards.q: Why is insulin preferred over oral diabetes drugs in pregnancy?

cards.a: Congenital malformations, especially heart defects and neural tube defects, miscarriage, a large baby (macrosomia), stillbirth, and newborn low glucose. The malformation risk is highest in the first trimester, so glucose control must be achieved before conception.
cards.q: What are the fetal risks of uncontrolled pregestational diabetes?

cards.a: Achieve tight glucose control with a haemoglobin A1c below 6.5 percent before conceiving, and take high-dose folic acid 4 mg daily. Good control before conception sharply reduces the risk of congenital malformations, which form in the first weeks before pregnancy is usually recognised.
cards.q: What is the most important preconception advice for a woman with type 1 diabetes who wants to become pregnant?

cards.a: Fasting below 95 mg/dL, 1-hour post-meal below 140 mg/dL, and 2-hour post-meal below 120 mg/dL. These targets are tighter than in non-pregnant adults because the fetus is exposed to the mother's glucose and excess glucose drives excessive fetal growth.
cards.q: What is the target fasting and post-meal glucose in pregnancy?

cards.a: Discuss delivery planning and consider caesarean section if the estimated weight is above 4,500 grams in a diabetic mother. A very large baby raises the risk of shoulder dystocia and birth injury, and the threshold for caesarean is lower in diabetes than in non-diabetic pregnancies.
cards.q: A woman with gestational diabetes has a baby estimated at 4,500 grams at 38 weeks. What is the management?

cards.a: Low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia). The baby's pancreas has been making extra insulin in response to the mother's high glucose, and after delivery the glucose supply stops but insulin remains high, so the baby's glucose falls and needs early feeding and monitoring.
cards.q: What is the most common complication for the newborn of a diabetic mother in the first hours of life?

cards.a: With a 75-gram oral glucose tolerance test at 6 to 12 weeks postpartum, then every 1 to 3 years. Gestational diabetes is a strong predictor of future type 2 diabetes, and many women already have undiagnosed diabetes that is only unmasked by pregnancy.
cards.q: When should a woman with gestational diabetes be screened for diabetes after delivery?

cards.a: Chronic hypertension is high blood pressure present before pregnancy or before 20 weeks, while gestational hypertension starts after 20 weeks without protein in the urine. The distinction matters because chronic hypertension needs medication review and early surveillance, while new hypertension after 20 weeks raises concern for preeclampsia.
cards.q: What defines chronic hypertension in pregnancy, and how is it distinguished from gestational hypertension?

cards.a: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers, because they cause fetal kidney damage and malformations, especially in the second and third trimesters. Switch to a safe drug such as labetalol, nifedipine, or methyldopa before conception.
cards.q: Which blood pressure drug should be stopped in a woman planning pregnancy?

cards.a: Methyldopa is the classic safest choice, and labetalol and extended-release nifedipine are also safe and commonly used. Diuretics are generally avoided because they reduce blood volume, and ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are contraindicated.
cards.q: What is the safest blood pressure drug to use during pregnancy?

cards.a: Plan delivery at 37 to 39 weeks. Continuing the pregnancy beyond this point increases the risk of superimposed preeclampsia and placental problems without benefit to the baby, who is mature by 37 weeks.
cards.q: A woman with chronic hypertension is at 37 weeks and her blood pressure is well controlled. What is the delivery plan?

cards.a: Superimposed preeclampsia. New proteinuria, worsening blood pressure, low platelets, or abnormal liver tests in a woman with chronic hypertension means preeclampsia has developed on top of it, and she needs close monitoring and likely delivery planning.
cards.q: A woman with chronic hypertension develops new protein in the urine at 30 weeks. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Chronic high blood pressure damages the blood vessels of the placenta, making it more likely to separate from the uterus before delivery. This is why these women need regular growth scans and monitoring for bleeding and pain.
cards.q: Why are women with chronic hypertension at higher risk of placental abruption?

cards.a: A systolic pressure of 160 mmHg or higher, or diastolic of 110 mmHg or higher, sustained over 15 minutes. Severe hypertension in pregnancy must be treated within 30 to 60 minutes to prevent stroke and seizures in the mother.
cards.q: What blood pressure threshold in pregnancy requires urgent treatment?

cards.a: TSH is the most useful test, but the normal range is lower in early pregnancy because hCG weakly stimulates the thyroid. A TSH that looks normal by non-pregnant standards may actually be high in pregnancy, so pregnancy-specific ranges must be used.
cards.q: What thyroid test is most useful in pregnancy, and why does the reference range change?

cards.a: Overt hypothyroidism, treated with levothyroxine. Untreated hypothyroidism increases the risk of miscarriage, preeclampsia, and impaired brain development in the baby, so treatment is started promptly and the dose is usually increased by about 30 percent in pregnancy.
cards.q: A pregnant woman has a TSH of 8 with a low free T4. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Increase the dose by about 30 percent as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, and recheck TSH every 4 weeks. Thyroid hormone needs rise early in pregnancy, and waiting for symptoms or a high TSH risks harming the developing fetal brain.
cards.q: A woman on levothyroxine becomes pregnant. What should be done with her dose?

cards.a: Propylthiouracil (PTU). Methimazole is associated with birth defects when used in the first trimester, so PTU is used early and the patient is switched to methimazole after the first trimester, because PTU carries a risk of liver damage with longer use.
cards.q: What is the treatment of choice for hyperthyroidism in the first trimester of pregnancy?

cards.a: It is associated with a specific pattern of birth defects including scalp defects and choanal atresia. PTU is used instead in the first trimester, then the patient switches to methimazole for the rest of the pregnancy to avoid PTU-related liver injury.
cards.q: Why is methimazole avoided in the first trimester of pregnancy?

cards.a: Thyroid storm, a life-threatening crisis with fever, rapid heart rate, and confusion, which can be triggered by labour, infection, or surgery. It is treated with PTU, beta blockers, and supportive care, and it is a reason to keep thyroid levels controlled throughout pregnancy.
cards.q: What is the most dangerous complication of uncontrolled hyperthyroidism in pregnancy?

cards.a: Neonatal thyrotoxicosis from maternal thyroid-stimulating antibodies crossing the placenta. These antibodies can overstimulate the baby's thyroid for weeks after birth, so the baby needs monitoring and sometimes treatment even though the mother was treated.
cards.q: A newborn of a mother with Graves disease develops a rapid heart rate and poor feeding. What is the cause?

cards.a: Levothyroxine. Antibody-positive subclinical hypothyroidism in pregnancy is treated because it increases the risk of miscarriage and preterm birth, whereas antibody-negative subclinical hypothyroidism with only mildly raised TSH is often just monitored.
cards.q: What is the treatment for a pregnant woman with subclinical hypothyroidism (high TSH, normal free T4) and positive thyroid antibodies?

cards.a: Congenital toxoplasmosis, which can cause brain calcifications, eye damage (chorioretinitis), and hearing loss. The risk of transmission rises as pregnancy advances, but the severity is worst when infection occurs early, so prevention by avoiding cat litter and undercooked meat is the key message.
cards.q: A pregnant woman is exposed to toxoplasmosis from cat litter. What is the main fetal risk?

cards.a: Counsel her to avoid exposure and give the MMR vaccine after delivery, before she leaves the hospital. The rubella vaccine is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy, and congenital rubella causes deafness, cataracts, and heart defects, so postpartum vaccination protects future pregnancies.
cards.q: A pregnant woman is not immune to rubella. What is the management?

cards.a: Cytomegalovirus (CMV). It is the most common congenital viral infection and the leading infectious cause of hearing loss and developmental delay. There is no vaccine and no routine screening, so prevention is hand hygiene, especially for women who work with young children.
cards.q: What is the most common cause of congenital hearing loss from infection in pregnancy?

cards.a: Offer caesarean delivery. A first episode of genital herpes near delivery carries a high risk of passing the virus to the baby during vaginal birth, causing neonatal herpes, which can be fatal, so caesarean is recommended if lesions are present at labour.
cards.q: A pregnant woman develops a painful genital ulcer and blisters at 38 weeks, her first episode of genital herpes. What is the management?

cards.a: Vaginal delivery is allowed, with suppressive acyclovir from 36 weeks to reduce the chance of an outbreak. Recurrent herpes carries a much lower transmission risk than a first episode, because the mother has antibodies that partially protect the baby.
cards.q: A pregnant woman has recurrent genital herpes with no active lesions at the time of labour. What is the management?

cards.a: A vaginal-rectal swab at 35 to 37 weeks. A positive result means the mother receives intravenous penicillin during labour to prevent the baby developing group B strep sepsis or meningitis, which are the most serious early newborn infections.
cards.q: When is group B streptococcus screening done, and what does a positive result mean?

cards.a: Clindamycin if the organism is sensitive, or vancomycin if sensitivity is unknown or the organism is resistant. Penicillin is first-line, but a severe allergy needs an alternative that still covers group B strep during labour.
cards.q: A woman who is group B strep positive arrives in labour and is allergic to penicillin with a history of anaphylaxis. What antibiotic is used?

cards.a: At the onset of labour or rupture of membranes, with the first dose given at least 4 hours before delivery if possible. Antibiotics given during labour reduce the baby's exposure during birth, which is when transmission occurs.
cards.q: A woman is group B strep positive and her membranes rupture at 37 weeks. When should antibiotics be started?

cards.a: Start or continue antiretroviral therapy throughout pregnancy, monitor viral load, give intravenous zidovudine during labour if the viral load is high, and avoid breastfeeding. With treatment and a suppressed viral load, the risk of passing HIV to the baby falls below 1 percent.
cards.q: What is the management of a pregnant woman with HIV?

cards.a: Scheduled caesarean section at 38 weeks. A high viral load means a higher risk of transmission during vaginal birth, so caesarean reduces the baby's exposure to the virus.
cards.q: A woman with HIV has a viral load above 1,000 copies per mL near delivery. What is the delivery plan?

cards.a: Penicillin, which is the only treatment proven to cure the mother and prevent congenital syphilis. There is no alternative in pregnancy; a penicillin-allergic woman must be desensitised and then treated with penicillin, because untreated syphilis causes stillbirth and severe congenital infection.
cards.q: A pregnant woman is diagnosed with syphilis. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Congenital syphilis, which causes stillbirth, bone and teeth abnormalities, deafness, and developmental delay. This is why syphilis screening is done at the first prenatal visit and repeated in the third trimester in high-risk women.
cards.q: What is the most important complication of untreated syphilis in pregnancy?

cards.a: The virus can cause severe fetal anaemia and hydrops (fluid accumulation) leading to fetal death. The next step is to check parvovirus IgM and IgG, and if infection is confirmed, monitor with ultrasound and middle cerebral artery Doppler to detect fetal anaemia, which may need an in-utero blood transfusion.
cards.q: A pregnant woman is exposed to parvovirus B19 (fifth disease) at work. What is the fetal risk and the next step?

cards.a: Give varicella zoster immune globulin within 10 days of exposure. This reduces the severity of the infection in the mother, because chickenpox in pregnancy can cause severe pneumonia, and early infection can cause congenital varicella syndrome with limb and eye defects.
cards.q: A pregnant woman who is not immune to varicella is exposed to chickenpox. What is the management?

cards.a: Listeria monocytogenes from unpasteurised dairy or deli meats. It causes miscarriage, stillbirth, and neonatal sepsis, so fever in pregnancy after eating high-risk food needs blood cultures and treatment with ampicillin, which covers Listeria.
cards.q: A pregnant woman eats unpasteurised cheese and develops fever and flu-like symptoms. What organism is suspected, and what is the treatment?

cards.a: Cephalosporins do not cover Listeria, while ampicillin does. Missing Listeria treatment risks fetal death, so when listeriosis is suspected the antibiotic must cover it, and ampicillin is the drug of choice.
cards.q: Why is ampicillin used instead of a cephalosporin for suspected listeriosis in pregnancy?

cards.a: Pyelonephritis, a kidney infection. She needs admission, intravenous antibiotics, and monitoring, because pyelonephritis in pregnancy can cause sepsis, preterm labour, and respiratory distress, and oral antibiotics alone are not enough.
cards.q: A pregnant woman has a urinary tract infection with fever and flank pain. What is the diagnosis and management?

cards.a: Tetracyclines, including doxycycline. They bind to developing teeth and bones, causing permanent discolouration and impaired bone growth, so they are avoided in pregnancy and in children under 8 years.
cards.q: Which antibiotic should be avoided in pregnancy because it causes tooth discolouration in the baby?

cards.a: Isotretinoin, which causes severe craniofacial, heart, and brain defects. It must never be used in pregnancy, and women taking it need two forms of contraception and monthly pregnancy tests, because even a brief exposure early in pregnancy is dangerous.
cards.q: Which drug is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy because it causes severe birth defects, and what must be done before prescribing it?

cards.a: Switch to heparin, usually low-molecular-weight heparin, at least during the first trimester and near delivery. Warfarin causes birth defects and fetal bleeding, while heparin does not cross the placenta, so the mother stays protected from clots without exposing the fetus.
cards.q: A woman on warfarin for a mechanical heart valve becomes pregnant. What is the management?

cards.a: Valproate carries the highest risk of birth defects and developmental delay of all antiepileptic drugs, so it should be switched to a safer drug such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam before conception if possible. If she is already pregnant and seizure control requires it, use the lowest effective dose with high-dose folic acid and specialist care.
cards.q: A woman taking valproate for epilepsy becomes pregnant. What is the counselling?

cards.a: Stop methotrexate at least 3 months before trying to conceive, because it is teratogenic and causes miscarriage and birth defects. She should switch to a pregnancy-safe drug and wait until the drug has cleared before conceiving.
cards.q: A woman taking methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis wants to become pregnant. What is the advice?

cards.a: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers. They cause fetal kidney failure, low amniotic fluid, and skull defects, especially in the second and third trimesters, so they must be stopped before or as soon as pregnancy is recognised.
cards.q: Which antihypertensive drugs are contraindicated in pregnancy?

cards.a: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) is the safest first choice. NSAIDs should be avoided, especially in the third trimester, because they can close the baby's ductus arteriosus early and reduce amniotic fluid.
cards.q: Which drugs are safe for pain relief in pregnancy?

cards.a: They can cause premature closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus, which the baby needs open before birth, and they reduce amniotic fluid by impairing fetal kidney function. This is why paracetamol is preferred and NSAIDs are stopped in late pregnancy.
cards.q: Why are NSAIDs avoided in the third trimester of pregnancy?

cards.a: Continue lamotrigine, which is one of the safer antiepileptic drugs in pregnancy, with high-dose folic acid and drug level monitoring. Stopping the drug risks seizures, which are more dangerous to mother and baby than the drug itself.
cards.q: A pregnant woman has a seizure disorder and is on lamotrigine. What is the management in pregnancy?

cards.a: Nitrofurantoin or cephalexin are commonly used, though nitrofurantoin is avoided near term because it can cause newborn haemolysis. Penicillins and cephalosporins are generally safe, while fluoroquinolones and trimethoprim in the first trimester are avoided.
cards.q: Which antibiotic is safe and commonly used for a urinary tract infection in pregnancy?

cards.a: Use the lowest effective dose of the drug with the longest safety record in pregnancy, and never stop a drug needed for the mother's health without a safe alternative. Untreated maternal illness, such as seizures or severe asthma, is often more dangerous to the baby than the drug.
cards.q: A pregnant woman is prescribed a new drug and asks if it is safe. What is the best general principle?

cards.a: Iron deficiency, from the increased blood volume and fetal iron needs. It is treated with oral ferrous sulfate, and intravenous iron is used if oral iron is not tolerated or the anaemia is severe, because anaemia increases the risk of preterm birth and poor tolerance of blood loss at delivery.
cards.q: What is the most common cause of anaemia in pregnancy, and how is it treated?

cards.a: Iron deficiency. A low MCV means small red blood cells, the classic pattern of iron deficiency, and the next step is to check ferritin and start iron, rather than assuming it is normal dilutional anaemia of pregnancy.
cards.q: A pregnant woman has anaemia with a low mean corpuscular volume (MCV). What is the likely cause?

cards.a: Folate and vitamin B12 levels. A high MCV means large red blood cells, which points to folate deficiency (more common in pregnancy) or B12 deficiency, and folate deficiency also raises the risk of neural tube defects.
cards.q: A pregnant woman has anaemia with a high MCV. What should be checked?

cards.a: Below 11 g/dL in the first and third trimesters, and below 10.5 g/dL in the second trimester. The second-trimester threshold is lower because blood volume expands faster than red cell mass, diluting the haemoglobin even in healthy women.
cards.q: What haemoglobin level defines anaemia in the first and third trimesters of pregnancy?

cards.a: When haemoglobin is very low (usually below 7 g/dL), or when there are symptoms such as chest pain, breathlessness, or heart failure, or active bleeding. Mild to moderate anaemia is treated with iron, because transfusion carries risks and iron usually corrects it.
cards.q: When is a blood transfusion indicated for anaemia in pregnancy?

cards.a: Worsening kidney function, preeclampsia, fetal growth restriction, and preterm birth. She needs close monitoring of blood pressure, kidney function, and urine protein, plus regular growth scans, and her care should be shared between obstetrics and nephrology.
cards.q: A woman with chronic kidney disease becomes pregnant. What is the main risk, and what should be monitored?

cards.a: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers, which protect the kidneys outside pregnancy but harm the fetal kidneys. They are stopped before conception and replaced with a pregnancy-safe blood pressure drug.
cards.q: Which drug for kidney disease must be stopped before pregnancy?

cards.a: Fetal growth restriction and preterm birth, because the underlying kidney disease and high blood pressure impair placental function. She needs close surveillance with growth scans and blood pressure monitoring.
cards.q: A pregnant woman has nephrotic syndrome with heavy protein in the urine. What is the main fetal risk?

cards.a: Pregnancy on dialysis is high risk, with high rates of miscarriage, preterm birth, and growth restriction, and dialysis usually needs to be intensified to daily sessions. She needs specialist preconception counselling before attempting pregnancy.
cards.q: A pregnant woman on dialysis asks about pregnancy. What is the key counselling point?

cards.a: Inhaled corticosteroids such as budesonide. They control airway inflammation with minimal drug reaching the baby, and uncontrolled asthma is far more dangerous than the inhaler, because it causes low oxygen for mother and baby.
cards.q: What is the safest controller drug for asthma in pregnancy?

cards.a: Give a short-acting bronchodilator and oral corticosteroids, and assess whether she needs admission. Asthma attacks in pregnancy must be treated promptly, because low oxygen harms the fetus and oral steroids are safer than an untreated severe attack.
cards.q: A pregnant woman with asthma has worsening wheeze and a peak flow below 70 percent of her best. What is the next step?

cards.a: After at least 6 months of inactive disease, on pregnancy-safe drugs. Active lupus at conception increases the risk of flare, preeclampsia, miscarriage, and preterm birth, so the disease should be quiet before pregnancy.
cards.q: A woman with systemic lupus erythematosus wants to become pregnant. When is the safest time?

cards.a: Hydroxychloroquine. It is safe in pregnancy and reduces flares, preeclampsia, and the risk of the baby developing heart block, so it should not be stopped.
cards.q: Which lupus drug must be continued in pregnancy to prevent flares?

cards.a: Congenital heart block. Anti-Ro antibodies cross the placenta and can damage the fetal heart's conduction system, so serial fetal echocardiograms are done from 16 to 26 weeks to detect it early.
cards.q: A woman with lupus has anti-Ro antibodies. What fetal complication must be monitored for?

cards.a: Influenza vaccine at any time in pregnancy, and Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria, pertussis) between 27 and 36 weeks. Flu vaccine protects the mother from severe flu, and Tdap in the third trimester passes antibodies to the baby, protecting the newborn from whooping cough.
cards.q: Which vaccines are recommended in every pregnancy?

cards.a: This timing produces the highest level of antibodies that cross the placenta to the baby, giving the newborn protection against whooping cough in the first months of life before the baby's own vaccines start.
cards.q: Why is Tdap given between 27 and 36 weeks of pregnancy rather than earlier?

cards.a: Live vaccines: MMR, varicella, and the nasal spray flu vaccine. Live vaccines carry a theoretical risk of infecting the fetus, so they are given after delivery, and the injected flu vaccine is used instead of the nasal spray.
cards.q: Which vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy?

cards.a: Give the rabies vaccine and immunoglobulin as indicated. Rabies is almost always fatal if it develops, and the vaccine is not a live vaccine, so the risk of rabies far outweighs any theoretical vaccine risk in pregnancy.
cards.q: A pregnant woman is bitten by a dog and needs rabies vaccination. What is the management?

cards.a: Yes, tetanus toxoid is safe in pregnancy and should be given when indicated. Tetanus is a killed toxoid vaccine, not a live vaccine, and preventing tetanus in the mother also protects the newborn.
cards.q: A pregnant woman needs a tetanus booster after a dirty wound. Is it safe?

cards.a: It is recommended in pregnancy, because pregnant women are at higher risk of severe COVID-19, preterm birth, and stillbirth. The vaccine reduces those risks and passes protective antibodies to the baby.
cards.q: A pregnant woman asks about the COVID-19 vaccine. What is the advice?

cards.a: Dietary measures such as small frequent meals and avoiding triggers, plus vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) with or without doxylamine. This combination is safe and effective for most women, and stronger anti-nausea drugs are reserved for those who do not improve.
cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy?

cards.a: Hyperemesis gravidarum, severe vomiting of pregnancy. It is diagnosed when vomiting causes weight loss of more than 5 percent, dehydration, and ketones, and it needs treatment rather than reassurance, because it can cause electrolyte disturbance and malnutrition.
cards.q: A pregnant woman at 9 weeks has persistent vomiting, weight loss, and ketones in the urine. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Admit for intravenous fluids, correct potassium and other electrolytes, give anti-nausea drugs, and give thiamine before glucose-containing fluids. Thiamine prevents Wernicke encephalopathy, a brain injury from vitamin B1 deficiency that can occur when vomiting has been prolonged.
cards.q: What is the management of hyperemesis gravidarum with dehydration and low potassium?

cards.a: Low potassium, which can cause heart rhythm problems, and low sodium from dehydration. Thiamine is given before intravenous glucose because giving glucose without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy in a thiamine-depleted patient.
cards.q: What electrolyte abnormality is most concerning in hyperemesis gravidarum, and why give thiamine first?

cards.a: Give anti-D immunoglobulin at 28 weeks, and again within 72 hours after delivery if the baby is Rh-positive. This prevents the mother forming antibodies against the baby's Rh-positive blood, which would attack the red cells of future Rh-positive babies.
cards.q: A Rh-negative woman at 28 weeks has no antibodies on screening. What is the next step?

cards.a: Yes, anti-D is given after any event that can mix fetal and maternal blood, including miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, amniocentesis, or bleeding. Even early in pregnancy, fetal blood cells can enter the mother's circulation and sensitise her.
cards.q: A Rh-negative woman has a miscarriage at 10 weeks. Should she receive anti-D?

cards.a: To measure how much fetal blood entered the mother's circulation, so the correct dose of anti-D can be given. A large bleed needs more than the standard dose, and missing it leaves the mother sensitised for the next pregnancy.
cards.q: What is the Kleihauer test used for after delivery in an Rh-negative woman?

cards.a: Monitor the baby for anaemia with ultrasound and middle cerebral artery Doppler, and be ready for in-utero transfusion if anaemia develops. Anti-D cannot help once sensitisation has occurred, so the focus shifts to detecting and treating fetal anaemia.
cards.q: A Rh-negative woman is already sensitised with anti-D antibodies. What is the management of her pregnancy?

cards.a: No, because the baby must be Rh-negative if both parents are Rh-negative, so there is no Rh incompatibility. Anti-D is only needed when the baby could be Rh-positive, which requires an Rh-positive father.
cards.q: A woman is Rh-negative and the father of the baby is Rh-negative. Does she need anti-D?

cards.a: Check a quantitative beta-hCG and perform a transvaginal ultrasound. Ectopic pregnancy must be ruled out first in any woman with bleeding and pain in early pregnancy, because a ruptured ectopic is life-threatening and needs urgent treatment.
cards.q: A woman at 7 weeks has vaginal bleeding and left-sided pelvic pain, with a positive pregnancy test. What is the first step?

cards.a: Around 1,500 to 2,000 IU/L for transvaginal ultrasound. Above this level, a pregnancy inside the uterus should be visible, so an empty uterus with a beta-hCG above the discriminatory zone raises strong suspicion for ectopic pregnancy.
cards.q: What is the discriminatory zone for beta-hCG, and why does it matter?

cards.a: A pregnancy of unknown location, most likely ectopic. In a normal early pregnancy beta-hCG roughly doubles every 48 hours, so a slow rise with an empty uterus means the pregnancy is not developing normally inside the uterus and needs close follow-up or treatment.
cards.q: A woman has a beta-hCG of 800 that rises by only 20 percent in 48 hours, with no pregnancy seen on ultrasound. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: A uterus full of grape-like vesicles with no fetus on ultrasound, and a very high beta-hCG. Treatment is suction evacuation of the uterus, followed by weekly beta-hCG monitoring until it is undetectable, because molar tissue can develop into choriocarcinoma.
cards.q: A woman has a complete molar pregnancy. What is the key diagnostic finding and the treatment?

cards.a: To detect persistent gestational trophoblastic disease, including choriocarcinoma. If beta-hCG stops falling or rises again, chemotherapy is needed, so follow-up continues until levels are normal and the woman is advised to avoid pregnancy for 6 to 12 months.
cards.q: Why must beta-hCG be followed after treatment of a molar pregnancy?

cards.a: A history-indicated cerclage, a stitch placed around the cervix at 12 to 14 weeks. Cervical insufficiency causes painless mid-trimester loss, and a cerclage placed before the cervix starts to open prevents it happening again.
cards.q: A woman has painless cervical dilation at 22 weeks in a previous pregnancy that ended in miscarriage. What is the management in her next pregnancy?

cards.a: About 11 to 16 kilograms (25 to 35 pounds). Gaining too little raises the risk of a small baby, while gaining too much raises the risk of gestational diabetes, large baby, and caesarean section, so weight gain is discussed at prenatal visits.
cards.q: How much weight should a woman with a normal pre-pregnancy body mass index gain during pregnancy?

cards.a: About 5 to 9 kilograms (11 to 20 pounds). Obese women need less weight gain than women of normal weight, because they already have energy reserves, and excess gain increases the risk of diabetes, hypertension, and delivery complications.
cards.q: How much weight should an obese woman gain during pregnancy?

cards.a: Advise complete abstinence, because there is no known safe amount of alcohol in pregnancy. Alcohol causes fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, with growth restriction, facial abnormalities, and lifelong learning problems, and stopping at any point still helps.
cards.q: A pregnant woman drinks alcohol regularly. What is the counselling?

cards.a: Behavioural counselling and an offer of support to quit, with nicotine replacement considered if counselling alone fails. Smoking causes growth restriction, placental abruption, and preterm birth, and quitting at any stage of pregnancy improves outcomes for the baby.
cards.q: A pregnant woman smokes cigarettes. What is the most effective intervention?

cards.a: Yes, moderate exercise such as walking or swimming for about 30 minutes most days is recommended in an uncomplicated pregnancy. It reduces the risk of gestational diabetes and excessive weight gain, and helps mood and sleep, but contact sports and activities with a high fall risk should be avoided.
cards.q: Should a woman with an uncomplicated pregnancy exercise, and what should she avoid?

cards.a: Blood loss of 500 mL or more after vaginal delivery, and 1000 mL or more after caesarean delivery. In practice, do not wait for an exact volume — any bleeding that causes haemodynamic instability, or ongoing bleeding that does not stop, is treated as postpartum haemorrhage because visual estimation underestimates true loss.
cards.q: What is the definition of postpartum haemorrhage after a vaginal delivery, and after a caesarean delivery?

cards.a: Tone (uterine atony), Trauma (lacerations, uterine rupture, uterine inversion), Tissue (retained placenta or membranes, abnormal placentation), and Thrombin (coagulopathy). Tone — uterine atony — is by far the most common cause, accounting for about 70 to 80 percent of cases.
cards.q: What are the 4 Ts that cause postpartum haemorrhage, and which is most common?

cards.a: Uterine atony. First, call for help, assess airway, breathing and circulation, give oxygen and large-bore IV access, and start continuous bimanual uterine massage while giving oxytocin. Massage stimulates uterine contraction, which compresses the spiral arteries and stops bleeding — a soft uterus cannot contract and will keep bleeding.
cards.q: A woman bleeds heavily immediately after delivery and her uterus feels soft and boggy on palpation. What is the most likely cause and what is the first step?

cards.a: Oxytocin is first line. It is given as an IV infusion, often after a slow IV bolus, and continued as an infusion. It causes strong uterine contractions with few side effects. A rapid bolus can cause hypotension, so it is given slowly. If oxytocin alone does not work, add a second uterotonic rather than waiting.
cards.q: What is the first-line uterotonic drug for postpartum haemorrhage due to atony, and how is it given?

cards.a: Methylergonovine (methergine) is usually next. Check blood pressure first — it is contraindicated in hypertension and preeclampsia because it causes vasoconstriction and can raise blood pressure sharply. It is given intramuscularly and causes sustained uterine contraction.
cards.q: Oxytocin has not controlled postpartum bleeding from uterine atony. What is the next uterotonic to add, and what must you check before giving it?

cards.a: Carboprost (15-methyl prostaglandin F2-alpha, Hemabate). It can cause bronchospasm, so avoid it in asthma. It is given intramuscularly every 15 to 90 minutes up to 8 doses. It also causes diarrhoea, vomiting and fever, but bronchospasm is the key contraindication to remember for the exam.
cards.q: Which uterotonic is contraindicated in asthma, and why?

cards.a: Misoprostol, a prostaglandin E1 analogue. It is given rectally (or orally/sublingually) and is safe in hypertension and asthma because it does not cause vasoconstriction or bronchospasm like the other second-line agents. Its main side effects are fever, shivering and diarrhoea.
cards.q: Which uterotonic is safe in both hypertension and asthma, and is given rectally?

cards.a: Oxytocin first, then methylergonovine (if blood pressure is normal) or carboprost (if no asthma), with misoprostol as an alternative that is safe in both hypertension and asthma. Do not delay moving to the next agent or to mechanical measures if bleeding continues — stepwise escalation saves lives.
cards.q: What is the correct order of uterotonics for atonic postpartum haemorrhage?

cards.a: Trauma — a genital tract laceration, cervical tear, or vaginal haematoma — or a coagulopathy (Thrombin). A contracted empty uterus that still bleeds points away from atony. Examine the cervix, vagina and perineum under good light, check for a haematoma, and send coagulation studies including fibrinogen.
cards.q: A woman continues to bleed after oxytocin and a second uterotonic. Her uterus is empty and contracted. What should you suspect next?

cards.a: Uterine balloon tamponade, such as a Bakri balloon. The balloon is placed inside the uterus and inflated with saline, pressing against the uterine wall and compressing bleeding vessels. It is a temporising measure that often stops bleeding and avoids surgery, but the patient still needs close monitoring, continued oxytocin, and blood products if needed.
cards.q: What is the next step when medical management fails to control postpartum haemorrhage from atony?

cards.a: First, uterine compression sutures such as B-Lynch sutures, or uterine artery ligation, or both. Next, internal iliac (hypogastric) artery ligation. Last resort is hysterectomy. Hysterectomy is life-saving when bleeding is uncontrollable, and should not be delayed so long that the patient develops irreversible coagulopathy.
cards.q: Balloon tamponade has failed to control postpartum haemorrhage. What are the surgical options, in order of increasing invasiveness?

cards.a: Transfuse when there is ongoing bleeding with haemodynamic instability, or a significant drop in haemoglobin, and do not wait for the haemoglobin result if she is exsanguinating. In massive haemorrhage use a balanced ratio of packed red cells, fresh frozen plasma and platelets, roughly 1 to 1 to 1, to replace clotting factors as well as red cells and prevent dilutional coagulopathy.
cards.q: When should blood transfusion be given in postpartum haemorrhage, and what ratio is used in massive bleeding?

cards.a: A falling fibrinogen level. Fibrinogen falls early in obstetric haemorrhage and a low fibrinogen predicts ongoing bleeding better than the INR or platelet count alone. Give cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate when fibrinogen is low, and give tranexamic acid early, within 3 hours of bleeding onset.
cards.q: What laboratory finding is the earliest and most useful marker of worsening coagulopathy in postpartum haemorrhage?

cards.a: Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic drug that stops clots from breaking down. Give it as early as possible, ideally within 3 hours of the onset of bleeding, alongside uterotonics. It reduces death from bleeding. It is an adjunct, not a substitute for uterotonics, tamponade or surgery.
cards.q: What is tranexamic acid and when should it be given in postpartum haemorrhage?

cards.a: Secondary postpartum haemorrhage from retained products of conception. Management is antibiotics plus evacuation of the uterus, usually with suction curettage, after correcting coagulopathy. Do not do curettage without antibiotic cover because the retained tissue is often infected. Send the tissue for histology.
cards.q: A woman has heavy bleeding 2 weeks after delivery, with a uterus that is enlarged and tender. Ultrasound shows echogenic material inside the uterus. What is the diagnosis and management?

cards.a: Primary postpartum haemorrhage occurs within 24 hours of delivery and is usually due to atony, trauma, retained placenta or coagulopathy. Secondary postpartum haemorrhage occurs from 24 hours to 6 weeks after delivery and is usually due to retained products of conception or endometritis. The timing points to the cause and changes the management.
cards.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary postpartum haemorrhage?

cards.a: Overdistension of the uterus — from twins, polyhydramnios or a large baby — is a classic risk factor. Others include prolonged labour, rapid labour, magnesium sulfate, general anaesthesia, chorioamnionitis, prior postpartum haemorrhage, and a full bladder. Knowing them helps you anticipate atony and give prophylactic oxytocin after delivery.
cards.q: What is the most important risk factor for uterine atony, and what other risk factors should you know?

cards.a: Active management of the third stage of labour: prophylactic oxytocin immediately after delivery of the baby, controlled cord traction, and uterine massage. Oxytocin after delivery is standard for all women because it reduces the risk of atony and haemorrhage.
cards.q: What prophylaxis is given routinely after delivery to prevent postpartum haemorrhage?

cards.a: Manual removal of the placenta under anaesthesia, with antibiotic cover and oxytocin after removal. Do not pull on the cord forcefully, which risks uterine inversion. If manual removal fails or the placenta is morbidly adherent, involve senior obstetric help and prepare for possible surgery.
cards.q: A woman has a retained placenta 30 minutes after delivery with ongoing bleeding. What is the next step?

cards.a: Uterine inversion is when the uterus turns inside out and prolapses through the cervix, usually after cord traction on a fundally implanted placenta. It presents with severe postpartum haemorrhage, shock out of proportion to blood loss, and a mass in the vagina. Management is immediate replacement of the uterus under anaesthesia with tocolysis to relax the uterus, and do NOT remove the placenta first if it is still attached — replace the uterus with the placenta attached, then remove it.
cards.q: What is uterine inversion, how does it present, and what is the emergency management?

cards.a: Postpartum endometritis — infection of the uterine lining after delivery. It typically presents 2 to 3 days after delivery with fever, uterine tenderness, foul lochia and sometimes tachycardia. It is more common after caesarean delivery and prolonged rupture of membranes.
cards.q: A woman on postpartum day 3 has fever of 38.5 C, lower abdominal pain, foul-smelling lochia and a tender, enlarged uterus. What is the most likely diagnosis?

cards.a: It is usually polymicrobial — vaginal and gut flora including group B streptococcus, anaerobes such as Bacteroides, and Gram-negative organisms such as E. coli. Standard treatment is IV clindamycin plus gentamicin, which covers Gram-positives, Gram-negatives and anaerobes. Add ampicillin if enterococcus is suspected or the patient does not improve.
cards.q: What organisms cause postpartum endometritis, and what is the standard antibiotic treatment?

cards.a: Clindamycin covers anaerobes and also covers group B streptococcus and Staphylococcus, and it penetrates the uterus well. It is the classic partner to gentamicin in this setting. Metronidazole covers anaerobes but not the Gram-positive organisms that are also involved, so clindamycin plus gentamicin is the standard exam answer.
cards.q: Why is clindamycin used in postpartum endometritis rather than metronidazole for anaerobic cover?

cards.a: Suspect retained products of conception, a pelvic abscess, wound infection, septic pelvic thrombophlebitis, or a resistant organism. Re-examine her, get an ultrasound to look for retained products or a collection, check blood cultures, and consider broadening antibiotics or imaging with CT if an abscess is suspected. Do not simply continue the same antibiotics without looking for a source.
cards.q: A woman with postpartum endometritis is not improving after 48 hours of clindamycin and gentamicin. What should you suspect and do next?

cards.a: When fever and bleeding persist despite antibiotics, the uterus remains enlarged and tender, and ultrasound shows echogenic material in the uterine cavity. Retained tissue acts as a nidus for infection that antibiotics alone cannot clear — she needs evacuation of the uterus with antibiotic cover.
cards.q: When should you suspect retained products of conception in a woman with postpartum endometritis?

cards.a: Infected clot in the pelvic veins, usually the ovarian vein, after delivery. Suspect it when a woman has persistent spiking fevers despite appropriate antibiotics for endometritis, with vague abdominal or flank pain and no clear source on examination or imaging. Diagnosis is often by CT showing a thrombosed ovarian vein, and treatment is antibiotics plus anticoagulation.
cards.q: What is septic pelvic thrombophlebitis, and when should you suspect it?

cards.a: Broad-spectrum antibiotics plus anticoagulation with heparin. Antibiotics alone often fail because the infected clot is a protected source. Continue anticoagulation for several weeks. The classic clue is fever that persists despite 48 to 72 hours of correct antibiotics for endometritis.
cards.q: What is the treatment for septic pelvic thrombophlebitis?

cards.a: Caesarean wound infection, usually from skin flora such as Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus. Management is to open the wound, drain any collection, send a swab for culture, debride necrotic tissue, and give antibiotics covering Staphylococcus and Streptococcus. Leave the wound open to heal by secondary intention if there is significant infection.
cards.q: A woman 5 days after caesarean delivery has fever, wound erythema and purulent discharge. What is the diagnosis and management?

cards.a: This is a surgical emergency — wound evisceration. Cover the exposed bowel with sterile saline-soaked dressings, keep her nil by mouth, give IV antibiotics and fluids, and take her to theatre urgently for surgical repair. Do not try to push the bowel back on the ward.
cards.q: A woman after caesarean delivery has wound dehiscence with bowel visible through the wound. What is the next step?

cards.a: Obesity, diabetes, prolonged rupture of membranes, prolonged labour, chorioamnionitis, emergency caesarean, blood loss, and smoking.
