cards.a: Clinical examination, imaging with mammography and ultrasound, and tissue diagnosis with core needle biopsy. All three are needed because no single part is reliable alone; a lump that feels benign can still be cancer, and imaging alone cannot make the diagnosis. Do not reassure on examination alone.
cards.q: A woman finds a breast lump. What is the triple assessment?

cards.a: Because a dominant, persistent mass needs tissue diagnosis even if imaging looks benign. Observation risks missing a cancer that is still curable, and a mass that does not resolve after a menstrual cycle should be biopsied. Age over 30 raises the pre-test probability enough that biopsy is the safe next step.
cards.q: Why should a dominant breast mass in a woman over 30 not simply be observed?

cards.a: Proceed to image-guided core needle biopsy. A normal examination does not exclude cancer, and mammographic abnormalities such as microcalcifications or a spiculated mass need histology. Do not repeat the mammogram in 6 months as the first step when the lesion is suspicious.
cards.q: What is the next step if mammography shows a suspicious lesion but examination is normal?

cards.a: BI-RADS 5 means highly suggestive of malignancy, with a greater than 95 percent chance of cancer. The next step is tissue biopsy and urgent referral to a breast surgeon. BI-RADS 4 also needs biopsy, while BI-RADS 3 is probably benign and can be followed, so the category decides urgency.
cards.q: What does BI-RADS 5 mean, and what is the next step?

cards.a: DCIS, ductal carcinoma in situ, is cancer cells confined to the ducts without invasion. It is treated with breast-conserving surgery plus radiation, or mastectomy if extensive, and endocrine therapy if hormone-receptor positive. It is not invasive cancer, but it can become invasive if left untreated, so treatment is needed.
cards.q: What is DCIS, and how is it treated?

cards.a: Invasive ductal carcinoma is the most common type and forms a distinct mass. Invasive lobular carcinoma grows in single file, is often harder to feel and to see on mammography, is more often bilateral and hormone-receptor positive, and can be harder to get clear margins on. Both are invasive and need staging and systemic therapy based on receptors.
cards.q: What is the difference between invasive ductal and invasive lobular carcinoma?

cards.a: ER and PR positive cancers respond to endocrine therapy. HER2 positive cancers benefit from HER2-targeted therapy such as trastuzumab plus chemotherapy. Triple negative cancers, negative for all three, do not respond to endocrine or HER2 therapy and need chemotherapy. Receptor status is therefore essential before choosing treatment.
cards.q: How do ER, PR and HER2 results guide breast cancer treatment?

cards.a: Tamoxifen blocks the oestrogen receptor and can be used before or after menopause. Aromatase inhibitors block oestrogen production and are used only after menopause, when the ovaries no longer make oestrogen. Choosing the wrong one, for example an aromatase inhibitor alone in a premenopausal woman, will not work because the ovaries will keep making oestrogen.
cards.q: What is the difference between tamoxifen and an aromatase inhibitor, and who gets which?

cards.a: HER2-positive cancer overexpresses the HER2 growth receptor and grows more aggressively. Trastuzumab is an antibody against HER2 that, added to chemotherapy, markedly improves survival. It can affect the heart, so cardiac function is checked before and during treatment.
cards.q: What is HER2-positive breast cancer, and why is trastuzumab added?

cards.a: Triple-negative cancer is negative for ER, PR and HER2, so it has no target for endocrine or HER2 therapy and is treated with chemotherapy. It tends to occur in younger women and BRCA1 carriers, grows faster, recurs earlier, and has a worse prognosis than hormone-receptor-positive cancers.
cards.q: What is triple-negative breast cancer, and why is its prognosis worse?

cards.a: Male breast cancer is rare but real, usually presents as a painless lump behind the nipple, and is strongly linked to BRCA2. Workup is the same triple assessment as in women, treatment is usually mastectomy plus systemic therapy based on receptors, and genetic counselling is essential because it signals a hereditary risk for the family.
cards.q: What should you know about male breast cancer?

cards.a: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory skin condition of the vulva causing intense itching, white atrophic plaques and scarring, most often after menopause. Treat with high-potency topical steroids, which control symptoms and may lower cancer risk, and biopsy any thickened, non-healing or suspicious area because lichen sclerosus raises the risk of vulvar squamous cancer.
cards.q: What is lichen sclerosus, and how is it managed?

cards.a: VIN, vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia, is a precancer of the vulva, often HPV-related in younger women or linked to lichen sclerosus in older women. It presents as raised, pigmented or white lesions that persist, and needs biopsy to confirm. Unlike lichen sclerosus, which is inflammatory, VIN is dysplasia and needs excision or ablation if confirmed.
cards.q: What is VIN, and how does it differ from lichen sclerosus?

cards.a: Vulvar cancer usually presents as a persistent vulvar lump, ulcer or itch that does not heal, most often squamous cell carcinoma in older women with lichen sclerosus or in younger women with HPV. Treatment is surgical excision with assessment of groin nodes, often with radiation if nodes are involved. Any non-healing vulvar lesion needs biopsy, not repeated antifungal cream.
cards.q: What is the presentation and treatment of vulvar cancer?

cards.a: Examine the vulva carefully and biopsy if there is a white plaque, thickening, ulcer or non-healing area. Repeated antifungal treatment without examination misses lichen sclerosus, VIN and vulvar cancer. Itching that persists is a reason to look and to biopsy, not to try another cream.
cards.q: A postmenopausal woman has persistent vulvar itching that has not responded to antifungals. What is the next step?

cards.a: Vaginal cancer is rare, usually squamous cell carcinoma, and presents with abnormal vaginal bleeding, especially postmenopausal bleeding, or discharge. It is often a recurrence or extension of cervical cancer rather than a primary tumour, so the cervix must be examined and prior cervical disease excluded before calling it primary vaginal cancer.
cards.q: What is vaginal cancer, and what is its usual presentation?

cards.a: Daughters exposed to diethylstilbestrol (DES) in utero have a higher risk of clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina and cervix, usually in adolescence or young adulthood, plus vaginal adenosis and structural abnormalities. They need lifelong specialist screening with careful examination of the vagina and cervix, and should tell every clinician about the exposure.
cards.q: What is the link between DES exposure in utero and vaginal cancer?

cards.a: Annual pelvic examination with careful inspection and palpation of the vagina and cervix, plus Pap testing, starting at puberty or when exposure is recognised, in a specialist clinic. Routine screening alone is not enough because clear cell adenocarcinoma can arise in the vagina, not just the cervix, so the whole vagina must be examined.
cards.q: What screening is needed for a DES daughter?

cards.a: A molar pregnancy is a gestational trophoblastic disease where the placenta grows abnormally without a viable fetus, with very high hCG. It presents with exaggerated pregnancy symptoms, hyperemesis, uterine size larger than dates, vaginal bleeding, and sometimes early pre-eclampsia or thyrotoxicosis. Ultrasound shows a snowstorm or grape-like pattern without a fetus.
cards.q: What is a molar pregnancy, and what is its classic presentation?

cards.a: A complete mole has no fetal tissue and is diploid, usually from an empty egg fertilised by a duplicated sperm. A partial mole has some fetal tissue and is triploid, from an egg fertilised by two sperm. Complete moles are more likely to develop persistent trophoblastic disease, so follow-up is closer after a complete mole.
cards.q: What is the difference between a complete and a partial mole?

cards.a: Evacuate the uterus by suction curettage, with blood available and oxytocics avoided until the uterus is empty because they can force trophoblastic tissue into the circulation. Give anti-D if Rh-negative, send tissue for histology, and check hCG and a chest X-ray. Do not attempt medical management alone, because evacuation is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
cards.q: How is a molar pregnancy managed, and what should be avoided before evacuation?

cards.a: Check hCG weekly until it is undetectable on three consecutive tests, then monthly for 6 months. Rising or plateauing hCG means persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia and needs chemotherapy. Use reliable contraception during follow-up because a new pregnancy would raise hCG and make it impossible to tell if disease has recurred.
cards.q: What is hCG follow-up after a molar pregnancy, and why is contraception advised?

cards.a: When hCG plateaus over 3 weeks, rises over 2 weeks, remains detectable 6 months after evacuation, or histology shows choriocarcinoma. It is a clinical diagnosis based on hCG, not a repeat biopsy, because the disease is highly chemosensitive and waiting for tissue would delay curative treatment.
cards.q: When is postmolar gestational trophoblastic neoplasia diagnosed?

cards.a: Choriocarcinoma is a malignant trophoblastic tumour that follows a molar pregnancy, abortion or normal pregnancy, with very high hCG and early spread to lung, vagina and brain. It is highly sensitive to chemotherapy, so even metastatic disease is often curable with multi-agent chemotherapy. Early recognition by hCG is the key to that cure rate.
cards.q: What is choriocarcinoma, and why is it highly curable despite metastases?

cards.a: Placental site trophoblastic tumour is a rare trophoblastic tumour that grows slowly, produces only mildly raised hCG, and is less sensitive to chemotherapy than choriocarcinoma. It usually needs surgery, often hysterectomy, as the main treatment, because chemotherapy alone is less effective. A low hCG with a uterine mass after pregnancy should raise suspicion.
cards.q: What is placental site trophoblastic tumour, and how does it differ from choriocarcinoma?

cards.a: Offer testing to people with breast cancer under 50, triple-negative breast cancer, ovarian cancer at any age, male breast cancer, or a strong family history of breast, ovarian, pancreatic or prostate cancer. BRCA1 and BRCA2 raise the risk of breast and ovarian cancer, and also pancreatic and prostate cancer. Testing should follow genetic counselling, not be ordered without it.
cards.q: Who should be offered BRCA testing, and what cancers are linked to BRCA1 and BRCA2?

cards.a: It is removal of both ovaries and fallopian tubes to prevent ovarian and fallopian tube cancer, usually at age 35 to 40 for BRCA1 and 40 to 45 for BRCA2, after childbearing is complete. It lowers ovarian cancer risk by most of the excess risk but causes surgical menopause, so hormone replacement and bone health need discussion.
cards.q: What is risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy for a BRCA carrier, and when is it done?

cards.a: Lynch syndrome is an inherited mismatch-repair gene mutation that raises the risk of colorectal, endometrial and ovarian cancer, plus other cancers. Endometrial cancer is often the first cancer in women with Lynch, so any endometrial cancer, especially under 50, should prompt consideration of Lynch testing.
cards.q: What is Lynch syndrome, and which gynaecologic cancers does it raise the risk of?

cards.a: Colonoscopy every 1 to 2 years from age 20 to 25, endometrial sampling or ultrasound surveillance, and discussion of risk-reducing hysterectomy with removal of ovaries after childbearing is complete. Aspirin may be discussed for colorectal prevention. Management should be in a high-risk programme with genetics input.
cards.q: What screening and prevention is offered to a woman with Lynch syndrome?

cards.a: Because a positive result affects not only the patient but her relatives, has implications for insurance and family planning, and a variant of uncertain significance can be misinterpreted without expert input. Counselling explains what the test can and cannot show, the options after a result, and the need to inform relatives, so testing is never just a blood test.
cards.q: Why is genetic counselling needed before BRCA or Lynch testing?

cards.a: Offer HPV vaccination, smoking cessation, weight management, and discussion of oral contraceptives where appropriate, plus screening on schedule. Smoking cessation matters for cervical cancer, weight loss matters for endometrial cancer, and vaccination matters for cervical, vulvar and vaginal cancer. Prevention is part of every gynaecology visit, not a separate service.
cards.q: What cancer prevention counselling should be given in gynaecologic oncology?

cards.a: Manage with diuretics if mild, therapeutic paracentesis for symptom relief when breathing or eating is impaired, and systemic chemotherapy to control the underlying cancer. Repeated paracentesis is a palliative measure, not a cure, and should be combined with attention to nutrition, pain and goals of care.
cards.q: How is malignant ascites in advanced ovarian cancer managed?

cards.a: Lymphedema after lymph node removal, menopause after removal of ovaries, sexual dysfunction after pelvic radiation or surgery, bladder and bowel effects of radiation, fatigue, and fear of recurrence. Survivorship care should screen for these at every visit, not just look for recurrence, because they affect quality of life for years.
cards.q: What survivorship issues follow treatment for gynaecologic cancer?

cards.a: Postmenopausal bleeding, postcoital bleeding, a palpable pelvic mass, persistent bloating and early satiety for more than 2 to 3 weeks, a non-healing vulvar ulcer, and unexplained weight loss with pelvic symptoms. Any of these needs urgent examination and referral, not routine follow-up, because early diagnosis changes outcome.
cards.q: What are the red-flag symptoms that need urgent gynaecologic oncology referral?

cards.a: It includes checking for late radiation effects on bladder and bowel, sexual health, lymphoedema, bone health, and psychological support, plus screening for second cancers and smoking cessation. Follow-up is not only about recurrence; it is about living well after treatment, so these issues should be asked about at every visit.
cards.q: What does follow-up after cervical cancer treatment include besides looking for recurrence?
A postmenopausal woman on tamoxifen for breast cancer develops vaginal bleeding. What is the next step, and why is she at risk?
cards.a: Work her up urgently for endometrial cancer with pelvic examination, transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial biopsy. Tamoxifen acts as an oestrogen agonist on the endometrium in postmenopausal women, raising the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and cancer, so bleeding on tamoxifen must never be assumed to be a drug side effect. Do not stop the tamoxifen without oncology input, but do not delay the biopsy.

Rotterdam criteria need 2 of 3 after excluding other causes: (1) oligo- or anovulation, (2) clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, (3) polycystic ovaries on ultrasound (12 or more follicles 2-9 mm or ovarian volume over 10 mL). Diagnosis is clinical plus exclusion of mimics such as thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, and non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
cards.q: A 28-year-old woman has irregular periods, acne, hirsutism, and ovaries with many small follicles on ultrasound. What are the Rotterdam criteria for PCOS, and how many are needed for diagnosis?

cards.a: Exclude other causes first: check pregnancy test, TSH, prolactin, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone for non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, plus testosterone and DHEAS if virilisation. PCOS is a diagnosis of exclusion, so missing thyroid disease or a prolactinoma leads to wrong treatment.
cards.q: What is the first step before diagnosing PCOS in a woman with irregular menses and androgen excess?

cards.a: Lifestyle modification is first line: diet, exercise, and even 5 to 10 percent weight loss. Weight loss lowers insulin resistance and androgen levels, which can restore ovulation spontaneously, so it should come before drugs in most overweight patients.
cards.q: A woman with PCOS is overweight and anovulatory. What is the first-line management, and why does it help fertility?

cards.a: Combined oral contraceptive pill is first line. It regulates cycles, protects the endometrium from unopposed oestrogen, lowers free testosterone by raising sex hormone-binding globulin, and improves acne and hirsutism.
cards.q: A woman with PCOS has irregular heavy bleeding but does not want pregnancy now. What is the best first-line treatment and why?

cards.a: Chronic anovulation means no progesterone to oppose oestrogen, so the endometrium keeps proliferating and can develop hyperplasia and cancer. Regular withdrawal bleeds from an oral contraceptive or cyclic progestin protect the endometrium.
cards.q: Why does unopposed oestrogen in PCOS increase endometrial cancer risk, and what prevents it?

cards.a: Metformin improves insulin sensitivity, lowers insulin and androgen levels, and can help restore ovulation and improve metabolic risk. It is most useful with obesity, impaired glucose tolerance, or diabetes risk, but it is less effective than letrozole for ovulation induction alone.
cards.q: A woman with PCOS and insulin resistance is started on metformin. What does metformin do, and when is it most useful?

cards.a: Letrozole is preferred first line for PCOS. It is an aromatase inhibitor that lowers oestrogen, increases FSH release, and gives higher live birth rates and lower multiple pregnancy rates than clomiphene in PCOS.
cards.q: A woman with PCOS wants to conceive. Which ovulation induction drug is now preferred over clomiphene, and why?

cards.a: Stop clomiphene and seek urgent review, especially for visual symptoms, which can signal a pituitary issue or drug effect. Clomiphene commonly causes hot flushes and mood changes, and visual disturbance is a reason to stop and not rechallenge without specialist input.
cards.q: A woman with PCOS on clomiphene develops hot flushes, mood changes, and visual blurring. What is the next best step?

cards.a: Screen for impaired glucose tolerance or diabetes with a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test, check blood pressure, lipids, and BMI, and assess for obstructive sleep apnoea if obese. PCOS carries a high risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, so metabolic screening is part of routine care, not optional.
cards.q: What metabolic screening should every woman with PCOS have at diagnosis?

cards.a: Add an anti-androgen such as spironolactone, with reliable contraception because it is teratogenic in a male fetus. Anti-androgens block androgen receptors and take 6 to 12 months for visible hair reduction; they should not be used alone in a woman who could become pregnant.
cards.q: A woman with PCOS has severe hirsutism despite 6 months on an oral contraceptive. What is the next best step?

cards.a: Eflornithine slows facial hair growth by inhibiting an enzyme in the hair follicle. It helps cosmetically but does not remove existing hair or treat the underlying androgen excess, so it is an adjunct to systemic treatment and hair removal, not a substitute.
cards.q: Why is eflornithine cream sometimes used for facial hirsutism in PCOS, and what should the patient expect?

cards.a: No. In a lean woman without insulin resistance, letrozole for ovulation induction is the priority, and metformin adds little. Metformin is targeted at metabolic dysfunction, not at every woman with PCOS.
cards.q: A lean woman with PCOS is normoglycaemic but anovulatory. Is metformin still first line for fertility?

cards.a: Higher risk of gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, and miscarriage. Early glucose screening in pregnancy and close antenatal surveillance are needed, and weight and blood pressure should be optimised before conception.
cards.q: A woman with PCOS becomes pregnant. What pregnancy risks should she be counselled about?

cards.a: Explain that PCOS is a long-term metabolic and reproductive condition, not just irregular periods: lifestyle, weight, and regular cycles matter for future fertility and for preventing diabetes and endometrial disease. Reassure her that fertility can usually be helped later with ovulation induction.
cards.q: What is the most important counselling point for a teenager newly diagnosed with PCOS?

cards.a: Refer to reproductive endocrinology and consider weight management, including bariatric surgery referral if appropriate, plus gonadotropin ovulation induction or laparoscopic ovarian drilling in selected cases. Severe obesity lowers ovulation drug success and raises pregnancy risks, so weight and specialist review come before escalating to IVF.
cards.q: A woman with PCOS has a BMI of 38 and has failed letrozole. What is the next best step before IVF?

cards.a: Primary amenorrhoea is no menses by age 15, or by age 13 if no breast development. The first test in any amenorrhoea is a pregnancy test, regardless of history, because pregnancy is the commonest cause and changes all further management.
cards.q: What is the definition of primary amenorrhoea, and what is the first test in any woman with amenorrhoea?

cards.a: No menses for 3 months if cycles were previously regular, or for 6 months if previously irregular. After excluding pregnancy, the workup follows the same outflow, ovarian, pituitary, and hypothalamic pathway as primary amenorrhoea.
cards.q: What is the definition of secondary amenorrhoea?

cards.a: Think of an outflow obstruction such as imperforate hymen or transverse vaginal septum, with blood trapped behind it (haematocolpos). Examine the perineum and do pelvic ultrasound; surgical correction relieves pain and restores flow.
cards.q: A 16-year-old has normal breast development but no periods and cyclic pelvic pain. What is the most likely cause and the next step?

cards.a: Sheehan syndrome: postpartum pituitary necrosis after severe haemorrhage and hypotension. She cannot breastfeed, has fatigue and amenorrhoea, and needs pituitary hormone testing and replacement, starting with cortisol before thyroid hormone.
cards.q: A woman has amenorrhoea after a difficult delivery with heavy bleeding. What is the likely diagnosis and why?

cards.a: Asherman syndrome: intrauterine adhesions after curettage scar the endometrium so it cannot shed. Confirm with hysteroscopy, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic by dividing adhesions; hysterosalpingography can suggest it but hysteroscopy is definitive.
cards.q: A woman has amenorrhoea after a dilatation and curettage. What is the diagnosis, and how is it confirmed?

cards.a: Give a progestin for 5 to 10 days, then stop it. A bleed means the outflow tract is patent, the endometrium responds to oestrogen, and the cause is anovulation. No bleed means either outflow obstruction or an oestrogen-deficient endometrium.
cards.q: What is the progesterone challenge test, and what does a withdrawal bleed mean?

cards.a: Give combined oestrogen plus progestin. A bleed after this means the outflow is patent but she is oestrogen-deficient (ovarian failure or hypothalamic cause). No bleed after oestrogen-progestin suggests outflow obstruction such as Asherman syndrome.
cards.q: A woman has no withdrawal bleed after progesterone. What is the next step in the workup?

cards.a: Turner syndrome (45,X): gonadal dysgenesis with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. Management is growth hormone in childhood, oestrogen replacement at puberty, cardiac screening for coarctation and bicuspid aortic valve, and fertility counselling, as most need donor eggs.
cards.q: A 17-year-old with primary amenorrhoea is short, has a webbed neck and shield chest, and has high FSH. What is the diagnosis and the key management?

cards.a: High FSH and LH mean the ovaries have failed (hypergonadotropic, e.g. Turner syndrome or premature ovarian insufficiency). Low or normal FSH and LH mean the problem is central, in the hypothalamus or pituitary (hypogonadotropic, e.g. stress, weight loss, or pituitary disease).
cards.q: What labs distinguish hypergonadotropic from hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in amenorrhoea?

cards.a: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea from energy deficiency. First line is restoring energy balance: increased intake, reduced exercise, and weight gain. Hormones mask the problem and do not restore bone or fertility as well as addressing the cause.
cards.q: A woman with amenorrhoea has low FSH, low LH, and low oestrogen, with a history of excessive exercise and low weight. What is the diagnosis and first-line treatment?

cards.a: Prolonged low oestrogen causes bone loss and raises fracture risk, even in young women. Check bone mineral density with DEXA if amenorrhoea lasts more than 6 months, and counsel on calcium, vitamin D, and restoring menses.
cards.q: Why is bone health a concern in hypothalamic amenorrhoea, and what should be checked?

cards.a: Check TSH and review drugs, then arrange pituitary MRI if prolactin stays high. A prolactin this high suggests a prolactinoma, and MRI defines size before starting a dopamine agonist.
cards.q: A woman with secondary amenorrhoea has galactorrhoea and a prolactin of 120 ng per mL. What is the next best step?

cards.a: Polycystic ovary syndrome and functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea are the commonest non-pregnancy causes, followed by thyroid disease and hyperprolactinaemia. That is why TSH, prolactin, and androgen assessment are part of the first-line workup.
cards.q: What is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhoea overall, after pregnancy?

cards.a: Do a progesterone challenge test to test endometrial oestrogen exposure and outflow patency, and consider pelvic ultrasound for ovarian and uterine anatomy. Normal gonadotropins point toward anovulation or outflow problems rather than ovarian failure.
cards.q: A woman with amenorrhoea has normal FSH, normal prolactin, and normal TSH. What is the next best investigation?

cards.a: Menopause is diagnosed retrospectively after 12 months without a period, usually around age 51. In a woman over 45 with typical symptoms, no lab test is needed; FSH is only useful if diagnosis is uncertain, such as after hysterectomy or at a younger age.
cards.q: At what age is menopause diagnosed, and what confirms it clinically?

cards.a: Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) is the most effective treatment for hot flushes and night sweats. Systemic oestrogen relieves vasomotor symptoms and vaginal dryness, and the decision balances symptom severity against risks and contraindications.
cards.q: A 52-year-old woman has hot flushes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. What is the most effective treatment for her vasomotor symptoms?

cards.a: Unopposed oestrogen causes endometrial hyperplasia and cancer in a woman with a uterus. Adding a progestogen for at least 12 days per month, or continuously, protects the endometrium. Women after hysterectomy can take oestrogen alone.
cards.q: A postmenopausal woman has a uterus and is started on oestrogen. Why must a progestogen be added?

cards.a: Unexplained vaginal bleeding, active or past breast cancer, active venous thromboembolism, active liver disease, and known oestrogen-sensitive cancer. These patients need non-hormonal alternatives and specialist advice.
cards.q: What are absolute contraindications to systemic HRT?

cards.a: Stop HRT immediately and assess urgently for venous thromboembolism with imaging. Oral oestrogen raises clot risk; transdermal oestrogen has lower clot risk and is preferred in women with clot risk factors.
cards.q: A woman on HRT develops a painful swollen calf and breathlessness. What is the next best step?

cards.a: Transdermal oestrogen bypasses first-pass liver metabolism, so it has less effect on clotting factors and a lower venous thromboembolism risk, and it is safer in migraine with aura. Oral oestrogen is avoided in these women.
cards.q: Why is transdermal oestrogen preferred over oral oestrogen in a woman with migraine with aura or clot risk?

cards.a: SSRIs or SNRIs such as paroxetine or venlafaxine, gabapentin, and clonidine can reduce hot flushes. Lifestyle measures, avoiding triggers, and cognitive behavioural therapy also help; counsel that they are less effective than HRT but useful when HRT is contraindicated.
cards.q: A 55-year-old woman cannot take HRT for hot flushes. What non-hormonal options help?

cards.a: Vaginal oestrogen (cream, tablet, or ring) is best. It treats local atrophy with minimal systemic absorption, so it is safe even in many women who cannot take systemic HRT, and it does not need a progestogen.
cards.q: A postmenopausal woman has only vaginal dryness and dyspareunia, with no hot flushes. What is the best treatment?

cards.a: Oestrogen prevents bone loss and reduces fracture risk. HRT is used for osteoporosis prevention mainly in women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause who also have vasomotor symptoms; otherwise bisphosphonates are first line for osteoporosis alone.
cards.q: How does HRT affect bone health after menopause, and when is it used for osteoporosis prevention?

cards.a: Starting HRT more than 10 years after menopause or after age 60 carries higher cardiovascular and clot risk with less benefit, so the risk-benefit balance is less favourable. Discuss this timing window and consider non-hormonal options or specialist referral.
cards.q: A 60-year-old woman 10 years after menopause asks to start HRT for the first time. What is the key counselling point?

cards.a: Investigate urgently: pelvic examination, transvaginal ultrasound, and endometrial biopsy if the endometrium is thickened. Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise, even on HRT.
cards.q: A postmenopausal woman on HRT has unexpected vaginal bleeding. What is the next best step?

cards.a: Infertility is failure to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse. Evaluate after 6 months if the woman is over 35, and immediately if there is known tubal disease, severe endometriosis, irregular cycles, or male factor, because waiting wastes fertile time.
cards.q: What is the definition of infertility, and when should evaluation start earlier than 12 months?

cards.a: Ovulation (history, mid-luteal progesterone, or ovulation kits), tubal patency (hysterosalpingography), and semen analysis in the male partner. These cover the three commonest causes, and all three should be assessed in parallel rather than one at a time.
cards.q: What are the three basic components of the infertility workup, and what does each test?

cards.a: Do a semen analysis now, alongside ovulation and tubal testing. Male factor contributes to about half of infertility, so the male partner must be tested early, not after months of female-only investigations.
cards.q: A couple has been trying for 14 months. The woman has regular cycles and the man has never had a semen analysis. What is the next best step?

cards.a: A mid-luteal progesterone level above 3 ng per mL, drawn about 7 days before the expected period, confirms ovulation. Basal body temperature and urine LH kits can suggest it, but progesterone is the standard confirmatory test.
cards.q: How is ovulation confirmed in a woman with regular cycles?

cards.a: Hysterosalpingography: dye through the cervix under X-ray shows whether tubes are open and outlines the uterine cavity. It can also show fibroids, polyps, or a septum, and should be done in the follicular phase after a negative pregnancy test.
cards.q: What is the first-line test for tubal patency, and what else can it show?

cards.a: Avoid hysterosalpingography as the first test if there is active pelvic infection or a history suggesting tubal damage with hydrosalpinx, because it can flare infection; treat infection first and consider laparoscopy or specialist referral.
cards.q: A woman with a history of pelvic inflammatory disease is being worked up for infertility. Which test should be avoided as first line, and why?

cards.a: Female fertility falls sharply after 35, and ovarian reserve declines with age. Guidelines advise evaluation after 6 months over age 35, so a 38-year-old should be assessed and referred promptly rather than told to wait a full year.
cards.q: A 38-year-old woman has been trying for 7 months. Why is early referral appropriate despite the 12-month definition?

cards.a: Anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) and antral follicle count on ultrasound estimate how many eggs remain. Low values predict poor response to stimulation and lower IVF success, but they do not predict natural conception well in a young woman, so they guide treatment choice, not a diagnosis of infertility alone.
cards.q: What is ovarian reserve testing, and what do AMH and antral follicle count tell you?

cards.a: Smoking, obesity, and alcohol: smoking reduces fertility in both partners, obesity impairs ovulation and IVF success, and heavy alcohol lowers conception rates. Stopping smoking, achieving a healthy weight, and limiting alcohol should be advised before starting treatment.
cards.q: A couple is counselled on lifestyle before fertility treatment. What three factors most affect success?

cards.a: Refer if the woman is over 35 with 6 months of trying, if basic tests show tubal blockage, severe male factor, anovulation not responding to first-line drugs, or endometriosis, or if the couple needs IVF or IUI. Early referral avoids delay when time-sensitive treatment is needed.
cards.q: When should a couple with infertility be referred to reproductive endocrinology rather than managed in primary care?

cards.a: Monitor with ultrasound for follicle growth and a mid-luteal progesterone to confirm ovulation, and advise timed intercourse. Monitoring prevents missing ovulation and detects multiple follicles, which raise the risk of multiple pregnancy.
cards.q: A woman with anovulatory infertility and normal prolactin and thyroid function is started on letrozole. How is response monitored?

cards.a: Clomiphene blocks oestrogen receptors in the hypothalamus, so the brain releases more GnRH and FSH, stimulating follicle growth. Its drawback is an anti-oestrogen effect on cervical mucus and endometrium, plus a higher multiple pregnancy rate than letrozole.
cards.q: How does clomiphene work to induce ovulation, and what is its main drawback compared with letrozole?

cards.a: Usually 3 to 6 ovulatory cycles. If pregnancy has not occurred after 6 ovulatory cycles, refer for further evaluation and consider gonadotropins or IVF, because continuing the same drug has diminishing returns.
cards.q: What is the maximum recommended duration of clomiphene or letrozole ovulation induction before moving on?

cards.a: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS). Stop the trigger or cancel the cycle, assess for ascites and haemoconcentration, and manage supportively with fluids and monitoring; severe OHSS needs hospital admission.
cards.q: A woman on gonadotropins for ovulation induction develops abdominal pain, bloating, and enlarged ovaries. What is the diagnosis and the next step?

cards.a: Counsel that ovulation induction raises the risk of twins and higher-order multiples, which increase preterm birth, pre-eclampsia, and perinatal mortality. Ultrasound monitoring and cancelling a cycle with too many follicles reduce this risk.
cards.q: What counselling must be given before ovulation induction about multiple pregnancy?

cards.a: Clomiphene works by increasing the brain's own GnRH and FSH, but in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism the hypothalamus or pituitary cannot respond. Gonadotropins replace FSH and LH directly, so they can stimulate the ovary.
cards.q: A woman with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism wants to conceive. Why are gonadotropins, not clomiphene, needed?

cards.a: Metformin alone is less effective than letrozole for live birth. It is most useful combined with letrozole or clomiphene in women with insulin resistance, or when letrozole alone has failed, rather than as sole first-line therapy.
cards.q: What is the role of metformin in ovulation induction for PCOS, alone versus combined with letrozole?

cards.a: Drilling makes small holes in the ovarian surface, lowering androgen production and restoring ovulation. Its main risks are pelvic adhesions and, rarely, premature ovarian failure, so it is reserved for women who fail medical induction and need laparoscopy anyway.
cards.q: A woman with PCOS has failed letrozole and is offered laparoscopic ovarian drilling. How does it work, and what is its main risk?

cards.a: Increase the dose stepwise in the next cycle, with ultrasound or progesterone monitoring. If she still does not ovulate at the maximum dose, switch to letrozole or gonadotropins under specialist care rather than continuing ineffective cycles.
cards.q: A woman is on clomiphene and has not ovulated at the starting dose. What is the next best step?

cards.a: IUI places washed, concentrated sperm directly into the uterus around ovulation, bypassing cervical mucus. It is most useful for mild male factor, cervical factor, unexplained infertility, and donor sperm, often combined with ovulation induction.
cards.q: What is intrauterine insemination (IUI), and when is it most useful?

cards.a: IVF stimulates the ovaries to produce multiple eggs, retrieves them, fertilises them with sperm in the laboratory, and transfers an embryo into the uterus. It is indicated for tubal blockage, severe male factor, endometriosis, failed IUI, and older women with low reserve.
cards.q: What is IVF, in simple terms, and when is it indicated?

cards.a: Female age, because egg quality and quantity fall with age. Younger women have higher live birth rates per cycle; age also predicts miscarriage risk, so counselling must be honest about declining success after 40.
cards.q: A couple is counselled before IVF. What is the single strongest predictor of IVF success?

cards.a: Transferring one embryo greatly reduces twin pregnancy and its complications, while cumulative live birth rates with frozen embryos remain similar. Multiple embryo transfer raises preterm birth and perinatal risk without a large gain in overall success.
cards.q: Why is single embryo transfer now recommended in many IVF cycles?

cards.a: Fresh transfer uses an embryo in the same cycle as egg retrieval; frozen transfer thaws a stored embryo in a later cycle. Frozen is preferred if there is OHSS risk, a thin endometrium, or preimplantation genetic testing, because it lets the uterus recover.
cards.q: What is the difference between fresh and frozen embryo transfer, and when is frozen preferred?

cards.a: Fluid from a blocked, fluid-filled tube can leak into the uterus and wash out or harm the embryo, halving implantation rates. Removing or clipping the tube before IVF improves success.
cards.q: A woman undergoing IVF is told she has a hydrosalpinx. Why should it be treated before embryo transfer?

cards.a: Intracytoplasmic sperm injection injects a single sperm directly into each egg. It is used for severe male factor such as very low count or poor motility, prior fertilisation failure, or when few eggs are retrieved.
cards.q: What is ICSI, and when is it used instead of standard IVF fertilisation?

cards.a: Counsel that IVF is physically, emotionally, and financially demanding, success is not guaranteed, multiple cycles are often needed, and support and realistic expectations matter. Offer psychological support and discuss stopping rules and alternatives such as donor eggs or adoption.
cards.q: A couple asks about the emotional and financial burden of IVF. What should counselling cover?

cards.a: It tests embryos for chromosomal abnormalities or a known single-gene disorder before transfer. It can reduce miscarriage and help select embryos, but it does not guarantee a healthy baby, adds cost, and mosaic results can be uncertain, so specialist genetic counselling is needed.
cards.q: What is the role of preimplantation genetic testing in IVF, and what are its limits?

cards.a: Progressive dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, chronic pelvic pain, dyschezia, and infertility. Diagnosis is delayed because pain is often normalised, symptoms overlap with irritable bowel and other causes, and definitive diagnosis needs laparoscopy, so years can pass before it is recognised.
cards.q: What are the classic symptoms of endometriosis, and why is diagnosis often delayed?

cards.a: Endometriosis with deep infiltrating disease and adhesions. A fixed uterus and tender nodules suggest endometriotic implants and scarring, and referral for imaging and laparoscopy is needed.
cards.q: A 30-year-old woman has severe dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia, and infertility. Examination shows a fixed retroverted uterus and tender nodules in the pouch of Douglas. What is the likely diagnosis?

cards.a: Laparoscopy with biopsy is the gold standard. Transvaginal ultrasound can show endometriomas (chocolate cysts) and deep disease, but a normal ultrasound does not exclude superficial peritoneal endometriosis.
cards.q: What is the gold standard for diagnosing endometriosis, and what can ultrasound show?

cards.a: NSAIDs for pain relief are first line when trying to conceive, because hormonal treatments suppress ovulation and delay pregnancy. She should be referred promptly for fertility assessment rather than kept on suppressive hormones.
cards.q: A woman with endometriosis has pain but wants to conceive soon. What is the best first-line medical treatment, and what should be avoided?

cards.a: Combined oral contraceptive or a progestin, which suppresses menstruation and endometriotic tissue growth and reduces pain. These are first line for pain control when fertility is not an immediate goal.
cards.q: A woman with endometriosis does not want pregnancy now. What is first-line medical management?

cards.a: Surgery is indicated for severe pain not responding to medical treatment, large endometriomas, bowel or bladder involvement, or infertility with anatomical distortion. The goal is excision of lesions and restoration of anatomy, not just symptom relief.
cards.q: When is surgery indicated for endometriosis, and what is its goal?

cards.a: Endometriosis distorts pelvic anatomy with adhesions, causes inflammation that harms eggs, sperm, and embryos, and impairs implantation. Even mild disease can reduce fertility through inflammation, so treatment must address both pain and fertility.
cards.q: How does endometriosis cause infertility, even when tubes are open?

cards.a: Not always. Removing a large endometrioma can reduce ovarian reserve and damage healthy tissue, so small cysts are often left and IVF proceeds. Large, painful, or rapidly growing cysts, or suspicion of malignancy, favour surgery before IVF.
cards.q: A woman with an endometrioma is planning IVF. Should the cyst be removed first?

cards.a: GnRH agonists create a temporary menopause that shrinks endometriotic tissue and relieves pain. Their main side effects are hot flushes and bone loss, so add-back HRT is given and use is usually limited to 6 months.
cards.q: What is the role of GnRH agonists in endometriosis, and what is their main side effect?

cards.a: Heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure, urinary frequency, constipation, and dyspareunia. Heavy bleeding with anaemia is the commonest presenting complaint, and large fibroids can cause a palpable abdominal mass.
cards.q: What are the typical symptoms of uterine fibroids, and which symptom most often brings women to care?

cards.a: Submucosal fibroids distort the uterine cavity and cause heavy bleeding and infertility even when small, while large subserosal fibroids may cause only pressure. Location determines symptoms and which treatment will help.
cards.q: A woman with heavy bleeding has a pelvic ultrasound showing a submucosal fibroid. Why does location matter more than size?

cards.a: Tranexamic acid during menses reduces bleeding, and NSAIDs help pain. Hormonal options such as a levonorgestrel intrauterine system or oral contraceptive can also reduce bleeding, but they do not shrink fibroids.
cards.q: What is first-line medical management for heavy bleeding from fibroids in a woman who wants to preserve fertility?

cards.a: GnRH agonists shrink fibroids by creating a low-oestrogen state, reducing bleeding and size before myomectomy or hysterectomy. Long-term use is limited by menopausal symptoms and bone loss, so they are a bridge to surgery, not a permanent treatment.
cards.q: How do GnRH agonists help fibroids before surgery, and what limits their long-term use?

cards.a: Hysteroscopic myomectomy to remove the submucosal fibroid and restore the cavity. This improves fertility and reduces miscarriage risk, whereas leaving a cavity-distorting fibroid lowers implantation.
cards.q: A woman with fibroids wants to conceive and has a submucosal fibroid distorting the cavity. What is the best treatment?

cards.a: Myomectomy is preferred when the woman wants to preserve fertility or the uterus, and fibroids are accessible. Hysterectomy is definitive but ends fertility, so it is chosen when childbearing is complete and symptoms are severe or other treatments have failed.
cards.q: When is myomectomy preferred over hysterectomy for fibroids?

cards.a: Embolisation blocks the blood supply to fibroids, causing them to shrink. It is suitable for women with symptomatic fibroids who want to avoid surgery and do not plan future pregnancy, as pregnancy after embolisation carries higher risks.
cards.q: What is uterine artery embolisation, and who is it suitable for?

cards.a: Red degeneration: the fibroid outgrows its blood supply and infarcts, causing acute pain. Management is conservative with analgesia and rest; surgery in pregnancy is avoided unless there is a complication.
cards.q: A pregnant woman has a known fibroid and develops severe localised pain in the second trimester. What is the likely cause and management?

cards.a: Fibroids are oestrogen- and progesterone-sensitive, so they grow when hormone levels are high in pregnancy and shrink when hormones fall after menopause. This is why menopause often relieves fibroid symptoms without surgery.
cards.q: Why do fibroids often grow in pregnancy and shrink after menopause?

cards.a: Prolactinoma, hypothyroidism, drugs, and physiological causes such as pregnancy and breastfeeding. Common drugs are antipsychotics, metoclopramide, and some antidepressants, so a drug history is essential before ordering MRI.
cards.q: What are the commonest causes of hyperprolactinaemia, and which drugs are culprits?

cards.a: Check TSH, because hypothyroidism raises TRH and prolactin, and review medicines. A mildly raised prolactin with hypothyroidism often normalises with thyroxine, avoiding unnecessary imaging.
cards.q: A woman has galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, and a prolactin of 45 ng per mL. What should be checked before assuming a prolactinoma?

cards.a: A dopamine agonist such as cabergoline is first line. It shrinks the tumour and lowers prolactin, restoring ovulation and menses in most women, and surgery is reserved for drug resistance or visual compromise.
cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for a prolactinoma, and how does it work?

cards.a: Monitor vision and symptoms closely, because the tumour can enlarge in pregnancy when oestrogen rises. Dopamine agonists are usually stopped in pregnancy for microadenomas, but macroadenomas need specialist follow-up and visual field testing.
cards.q: A woman with a macroprolactinoma becomes pregnant. What monitoring is needed?

cards.a: Surgery is indicated if the tumour does not shrink on dopamine agonists, if there is acute visual loss or apoplexy, or if the patient cannot tolerate the drug. Most prolactinomas respond well to medical treatment, so surgery is uncommon.
cards.q: When is surgery indicated for a prolactinoma rather than medical treatment?

cards.a: The tumour is compressing the optic chiasm. Urgent ophthalmology and MRI are needed, and a dopamine agonist is started promptly; if vision worsens rapidly, neurosurgical review is urgent.
cards.q: A woman with hyperprolactinaemia has bitemporal hemianopia. What does this finding mean, and what is urgent?

cards.a: Prolactin rises with stress, sleep, exercise, and nipple stimulation, so a single mildly raised level can be a false positive. Repeat a fasting morning sample, and check macroprolactin if the level stays high without symptoms.
cards.q: Why should prolactin be rechecked if the first level is mildly raised and the patient was stressed or had a breast examination?

cards.a: Hypothyroidism raises TRH, which raises prolactin, and it disrupts GnRH pulsatility and ovulation. It causes irregular or heavy bleeding and anovulation, and treating with thyroxine often restores cycles and fertility.
cards.q: How does hypothyroidism cause menstrual irregularity and infertility?

cards.a: Start levothyroxine and recheck TSH, aiming for a normal range before conception. Untreated hypothyroidism raises miscarriage and obstetric risks, so thyroid function should be optimised before trying to conceive.
cards.q: A woman with irregular periods has a TSH of 8 mIU per L and a low free T4. What is the next best step for her fertility?

cards.a: Hyperthyroidism causes light, infrequent, or absent periods and anovulation. Check TSH and free T4, treat the thyroid disease, and counsel that cycles usually normalise once thyroid function is controlled.
cards.q: How does hyperthyroidism affect menstruation, and what should be checked?

cards.a: It is a mild 21-hydroxylase deficiency causing excess adrenal androgens. It presents with hirsutism, acne, irregular periods, and infertility, mimicking PCOS, and is diagnosed by a raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone, especially in the early morning follicular phase.
cards.q: What is non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and how does it present in a woman with hirsutism?

cards.a: A very high DHEAS suggests an adrenal source such as an adrenal tumour. Arrange adrenal imaging urgently and refer to endocrinology, rather than treating as PCOS.
cards.q: A woman with hirsutism has a DHEAS level markedly raised. What does this suggest, and what is the next step?

cards.a: Excess cortisol suppresses GnRH and causes amenorrhoea or irregular periods, with weight gain, central obesity, purple striae, and hypertension. If these features are present, screen with a dexamethasone suppression test or urinary cortisol rather than assuming PCOS.
cards.q: How does Cushing syndrome cause menstrual disturbance, and what clues point to it?

cards.a: Hirsutism is excess terminal hair in a male pattern; virilisation adds deepening voice, clitoromegaly, male-pattern baldness, and increased muscle mass. Virilisation suggests a much higher androgen level and an androgen-secreting tumour, so it needs urgent workup.
cards.q: What is the difference between hirsutism and virilisation, and why does it matter?

cards.a: Measure total testosterone, DHEAS, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone urgently and arrange imaging for an ovarian or adrenal androgen-secreting tumour. Rapid progression with virilisation is a red flag for tumour, not PCOS.
cards.q: A woman has rapidly progressive hirsutism with virilisation over 6 months. What is the next best step?

cards.a: Combined oral contraceptive, which lowers free testosterone and ovarian androgen production. Add spironolactone if the response is inadequate after 6 months, and counsel that hair reduction takes months.
cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for hirsutism in a woman who does not want pregnancy?

cards.a: Total testosterone is low in women and many assays are inaccurate at that range. A raised total testosterone with a raised free androgen index is more informative, and the result must be interpreted with the clinical picture, not in isolation.
cards.q: Why is testosterone measurement tricky in women, and which test is most useful?

cards.a: PCOS can still be the diagnosis, because androgen excess can be clinical (hirsutism and acne) without a raised blood testosterone. Rotterdam criteria allow clinical hyperandrogenism alone, so a normal testosterone does not exclude PCOS.
cards.q: A woman has hirsutism, acne, and irregular periods, but her testosterone is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

cards.a: Loss of ovarian function before age 40, with amenorrhoea or irregular periods and raised FSH on two occasions at least 4 weeks apart. It causes infertility and oestrogen deficiency, and needs hormone replacement until the average age of menopause.
cards.q: What is premature ovarian insufficiency, and how is it diagnosed?

cards.a: Premature ovarian insufficiency. Counsel that pregnancy with her own eggs is unlikely but not impossible, so contraception is still needed if pregnancy is not wanted, and donor eggs are the main fertility option.
cards.q: A 32-year-old woman has amenorrhoea, hot flushes, and FSH of 65 IU per L. What is the diagnosis and the key counselling?

cards.a: To protect bone and cardiovascular health, because early oestrogen loss causes premature bone loss and higher cardiovascular risk. HRT replaces what the ovaries would have made until the natural age of menopause.
cards.q: Why is HRT recommended until age 51 in premature ovarian insufficiency, even if the woman has no hot flushes?

cards.a: Autoimmune thyroid disease and adrenal insufficiency, and a karyotype if there is Turner mosaicism or a family history. Screening matters because autoimmune disease is a common cause and adrenal failure can be life-threatening if missed.
cards.q: What associated conditions should be screened for in premature ovarian insufficiency?

cards.a: Two or more consecutive miscarriages. Basic workup includes parental karyotypes, antiphospholipid antibodies, thyroid function, uterine anatomy with ultrasound or hysteroscopy, and assessment for diabetes and prolactin, plus lifestyle and age counselling.
cards.q: What is recurrent pregnancy loss, and what is the basic workup?

cards.a: Antiphospholipid syndrome. Treat the next pregnancy with low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic heparin, starting early, which greatly improves live birth rates. Refer to obstetrics and haematology for a plan.
cards.q: A woman has had three first-trimester miscarriages and tests positive for lupus anticoagulant. What is the diagnosis and treatment in the next pregnancy?

cards.a: Hysteroscopic resection of the septum, which restores the cavity and reduces miscarriage risk. A septum is a correctable anatomical cause, so surgical correction is offered before the next pregnancy.
cards.q: A woman with recurrent miscarriage has a uterine septum on imaging. What is the next best step?

cards.a: Explain that even with a normal workup, the chance of a successful next pregnancy is high, often 60 to 70 percent, and that no specific treatment is proven to help. Offer supportive care, early ultrasound, and emotional support.
cards.q: What is the most important counselling point after recurrent pregnancy loss when all tests are normal?

cards.a: Male factor is infertility due to abnormal sperm production, function, or delivery. The first test is semen analysis, which assesses volume, count, motility, and morphology, and should be done early in every infertility workup.
cards.q: What is the definition of male factor infertility, and what is the first test?

cards.a: Non-obstructive azoospermia from testicular failure, suggested by high FSH and small or normal testes with no sperm production. Obstructive azoospermia, by contrast, usually has normal FSH and normal testicular volume.
cards.q: A semen analysis shows no sperm (azoospermia) with normal testicular volume and high FSH. What does this suggest?

cards.a: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism: the pituitary is not stimulating the testes. Treat with gonadotropins (hCG plus FSH) to stimulate sperm production, rather than testosterone, which suppresses sperm production.
cards.q: A man has low sperm count, low testosterone, and low LH and FSH. What is the cause and treatment for fertility?

cards.a: Exogenous testosterone suppresses GnRH, LH, and FSH, shutting down sperm production and causing infertility. Men who need androgen treatment and want fertility need specialist care with gonadotropins instead.
cards.q: Why should a man trying to conceive avoid testosterone replacement and anabolic steroids?

cards.a: First line is nutritional rehabilitation and weight restoration with multidisciplinary support. Oestrogen alone gives false reassurance and does not restore bone, fertility, or the underlying energy deficit, so it should not replace treating the eating disorder.
cards.q: A woman has hypothalamic amenorrhoea from an eating disorder. What is the first-line treatment, and why is oestrogen alone not enough?

cards.a: A 46,XY person with a non-functioning androgen receptor develops as a phenotypic female with normal breast development, absent uterus, and primary amenorrhoea, with testes in the abdomen or groin. Diagnosis is by karyotype and hormone testing.
cards.q: What is androgen insensitivity syndrome, and how does it present?

cards.a: Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome. Management is explaining the diagnosis sensitively, removing testes after puberty because of malignancy risk, oestrogen replacement, and psychological support, with fertility counselling about donor eggs and surrogacy.
cards.q: A 16-year-old girl has primary amenorrhoea, normal breast development, no pubic hair, and a blind-ending vagina. What is the likely diagnosis and the key management?
A woman with mild endometriosis and infertility has open tubes and normal ovulation. Does laparoscopic treatment of the endometriosis improve her chance of pregnancy?
cards.a: Yes. In mild to moderate endometriosis, laparoscopic ablation or excision of visible lesions modestly improves pregnancy rates by reducing pelvic inflammation and restoring normal anatomy. If pregnancy does not follow within a reasonable time after surgery, move promptly to IVF rather than repeating surgery.

Sleep change, Interest loss, Guilt, Energy loss, Concentration problems, Appetite or weight change, Psychomotor change, and Suicidal thoughts. Remembering SIGECAPS helps you check all eight features instead of stopping at low mood alone, because Step 3 cases often hide depression behind poor sleep, fatigue, or poor concentration.
cards.q: What are the SIGECAPS symptoms of major depression?

cards.a: At least 5 of the 9 DSM symptoms for at least 2 weeks, and one must be depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure. The 2-week rule matters because a few bad days after a stressor is not major depression, while persistent symptoms with functional impairment are.
cards.q: How many symptoms and for how long are needed to diagnose major depressive disorder?

cards.a: Take a full history, confirm the diagnosis with a clinical interview, assess safety and suicide risk, and check for mania, psychosis, substance use, and medical causes such as hypothyroidism. A screening score alone never makes the diagnosis or starts treatment, because it cannot separate depression from bipolar disorder, grief, or a medical illness.
cards.q: What is the first step when a patient screens positive for depression on the PHQ-9?

cards.a: Check TSH, CBC, basic metabolic panel, and review medicines and substances, plus screen for anaemia, thyroid disease, and vitamin B12 deficiency when indicated. Treating depression without this workup risks missing hypothyroidism or another reversible cause that looks exactly like depression.
cards.q: A patient has low mood, poor sleep, and weight loss for 3 weeks. What medical workup should you do before calling it depression?

cards.a: Adjustment disorder starts within 3 months of a clear stressor, does not meet full major depression criteria, and resolves within 6 months after the stressor ends. Major depression meets full criteria and lasts at least 2 weeks regardless of a trigger, so do not downgrade a full syndrome to adjustment disorder just because a stressor is present.
cards.q: What is the difference between major depression and adjustment disorder with depressed mood?

cards.a: Major depression with psychotic features, usually mood-congruent delusions of guilt or nihilism. Treat with an antidepressant plus an antipsychotic, and consider ECT early because psychotic depression responds poorly to an antidepressant alone and carries high suicide risk.
cards.q: A depressed patient has delusions that they are guilty of terrible sins and are already dead. What is the diagnosis and next step?

cards.a: Melancholic depression is severe depression with loss of pleasure in almost everything, worse mood in the morning, early morning awakening, marked weight loss, and excessive guilt. It responds better to medication or ECT than to psychotherapy alone, so do not rely on talk therapy only for this severe subtype.
cards.q: What is melancholic depression and why does it matter for treatment?

cards.a: Atypical depression has mood that lifts briefly with good news, plus oversleeping, overeating or weight gain, heavy leaden limbs, and sensitivity to rejection. Monoamine oxidase inhibitors are classically most effective, but SSRIs are used first in practice because MAOIs carry dietary and drug interaction risks.
cards.q: What is atypical depression and which drug class is classically most effective?

cards.a: This fits atypical features, not laziness or simple overeating. Do not assume it is hypothyroidism alone or a character problem; confirm the full depression syndrome, check TSH, and treat the depression, because hypersomnia and hyperphagia are real depressive symptoms.
cards.q: A patient with depression has no energy, sleeps 12 hours a day, and has gained weight. What subtype is this and what should you avoid assuming?

cards.a: Catatonia is mutism, stupor, staring, refusal to eat or move, and waxy flexibility or posturing in a depressed patient. Give a lorazepam challenge first, because benzodiazepines often reverse catatonia quickly, and use ECT if lorazepam fails or the patient cannot eat or drink safely.
cards.q: What is catatonia in depression and what is the first treatment?

cards.a: No. Some pleasure does not rule out depression, especially in atypical depression where mood can lift briefly. Judge the overall pattern over 2 weeks, including sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, and function, rather than one pleasant moment.
cards.q: A depressed patient says they feel sad but still enjoy time with grandchildren. Does this rule out major depression?

cards.a: Ask how symptoms affect work, school, relationships, self-care, and daily function, and for how long. Normal sadness is brief and does not cause sustained impairment, while major depression causes persistent functional decline, which is what makes treatment necessary.
cards.q: What functional question best separates true depression from normal sadness on Step 3?

cards.a: Abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy for at least 7 days, or any length if hospitalisation is needed, plus at least 3 symptoms such as grandiosity, less need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, distractibility, increased goal-directed activity, and risky behaviour. The key Step 3 point is marked impairment, psychosis, or hospitalisation, which separates mania from hypomania.
cards.q: What defines a manic episode?

cards.a: Elevated or irritable mood with increased energy for at least 4 days with at least 3 manic symptoms, but no psychosis, no marked impairment, and no hospitalisation. If function is clearly impaired or psychosis appears, it is mania, not hypomania, and the diagnosis changes.
cards.q: What defines a hypomanic episode?

cards.a: Bipolar I requires at least one manic episode, while bipolar II requires at least one hypomanic episode plus at least one major depressive episode and never a full manic episode. A single manic episode makes it bipolar I even if depression dominates later, so always ask about past periods of high energy and little sleep.
cards.q: What is the difference between bipolar I and bipolar II disorder?

cards.a: Bipolar I disorder, because that week meets mania criteria. Do not keep calling it unipolar depression, because an antidepressant alone in bipolar disorder can trigger mania, so a mood stabiliser must be part of treatment.
cards.q: A patient has recurrent depression and one past week of feeling euphoric, sleeping 2 hours a night, and spending recklessly. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Bipolar II disorder, because the episode is hypomania, not mania, plus recurrent major depression. It still needs a mood stabiliser, because antidepressant monotherapy can cause a switch to hypomania or rapid cycling.
cards.q: A patient has recurrent depression and a 5-day period of high energy, fast talking, and little sleep, but kept working fine. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Because an antidepressant alone can trigger mania or hypomania in undiagnosed bipolar disorder. Always ask about past episodes of decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, grandiosity, and impulsive spending before prescribing, and add a mood stabiliser if bipolar disorder is present.
cards.q: Why must you ask about mania before starting an antidepressant for depression?

cards.a: Four or more mood episodes of mania, hypomania, or depression within 12 months. It is harder to treat and is often worsened by antidepressants, so the next step is to stop the antidepressant, optimise a mood stabiliser such as lithium or valproate, and treat thyroid disease if present.
cards.q: What is rapid cycling bipolar disorder?

cards.a: Start an antipsychotic such as olanzapine, risperidone, or haloperidol, often with lithium or valproate, and use a benzodiazepine for acute agitation. Do not give an antidepressant during mania, because it can worsen the episode, and hospitalise if the patient is unsafe or psychotic.
cards.q: A bipolar patient is currently manic, agitated, and psychotic. What is the first-line acute treatment?

cards.a: Use a mood stabiliser with antidepressant effect, such as lamotrigine or lithium, or quetiapine or lurasidone, which are approved for bipolar depression. Avoid antidepressant monotherapy, because it risks a switch to mania without preventing future depressive episodes.
cards.q: A bipolar patient is currently depressed. What is the best next step?

cards.a: Take it every day even when feeling well, keep fluid and salt intake steady, and get regular blood levels, kidney function, and thyroid checks. Stopping lithium suddenly greatly increases relapse risk, and dehydration or low salt can push levels into toxicity.
cards.q: What is the most important counselling point for a bipolar patient starting lithium?

cards.a: Explain that bipolar disorder is a lifelong relapsing illness and maintenance treatment prevents future mania and depression, then explore side effects and simplify the regimen if possible. Do not agree to stop everything, because abrupt discontinuation is a common trigger for relapse.
cards.q: A patient with bipolar disorder wants to stop all medicines because they feel well. What do you do?

cards.a: At least 2 years of many periods of hypomanic symptoms and depressive symptoms that never meet full criteria for mania, hypomania, or major depression. It is a milder but chronic bipolar spectrum illness, so treat with psychoeducation and a mood stabiliser if symptoms impair function, and watch for progression to bipolar I or II.
cards.q: What is cyclothymia?

cards.a: Hospitalise involuntarily if needed for safety, because mania with psychosis, refusal of treatment, and no sleep is unsafe in the community. Start an antipsychotic and a mood stabiliser in hospital, and do not send the patient home hoping sleep will return on its own.
cards.q: A manic patient has not slept for 3 nights, is grandiose, and refuses medicines. What is the next step?

cards.a: Mania is episodic, with mood symptoms dominating and psychosis that is usually mood-congruent and resolves between episodes, while schizophrenia has persistent psychosis with negative symptoms and functional decline between episodes. Always take a longitudinal history, because a single cross-section of psychosis can look the same in both.
cards.q: What is the difference between bipolar mania and schizophrenia on Step 3?

cards.a: Lithium side effects, likely nephrogenic diabetes insipidus causing polyuria and polydipsia, plus tremor. Check a lithium level, kidney function, and electrolytes, review fluid and salt intake and interacting drugs, and do not simply stop lithium abruptly without a plan, because relapse risk is high.
cards.q: A patient with bipolar disorder is stable on lithium but now has tremor, frequent urination, and thirst. What is the cause and next step?

cards.a: Depressed mood for most of the day, most days, for at least 2 years, with at least 2 of poor appetite or overeating, insomnia or hypersomnia, low energy, low self-esteem, poor concentration, and hopelessness. It is chronic low-grade depression, not just a bad month, so it needs long-term treatment, not reassurance alone.
cards.q: What is persistent depressive disorder?

cards.a: Dysthymia is the older name for the milder chronic form now included under persistent depressive disorder. The key point is duration of at least 2 years with persistent low mood, which separates it from a single major depressive episode.
cards.q: How does dysthymia relate to persistent depressive disorder?

cards.a: Persistent depressive disorder. Treat with an SSRI plus psychotherapy, because chronic depression responds best to combined treatment, and do not dismiss it as a personality trait just because it is long-standing.
cards.q: A patient has felt mildly depressed almost every day for 3 years but never had a full major depressive episode. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: A major depressive episode superimposed on persistent depressive disorder, so a patient with chronic low mood suddenly gets much worse. Treat the acute major episode actively with medication and psychotherapy, and continue maintenance treatment afterwards, because the underlying chronic depression remains.
cards.q: What is double depression?

cards.a: Persistent depressive disorder often starts in childhood or adolescence and can last decades, which is why it is easily mistaken for personality. Treat it actively with medication plus psychotherapy, because long duration does not mean untreatable.
cards.q: Why is persistent depressive disorder often missed or mistaken for personality?

cards.a: Yes, persistent depressive disorder can occur in children and adolescents, with a duration of at least 1 year instead of 2 years and irritability often replacing depressed mood. Do not dismiss chronic irritability and low mood in a teenager as normal adolescence without a full assessment.
cards.q: Can persistent depressive disorder occur in children, and how is the duration different?

cards.a: Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plans, intent, access to means, prior attempts, and protective factors, in a calm non-judgmental way. Asking does not plant the idea; it is the only reliable way to find risk, and it opens the door to safety planning.
cards.q: What is the first step in suicide risk assessment for a depressed patient?

cards.a: Active suicidal intent with a specific plan, access to lethal means, prior attempt, recent loss or stressor, substance use, psychosis, agitation, and poor social support. The strongest single predictor is a prior suicide attempt, so always ask about it directly.
cards.q: What factors increase suicide risk the most?

cards.a: Admit the patient, preferably voluntarily, keep them under close observation, remove access to means, involve family, and start treatment urgently. Do not send a patient with active intent and a plan home with a follow-up appointment, because risk is immediate.
cards.q: A depressed patient says they plan to take an overdose tonight and have the pills at home. What is the next step?

cards.a: Make a safety plan together: recognise warning signs, use coping strategies, contact supportive people, remove or restrict lethal means, and list crisis numbers and emergency services. A written plan plus means restriction is more useful than a no-suicide contract alone, which has no evidence of preventing suicide.
cards.q: What is a safety plan and why is it better than a no-suicide contract?

cards.a: Ask about access to firearms, medicines, and other lethal means, and involve family to lock up or remove them. Means restriction saves lives because many attempts are impulsive, and a less lethal method gives time for rescue and treatment.
cards.q: Why is asking about access to means part of suicide assessment?

cards.a: Patients with passive thoughts but no plan or intent, good insight, strong support, and willingness to follow up can often be managed as outpatients with close follow-up, safety planning, and family involvement. The decision depends on the full risk picture, not on the word passive alone.
cards.q: When can a patient with passive suicidal thoughts be managed as an outpatient?

cards.a: Suicidal thoughts are common in severe depression and do not by themselves prove the patient will act, but they always need a full risk assessment. Never dismiss them as attention-seeking, and always assess plan, intent, means, and protective factors before deciding on disposition.
cards.q: A patient says life is not worth living but denies any plan. How should you interpret this?

cards.a: Involuntary hospitalisation is justified when the patient is an imminent danger to themselves and refuses voluntary admission. Document capacity, risk, and least restrictive alternatives tried, and involve the team and family, because safety overrides autonomy when capacity is impaired by severe illness.
cards.q: When is involuntary hospitalisation appropriate for a suicidal patient?

cards.a: Ask about command hallucinations, delusions, severe agitation, and loss of impulse control, because psychotic depression carries very high suicide risk. Treat urgently with an antidepressant plus an antipsychotic or ECT, and hospitalise if risk is high.
cards.q: Why does psychotic depression carry a higher suicide risk?

cards.a: Suicide risk can rise early in antidepressant treatment because energy and motivation return before mood fully lifts, giving the patient the energy to act on pre-existing thoughts. Monitor closely in the first weeks, involve family, and warn them about worsening agitation or new suicidal thoughts.
cards.q: Why is suicide risk highest in the first few weeks after starting an antidepressant?

cards.a: Ask about recent loss, relationship breakdown, job loss, financial stress, chronic pain, substance use, and access to means, because acute stressors often trigger an attempt in a vulnerable patient. Addressing the stressor and involving support is part of treatment, not separate from it.
cards.q: What acute stressors should you ask about in a suicidal patient?

cards.a: Ask about any prior attempt, how lethal it was, whether help was sought, and what has changed since. A prior attempt is the strongest predictor of a future attempt, so a history of one attempt raises risk even if the patient now seems calm.
cards.q: Why is a history of prior suicide attempt the most important question?

cards.a: Start an antidepressant and psychotherapy together, arrange close follow-up within days, involve family, and give crisis resources. Do not wait for psychotherapy alone in moderate to severe depression, because combined treatment works faster and reduces relapse.
cards.q: A patient with moderate depression has fleeting suicidal thoughts but no plan or intent. What is the management?

cards.a: Assess risk, hospitalise if needed, treat the underlying depression, and arrange close psychiatric follow-up after discharge, because the weeks after discharge are high risk. Do not discharge without a safety plan, means restriction, and a definite follow-up appointment.
cards.q: What is the management after a suicide attempt?

cards.a: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as sertraline, escitalopram, and fluoxetine are first-line for major depression because they are effective, well tolerated, and safe in overdose compared with older drugs. Start low, warn about a 4 to 6 week delay, and monitor for agitation and suicidal thoughts early on.
cards.q: What is the first-line drug class for major depression and why?

cards.a: Serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors such as venlafaxine and duloxetine help depression and also help chronic pain and neuropathic pain. They are useful when depression coexists with pain, but watch for raised blood pressure with venlafaxine and for a worse discontinuation syndrome.
cards.q: When are SNRIs preferred over SSRIs for depression?

cards.a: Bupropion blocks reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine, so it causes little sexual dysfunction or weight gain and can help fatigue. Avoid it in seizure disorder and eating disorders, because it lowers the seizure threshold, and avoid it in severe anxiety because it can worsen agitation.
cards.q: What is bupropion best for in depression, and when must you avoid it?

cards.a: Mirtazapine blocks alpha-2 and certain serotonin receptors, causing sedation and increased appetite. It is useful for a depressed patient with insomnia and weight loss, but avoid it when weight gain is a problem, because sedation and appetite increase are common.
cards.q: What is mirtazapine best for in depression?

cards.a: Sexual dysfunction, weight gain, and gastrointestinal upset are common, with hyponatraemia and increased bleeding risk in older adults. Counsel patients before starting, because sexual side effects are a common reason for stopping, and switching to bupropion or adding bupropion can help.
cards.q: What are the most common side effects of SSRIs?

cards.a: Serotonin syndrome is agitation, confusion, sweating, tremor, muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, and clonus from excess serotonin, often after combining an SSRI with another serotonergic drug. Stop all serotonergic drugs, give supportive care and benzodiazepines, and cool the patient, because it can be fatal if missed.
cards.q: What is serotonin syndrome and how is it managed?

cards.a: Wait at least 5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine before starting an MAOI, and at least 2 weeks for other SSRIs, because fluoxetine has a very long half-life. Starting too soon risks serotonin syndrome, so always check the washout period on Step 3.
cards.q: How long must you wait after stopping fluoxetine before starting an MAOI?

cards.a: Tricyclic antidepressants such as amitriptyline cause dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, orthostatic hypotension, sedation, and weight gain, and are lethal in overdose due to cardiac conduction block and seizures. They are second-line now, reserved for depression with chronic pain or insomnia when SSRIs have failed.
cards.q: What are the side effects of tricyclic antidepressants and why are they second-line?
