cards.a: Amitriptyline and nortriptyline are used for neuropathic pain, migraine prevention, and fibromyalgia, even when depression is not the main problem. Nortriptyline is better tolerated than amitriptyline in older adults, but still needs an ECG and caution about falls.
cards.q: When are tricyclic antidepressants still useful despite their side effects?

cards.a: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors such as phenelzine require a tyramine-free diet to avoid hypertensive crisis from aged cheese, cured meats, and fermented foods, and interact dangerously with many drugs. They are reserved for atypical or treatment-resistant depression, because safer drugs are tried first.
cards.q: What dietary restriction is needed with MAOIs and why?

cards.a: SSRIs can cause hyponatraemia from SIADH, especially in older adults, with confusion, falls, and seizures. Check sodium if an older patient becomes confused or lethargic after starting an SSRI, and stop the drug if hyponatraemia is severe.
cards.q: An older patient becomes confused 2 weeks after starting sertraline. What is the likely cause?

cards.a: SSRIs inhibit platelets, so they increase bleeding risk, especially with NSAIDs, aspirin, or anticoagulants. Ask about bruising and bleeding, and be cautious in patients on warfarin or with a bleeding disorder, because the combination raises gastrointestinal bleeding risk.
cards.q: Why do SSRIs increase bleeding risk?

cards.a: Fluoxetine has the longest half-life of the SSRIs, so it causes the least discontinuation syndrome but takes longest to wash out. Paroxetine has the shortest half-life and the worst discontinuation symptoms, so never stop it abruptly.
cards.q: Which SSRI has the longest half-life and why does it matter?

cards.a: Sertraline is usually preferred in pregnancy and breastfeeding because it has the most safety data and low transfer into breast milk. Paroxetine is avoided in pregnancy when possible because of a possible association with cardiac defects, so check the drug choice carefully in this setting.
cards.q: Which SSRI is preferred in pregnancy and which is avoided?

cards.a: Continue for at least 6 to 12 months after remission of a first episode, then taper slowly. Stopping too early is the commonest cause of relapse, so do not stop at 6 weeks just because the patient feels better.
cards.q: How long should an antidepressant be continued after a first episode of depression?

cards.a: Continue maintenance treatment for at least 2 years, often indefinitely, after 3 or more episodes, or after a severe episode with suicidality or psychosis. Recurrent depression is a relapsing illness, so long-term prevention matters more than short-term symptom relief.
cards.q: How long should maintenance antidepressant treatment last after recurrent depression?

cards.a: Check adherence, dose, duration, substance use, thyroid function, and whether the diagnosis is really bipolar depression or a medical cause. Do not call it treatment-resistant until an adequate dose has been taken for at least 6 weeks with good adherence.
cards.q: A patient has no improvement after 3 weeks on a low dose of sertraline. What should you check before switching drugs?

cards.a: Switch to another antidepressant, often from a different class, or add psychotherapy. Augmentation with bupropion, an atypical antipsychotic, or lithium is used when switching alone has failed, so the next step depends on what has already been tried.
cards.q: What is the next step when a first SSRI fails after an adequate trial?

cards.a: Cognitive behavioural therapy helps patients recognise and change negative thought patterns and is effective for mild to moderate depression. It works best combined with medication in moderate to severe depression, because drugs alone do not teach coping skills.
cards.q: What is cognitive behavioural therapy and when is it used for depression?

cards.a: Lithium is the gold-standard mood stabiliser for bipolar disorder, especially for preventing mania and reducing suicide risk. It has a narrow therapeutic range, so levels, kidney function, and thyroid function must be monitored regularly.
cards.q: What is lithium used for in bipolar disorder and why does it need monitoring?

cards.a: Lithium toxicity causes coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, vomiting, diarrhoea, and polyuria, and can progress to seizures and coma. Stop lithium, give intravenous fluids, check levels and kidney function, and consider dialysis in severe cases, because toxicity is worsened by dehydration and kidney failure.
cards.q: What are the signs of lithium toxicity and how is it managed?

cards.a: Thiazide diuretics, NSAIDs, and ACE inhibitors raise lithium levels by reducing its clearance, while dehydration, low salt intake, and vomiting do the same. Always review new medicines in a patient on lithium, because a routine prescription can cause toxicity.
cards.q: Which drugs raise lithium levels?

cards.a: Lithium can cause hypothyroidism and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, leading to polyuria, polydipsia, and weight gain. Check TSH and kidney function before starting and regularly afterwards, and treat hypothyroidism with levothyroxine rather than stopping lithium abruptly if the patient is stable.
cards.q: What are the long-term side effects of lithium on thyroid and kidney?

cards.a: Valproate is effective for acute mania and maintenance, especially in rapid cycling and mixed episodes. It is teratogenic, causing neural tube defects, so avoid it in women of childbearing age unless no alternative works and reliable contraception is in place.
cards.q: What is valproate used for and why must it be avoided in pregnancy?

cards.a: Valproate can cause weight gain, hair loss, tremor, liver injury, pancreatitis, and polycystic ovary syndrome. Check liver function and platelets, warn about abdominal pain, and stop the drug urgently if pancreatitis is suspected.
cards.q: What are the main side effects of valproate?

cards.a: Lamotrigine is most useful for preventing depressive episodes in bipolar disorder, not for acute mania. It is started very slowly because a fast increase raises the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome, a severe skin reaction.
cards.q: What is lamotrigine best for in bipolar disorder?

cards.a: A serious rash, blistering, or mucosal involvement after starting lamotrigine, most often from too rapid dose escalation or combining it with valproate, which raises lamotrigine levels. Stop lamotrigine immediately and seek urgent dermatology care, because Stevens-Johnson syndrome can be fatal.
cards.q: What is the most dangerous side effect of lamotrigine and when does it occur?

cards.a: Carbamazepine is an alternative mood stabiliser for acute mania and maintenance, especially when lithium and valproate fail. It induces its own metabolism, interacts with many drugs, and can cause hyponatraemia, rash, and blood dyscrasias, so check blood counts and sodium.
cards.q: When is carbamazepine used for bipolar disorder and what must you monitor?

cards.a: Carbamazepine can cause agranulocytosis and aplastic anaemia, so check a baseline CBC and warn the patient to report fever, sore throat, or unusual bruising urgently. It is also teratogenic, so avoid it in pregnancy when possible.
cards.q: What blood problem can carbamazepine cause?

cards.a: Second-generation antipsychotics such as quetiapine, olanzapine, and lurasidone are used for acute mania, bipolar depression, and maintenance. They can cause weight gain, diabetes, and dyslipidaemia, so monitor weight, glucose, and lipids regularly.
cards.q: What role do second-generation antipsychotics play in bipolar disorder?

cards.a: Monitor weight, blood pressure, fasting glucose, lipids, and movement disorders, because metabolic syndrome is the main long-term harm of second-generation antipsychotics. Early monitoring allows a switch to a lower-risk drug before diabetes or heart disease develops.
cards.q: What metabolic monitoring is needed on a second-generation antipsychotic?

cards.a: Check a lithium level 5 to 7 days after starting or changing the dose, then every 3 to 6 months once stable, plus kidney function, electrolytes, calcium, and TSH. Levels are usually drawn 12 hours after the last dose, because a random level is hard to interpret.
cards.q: How often should lithium levels and labs be checked?

cards.a: Valproate levels, liver function, platelets, and pregnancy testing in women of childbearing age. Baseline labs matter because valproate can cause liver injury and thrombocytopenia, and pregnancy must be excluded before starting.
cards.q: What monitoring is needed before and during valproate treatment?

cards.a: Because valproate inhibits the metabolism of lamotrigine, doubling its level and raising the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome. When both are used together, lamotrigine must be started at a much lower dose and increased very slowly.
cards.q: Why must lamotrigine be started at a lower dose when combined with valproate?

cards.a: A mood stabiliser alone is preferred for maintenance, because adding an antidepressant long-term raises the risk of a switch to mania and rapid cycling. If an antidepressant is used for bipolar depression, it should be short-term and always with a mood stabiliser, then tapered off.
cards.q: Should a bipolar patient stay on an antidepressant long-term?

cards.a: Lithium reduces suicide risk in bipolar disorder more than other mood stabilisers, which is one reason it is preferred when suicide risk is high. This protective effect is separate from its effect on mood episodes, so do not switch away from lithium lightly in a high-risk patient.
cards.q: Which mood stabiliser best reduces suicide risk in bipolar disorder?

cards.a: Electroconvulsive therapy is indicated for severe depression with psychosis, catatonia, severe suicidality, refusal to eat, or failure of multiple drug trials. It is the fastest effective treatment for life-threatening depression, so do not delay referral when the patient is deteriorating.
cards.q: What are the main indications for ECT in depression?

cards.a: ECT works by inducing a brief controlled seizure under anaesthesia, which rapidly improves severe depression. It is not a punishment and does not cause brain damage in the way patients fear, so explain the procedure, anaesthesia, and temporary memory effects clearly before consent.
cards.q: How does ECT work and what should you tell a fearful patient?

cards.a: Temporary confusion and short-term memory loss, especially for events around the treatment, plus headache and muscle aches. Memory usually improves over weeks, and bilateral ECT causes more memory problems than unilateral ECT, so technique is chosen to balance speed and side effects.
cards.q: What are the main side effects of ECT?

cards.a: ECT is relatively safe in pregnancy and is often used for severe depression or psychosis in pregnancy when drugs have failed or are unsafe. It avoids fetal drug exposure, but needs obstetric and anaesthetic involvement, because airway and monitoring needs change in pregnancy.
cards.q: Is ECT safe in pregnancy?

cards.a: ECT is not first-line for mild to moderate depression, because drugs and psychotherapy are safer and effective for most patients. Reserve it for severe, psychotic, catatonic, or treatment-resistant depression, or when rapid improvement is needed for safety.
cards.q: Why is ECT not first-line for mild depression?

cards.a: ECT is given as a course, usually 6 to 12 sessions over 2 to 4 weeks, and maintenance medication is started afterwards to prevent relapse. A single session is not enough, because relapse is common without follow-up treatment.
cards.q: How many ECT sessions are usually given and what follows them?

cards.a: Patients with a pacemaker, recent stroke, raised intracranial pressure, or unstable heart disease need careful assessment, but there are few absolute contraindications to ECT. Anaesthetic and medical review is essential, because the seizure causes a brief rise in blood pressure and heart rate.
cards.q: What medical conditions need caution before ECT?

cards.a: Treatment-resistant depression is failure to respond to at least 2 adequate antidepressant trials of different classes at adequate dose and duration. Confirm adherence, dose, duration, and diagnosis first, because apparent resistance is often inadequate treatment or undiagnosed bipolar disorder.
cards.q: What defines treatment-resistant depression?

cards.a: Switch to a different class, add psychotherapy, or augment with lithium, an atypical antipsychotic such as aripiprazole or quetiapine, or bupropion. Augmentation is preferred when there was a partial response, because keeping some benefit is better than starting from scratch.
cards.q: What is the next step after two failed antidepressant trials?

cards.a: Ketamine and its nasal form esketamine can rapidly reduce severe treatment-resistant depression and suicidal thoughts, often within hours to days. They are given under supervision because of dissociation, blood pressure rise, and abuse potential, so they are not first-line or take-home drugs.
cards.q: What is the role of ketamine in treatment-resistant depression?

cards.a: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation uses magnetic pulses to stimulate the prefrontal cortex and can help treatment-resistant depression without anaesthesia or memory loss. It is less effective than ECT for severe psychotic depression, so ECT remains preferred when rapid or stronger treatment is needed.
cards.q: What is transcranial magnetic stimulation and when is it used?

cards.a: Augmentation means adding a second drug to boost the effect of the antidepressant, while switching means stopping it and starting a different one. Augment when there was a partial response, and switch when there was no response or intolerable side effects.
cards.q: What is the difference between augmentation and switching in depression?

cards.a: Check thyroid function, vitamin B12, substance use, sleep apnoea, and medical illness, because all can mimic or worsen treatment-resistant depression. Treating an underlying cause can restore response to antidepressants.
cards.q: What medical causes should you check in treatment-resistant depression?

cards.a: Refer to psychiatry urgently for ECT, ketamine, or a specialist regimen, and do not keep cycling through SSRIs alone. Specialist input is the next step when standard augmentation has failed, because the risk of suicide rises with each failed trial.
cards.q: When should treatment-resistant depression be referred to psychiatry?

cards.a: Sertraline is usually the first choice in pregnancy because it has the most reassuring safety data. Untreated depression in pregnancy is itself harmful, causing poor antenatal care, substance use, and preterm birth, so treatment is usually continued rather than stopped.
cards.q: Which antidepressant is preferred in pregnancy and why continue treatment?

cards.a: Paroxetine is avoided in early pregnancy when possible because of a possible association with cardiac defects, and valproate must be avoided because of neural tube defects. If a patient is already stable on paroxetine, discuss risks and benefits rather than stopping abruptly.
cards.q: Which psychiatric drugs must be avoided in pregnancy?

cards.a: Postpartum depression is major depression starting during pregnancy or within 4 weeks after delivery, though in practice it is screened for throughout the first year. It is more severe and persistent than the baby blues, with impaired bonding and functioning, so it needs active treatment.
cards.q: What is postpartum depression and how is it different from the baby blues?

cards.a: The baby blues are mild mood swings, tearfulness, and anxiety in the first few days after delivery, resolving within 2 weeks without treatment. Postpartum depression lasts longer, is more severe, and impairs function, so it needs treatment and follow-up.
cards.q: What are the baby blues?

cards.a: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency with delusions, hallucinations, confusion, and disorganised behaviour, usually within 2 weeks of delivery. Admit the patient urgently, do not leave the baby unsupervised with her, and treat with an antipsychotic and a mood stabiliser, often with ECT.
cards.q: What is postpartum psychosis and why is it an emergency?

cards.a: Screen all women for postpartum depression with a validated tool such as the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale at postpartum visits. Early screening matters because many women do not volunteer symptoms, and untreated depression harms both mother and baby.
cards.q: How and when should postpartum depression be screened for?

cards.a: Brexanolone is an intravenous neurosteroid given over 60 hours for moderate to severe postpartum depression, acting rapidly on GABA receptors. It requires monitoring for sedation and loss of consciousness, so it is given in a supervised setting, not at home.
cards.q: What is brexanolone used for?

cards.a: Continue the antidepressant that worked in pregnancy into the postpartum period, and counsel that most SSRIs, especially sertraline, have low transfer into breast milk. Stopping treatment after delivery raises relapse risk, so do not stop a working drug without a plan.
cards.q: Should antidepressants be continued after delivery and during breastfeeding?

cards.a: Lithium is teratogenic in the first trimester, with a small increased risk of Ebstein anomaly, so it is usually stopped or minimised then, but it can be restarted later in pregnancy because relapse risk is high. This is a specialist decision, with fetal echocardiography and close monitoring.
cards.q: What is the risk of lithium in pregnancy?

cards.a: Seasonal affective disorder is recurrent major depression with a seasonal pattern, usually starting in autumn or winter and remitting in spring. Light therapy, SSRIs, and bupropion are effective, because reduced daylight is thought to disrupt circadian rhythm and serotonin.
cards.q: What is seasonal affective disorder?

cards.a: Bright light therapy, usually 10,000 lux for 30 minutes each morning, is first-line for seasonal affective disorder. It is safe and fast, but can trigger mania in bipolar disorder, so screen for bipolar disorder first.
cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for seasonal affective disorder?

cards.a: Bupropion XL is approved for prevention of seasonal affective disorder and can be started in autumn before symptoms begin. It is useful because it does not cause the sexual dysfunction or weight gain seen with SSRIs.
cards.q: Which drug can prevent seasonal affective disorder?

cards.a: Normal bereavement is intense grief with waves of sadness, preserved self-esteem, and a sense of loss focused on the deceased, while depression is persistent low mood, worthlessness, and inability to function. Grief comes in waves and improves over time, while depression is constant and disabling.
cards.q: How do you distinguish normal bereavement from major depression?

cards.a: Persistent guilt, worthlessness, psychomotor slowing, suicidal thoughts, and inability to function for more than 2 months after a loss suggest major depression, not just grief. Treat it as depression, because bereavement does not protect against depression.
cards.q: When does grief after a loss become major depression?

cards.a: Support, counselling, and time are usually enough for uncomplicated grief, without antidepressants. Start treatment when full major depression criteria are met or when grief is prolonged and disabling, because normal grief is not a drug deficiency.
cards.q: When should bereavement be treated with antidepressants?

cards.a: Corticosteroids can cause depression, mania, psychosis, and insomnia, often within days of starting a high dose. Reduce the dose if possible, treat the mood symptoms, and warn patients before starting steroids, because the effect is dose-related and reversible on stopping.
cards.q: Which mood symptoms can corticosteroids cause?

cards.a: Interferon alpha can cause severe depression and suicidal thoughts, so screen for depression before and during treatment. Stop interferon or add an antidepressant and psychiatric input if depression develops, because it can be life-threatening.
cards.q: Why must you screen for depression in a patient starting interferon?

cards.a: Isotretinoin has been associated with depression and suicidal thoughts, so screen for mood symptoms before and during treatment. The association is debated, but on Step 3 the safe answer is to monitor mood, involve psychiatry if symptoms appear, and stop the drug if severe depression develops.
cards.q: What mood risk is associated with isotretinoin?

cards.a: Reserpine, methyldopa, and beta blockers have been associated with depression, as have some hormonal contraceptives. Review the drug list in any new depression, because stopping the culprit drug can resolve symptoms without an antidepressant.
cards.q: Which antihypertensive drugs can cause depression?

cards.a: Alcohol and cannabis can cause or worsen depression, and withdrawal from stimulants such as cocaine can cause a crash with low mood and suicidal thoughts. Treat the substance use alongside the depression, because the mood disorder will not resolve while use continues.
cards.q: How do substances cause mood symptoms?

cards.a: Thyroid disease, Cushing syndrome, Parkinson disease, stroke, and multiple sclerosis can all cause depression. Always consider a medical cause in new depression, especially in older adults or when neurological signs are present, because treating the underlying disease improves mood.
cards.q: Which medical illnesses commonly cause depression?

cards.a: Levodopa and other dopaminergic drugs can cause mania or psychosis in Parkinson disease, while steroids and stimulants can also trigger mania. Reduce or stop the culprit drug if possible and involve psychiatry, because the mania may resolve without a mood stabiliser.
cards.q: Which drugs can trigger mania?

cards.a: In drug-induced depression, stop or reduce the culprit drug if possible, monitor mood, and only add an antidepressant if symptoms persist after stopping. Do not immediately label it as major depression and start lifelong treatment, because the cause is reversible.
cards.q: What is the management of drug-induced depression?

cards.a: Excessive, hard-to-control worry about many everyday things (work, health, money, family) on most days for at least 6 months, plus restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension or poor sleep. It is worry that is out of proportion and interferes with life, not just normal stress before an exam.
cards.q: What is the core feature of generalised anxiety disorder (GAD)?

cards.a: Generalised anxiety disorder. The key is chronic excessive worry lasting 6 months or more with somatic symptoms. Panic disorder needs recurrent unexpected panic attacks, and depression needs low mood or loss of interest as the main feature.
cards.q: A patient worries constantly for 7 months, has muscle tension, fatigue and trouble sleeping, but no panic attacks and no low mood. What is the most likely diagnosis?

cards.a: An SSRI such as escitalopram, paroxetine or sertraline, or an SNRI such as venlafaxine or duloxetine. They reduce worry over weeks and are safe for long-term use. Start low, warn that benefit takes 4 to 6 weeks, and that anxiety can briefly worsen at the start.
cards.q: What is the first-line drug treatment for GAD?

cards.a: Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), especially worry-focused CBT with cognitive restructuring and worry-time techniques. It teaches patients to challenge catastrophic thoughts and tolerate uncertainty. CBT plus an SSRI works better than either alone in moderate to severe GAD.
cards.q: What is the first-line non-drug treatment for GAD?

cards.a: Buspirone is a 5-HT1A partial agonist that reduces worry without sedation, dependence or withdrawal, so it is good for chronic GAD, especially in patients with a substance-use history. Its limitation is slow onset (1 to 2 weeks or more) and it does not help panic attacks or acute anxiety, so it is not a rescue drug.
cards.q: Why is buspirone useful in GAD, and what is its main limitation?

cards.a: Reassure and continue the SSRI at the current dose, explaining that SSRIs take 4 to 6 weeks for full effect in anxiety. Do not stop it or switch yet. Check adherence, side effects and sleep, and add CBT. Only consider a dose increase or switch after an adequate trial of 6 to 8 weeks.
cards.q: A patient with GAD has been on sertraline for 2 weeks and says it is not working. What is the next best step?

cards.a: Benzodiazepines such as alprazolam and lorazepam. They work fast but cause sedation, tolerance, dependence and withdrawal, and they blunt the learning that makes CBT work. Reserve them for short-term crisis use only, never as the main long-term plan.
cards.q: Which drugs should be avoided as long-term treatment for GAD and why?

cards.a: Explain that the SSRI treats the worry driving the tension and insomnia, but sleep hygiene and relaxation training help too, and that improvement is gradual. Avoid prescribing a nightly benzodiazepine for sleep, because dependence develops quickly and it worsens daytime anxiety when it wears off.
cards.q: A patient with GAD also has chronic muscle tension and insomnia. Which SSRI-related counselling point matters most?

cards.a: Hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, arrhythmia, hypoglycaemia, asthma or COPD exacerbation, and substance use or withdrawal (caffeine, cocaine, alcohol withdrawal). Check TSH, vitals, ECG if palpitations, and a substance history, because these mimics cause the same restlessness, palpitations and sweating.
cards.q: What medical conditions must be ruled out before diagnosing GAD?

cards.a: Blood pressure, because venlafaxine (an SNRI) can raise blood pressure in a dose-dependent way, plus nausea, sweating, insomnia and sexual side effects. Also warn about a discontinuation syndrome (dizziness, electric-shock sensations) if doses are missed or stopped abruptly, so taper slowly.
cards.q: A patient with GAD is started on venlafaxine. What must be monitored?

cards.a: Pregabalin reduces anxiety quickly and helps somatic symptoms, and it has no SSRI sexual side effects. It is avoided or used cautiously in patients with a substance-use history because it can be misused, and it causes sedation, dizziness and weight gain.
cards.q: Why is pregabalin sometimes used in GAD, and when is it avoided?

cards.a: Continue for at least 12 months after remission, then taper slowly if the patient is stable, because stopping early causes relapse in most patients. Longer treatment is needed if anxiety was severe, recurrent, or there are ongoing stressors. CBT skills help prevent relapse after stopping.
cards.q: A patient with GAD improves on escitalopram. How long should treatment continue?

cards.a: A sudden surge of intense fear that peaks within minutes, with at least 4 of: palpitations, sweating, shaking, shortness of breath, choking feeling, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, chills or hot flushes, numbness, derealisation, fear of losing control or fear of dying. It is a symptom, not a diagnosis by itself.
cards.q: What defines a panic attack?

cards.a: A panic attack is a single episode. Panic disorder needs recurrent unexpected panic attacks plus at least 1 month of persistent worry about more attacks, or maladaptive behaviour to avoid them (avoiding places, carrying water or medication). Expected attacks only in feared situations point to a phobia or social anxiety instead.
cards.q: What is the difference between a panic attack and panic disorder?

cards.a: Panic disorder with agoraphobia. The unexpected attacks plus a month of worry and avoidance of places where escape might be hard or help unavailable define it. Agoraphobia is the avoidance, not the attacks themselves.
cards.q: A patient has recurrent unexpected panic attacks and now avoids driving and shopping for fear of another attack. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Rule out a medical emergency first: ECG, troponin, vitals, oxygen saturation and glucose. Panic attacks mimic myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism and arrhythmia, and a first panic-like presentation must never be assumed to be anxiety until dangerous causes are excluded.
cards.q: A patient arrives in the emergency department with chest pain, palpitations and shortness of breath, convinced they are dying. What is the first step?

cards.a: An SSRI such as sertraline, paroxetine or fluoxetine, plus CBT with interoceptive exposure (deliberately inducing feared sensations like rapid breathing to learn they are harmless). SSRIs prevent attacks over weeks; CBT stops the fear-of-fear cycle and avoidance.
cards.q: What is the first-line long-term treatment for panic disorder?

cards.a: They stop an attack fast but cause dependence, tolerance and withdrawal, and withdrawal itself triggers panic. They also prevent the patient learning through exposure that the sensations are safe, so CBT works less well. Use only very short-term while an SSRI takes effect, if at all.
cards.q: Why are benzodiazepines not first-line for panic disorder despite working quickly?

cards.a: Continue the drug and reassure: SSRIs can briefly increase anxiety and jitteriness in the first 1 to 2 weeks before they help. Start at a low dose and increase slowly. Only stop if there is severe agitation, suicidal thoughts or intolerable side effects.
cards.q: A patient with panic disorder is started on paroxetine and reports worse anxiety in week 1. What do you do?

cards.a: Deliberately creating the feared bodily sensations in a safe setting, for example spinning in a chair to cause dizziness or breathing fast to cause tingling. It works because the patient learns the sensations are uncomfortable but not dangerous, breaking the cycle where a normal sensation is misread as a catastrophe.
cards.q: What is interoceptive exposure, and why does it work in panic disorder?

cards.a: Do not breathe into a paper bag. It can cause dangerous low oxygen and high carbon dioxide, especially if the cause is actually asthma, pulmonary embolism or cardiac disease. Instead, slow breathing, grounding, and reminding themselves the attack peaks in minutes and passes.
cards.q: A patient with panic disorder hyperventilates during an attack. What should you advise them NOT to do?

cards.a: Sertraline or paroxetine are commonly used. Start low (for example half the usual depression dose) because panic patients are very sensitive to the early activating side effects of SSRIs, and a full dose can trigger more anxiety and make them stop the drug.
cards.q: Which SSRI is often preferred in panic disorder and why is the starting dose low?

cards.a: Treat both together: explain alcohol gives brief relief but causes rebound anxiety and withdrawal panic the next day, worsening the disorder. Offer an SSRI plus CBT, and address the alcohol use with counselling and support, because panic will not remit while daily alcohol use continues.
cards.q: A patient with panic disorder also drinks alcohol daily to calm the attacks. What is the management priority?

cards.a: Panic attacks that wake the patient from sleep with palpitations, sweating and fear of dying, without a dream beforehand. Nightmares occur during REM sleep with a remembered frightening dream and the fear fades on waking, while nocturnal panic wakes the patient suddenly in non-REM sleep with full panic symptoms.
cards.q: What is nocturnal panic, and how is it distinguished from nightmares?

cards.a: CBT first, because it has no drug risk to the fetus and is highly effective for panic. If medication is needed, sertraline is usually preferred among SSRIs as it has the most pregnancy safety data. Avoid benzodiazepines, especially in the first trimester and near delivery, because of sedation and neonatal withdrawal.
cards.q: A patient with panic disorder is pregnant. Which treatment is preferred?

cards.a: Depression and agoraphobia, plus alcohol use disorder. Comorbid depression raises suicide risk and makes panic harder to treat, so screen every panic patient for low mood, suicidal thoughts and substance use, and treat both conditions, usually with the same SSRI.
cards.q: What is the most common comorbidity of panic disorder, and why does it matter?

cards.a: Fear of being judged, embarrassed or humiliated in social or performance situations, such as speaking, eating in public or meeting strangers. The patient fears others will notice their anxiety (blushing, shaking, sweating) and think badly of them, so they avoid or endure situations with intense distress.
cards.q: What is the core fear in social anxiety disorder?

cards.a: Shyness is mild discomfort that fades and does not stop a person living their life. Social anxiety disorder is persistent, intense fear lasting 6 months or more that causes avoidance, missed school or work, and real functional impairment, with physical symptoms such as blushing, tremor and nausea.
cards.q: How is social anxiety disorder distinguished from normal shyness?

cards.a: An SSRI such as sertraline, paroxetine or escitalopram, or the SNRI venlafaxine, plus CBT with exposure to feared social situations. Medication reduces the physical anxiety, and CBT changes the belief that others are judging them and builds social skills through graded practice.
cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for generalised social anxiety disorder?

cards.a: A beta-blocker such as propranolol taken 30 to 60 minutes before the performance. It blocks the physical symptoms (tremor, palpitations, sweating) without sedation. This is performance-only social anxiety; daily SSRIs are not needed when the fear is limited to one situation.
cards.q: A medical student has severe anxiety only before giving presentations, with shaking hands and a racing heart, but is fine socially otherwise. What is the best treatment?

cards.a: Reassurance and avoidance keep the false belief alive that social situations are dangerous. Graded exposure (starting with low-fear situations and building up) plus dropping safety behaviours like avoiding eye contact teaches the brain the feared judgment does not happen, which is what produces lasting improvement.
cards.q: Why is CBT with exposure the key treatment for social anxiety, not reassurance alone?

cards.a: Venlafaxine (an SNRI) is an alternative first-line option when SSRIs fail or are not tolerated. It works similarly but can raise blood pressure and causes a worse discontinuation syndrome, so monitor blood pressure and taper slowly.
cards.q: A patient with social anxiety does not improve on sertraline. What is an alternative first-line drug?

cards.a: Propranolol is contraindicated in asthma because beta-blockade can trigger bronchospasm, and it is also avoided in bradycardia, heart block and decompensated heart failure. In an asthmatic patient, use CBT and relaxation techniques instead, and treat the anxiety with an SSRI if it is generalised.
cards.q: A patient with asthma and performance anxiety asks for propranolol. What is the problem?

cards.a: Selective mutism: the child speaks normally at home but consistently fails to speak in specific social situations such as school, despite being able to speak. It is an anxiety disorder, not defiance or a speech problem, and it is treated with CBT, graded exposure and sometimes an SSRI.
cards.q: A 7-year-old speaks freely at home but has not spoken a word at school for 6 months. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Social anxiety disorder. Asking a patient to have a drink before a social event is a red flag: alcohol is being used as a safety behaviour and self-medication, which maintains the anxiety and risks dependence. Treat the social anxiety with CBT and an SSRI, and address the alcohol use.
cards.q: A patient drinks two glasses of wine before every work meeting to cope with fear of being judged. What does this suggest?

cards.a: Intense, persistent fear of a specific object or situation (heights, spiders, flying, blood, needles) lasting 6 months or more, out of proportion to the danger, causing avoidance or intense distress. The fear is recognised as excessive but the person cannot control it.
cards.q: What defines a specific phobia?

cards.a: Exposure therapy: gradual, repeated, controlled contact with the feared object or situation until the fear response fades (habituation). It is the most effective treatment for specific phobias. Drugs are not first-line, because the fear is situational and exposure cures it rather than masking it.
cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for a specific phobia?

cards.a: Blood-injection-injury phobia. Unlike other phobias, which cause a rise in heart rate and blood pressure, it causes a vasovagal response: heart rate and blood pressure drop, leading to fainting. That is why patients faint at the sight of blood or a needle.
cards.q: A patient faints every time they see blood or a needle. Which phobia is this, and why does fainting occur?

cards.a: Applied tension: tensing the muscles of the arms, chest and legs to raise blood pressure before and during the procedure. It counteracts the vasovagal drop that causes fainting, so the patient can tolerate blood draws and injections. Exposure therapy is combined with this technique.
cards.q: What technique helps a patient with blood-injection-injury phobia tolerate a blood draw?

cards.a: Virtual reality exposure is effective and practical when the real situation is hard to arrange (flying, heights). It produces the same fear and habituation as in-person exposure, and it is used when in-vivo exposure is unsafe, expensive or unavailable.
cards.q: A patient has a fear of flying but cannot afford repeated flights for exposure therapy. What is an alternative?

cards.a: Claustrophobia: fear of enclosed spaces. A patient may avoid lifts, tunnels, MRI scanners and crowded rooms, and may panic if trapped. Treat with exposure (starting with a lift for one floor, building up) and CBT to challenge catastrophic thoughts about being trapped.
cards.q: A patient refuses an MRI because they fear being inside the scanner and avoids lifts. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Post-traumatic stress disorder: intrusive symptoms after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence. Diagnosis needs intrusive re-experiencing, avoidance, negative changes in mood and thinking, and hyperarousal, lasting more than 1 month and causing functional impairment.
cards.q: What is the core definition of PTSD?

cards.a: Flashbacks, intrusive memories, nightmares about the event, and intense distress or physical reactions when reminded of it. The key is involuntary re-experiencing: the memory comes back unbidden and feels as if the event is happening again, not just remembering it.
cards.q: What are the intrusive (re-experiencing) symptoms of PTSD?

cards.a: Avoidance of thoughts, feelings, places, people or activities that remind the patient of the trauma. Avoidance maintains PTSD because the patient never learns the reminders are safe, so the fear stays. Treatment must gently reverse avoidance through exposure.
cards.q: Why is avoidance a maintaining factor in PTSD?

cards.a: Irritability and anger outbursts, reckless behaviour, hypervigilance, exaggerated startle response, poor concentration and sleep disturbance. These reflect a nervous system stuck on high alert after the trauma, as if danger is still present.
cards.q: What are the hyperarousal symptoms of PTSD?

cards.a: Persistent negative beliefs about oneself or the world (I am bad, the world is completely dangerous), self-blame, persistent negative emotions such as fear, guilt or shame, loss of interest, feeling detached from others, and inability to feel positive emotions.
cards.q: What are the negative mood and cognition symptoms of PTSD?

cards.a: Trauma-focused CBT (including prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy) and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR). They work by helping the patient process the traumatic memory safely and reduce avoidance. They are first-line, ahead of drugs.
cards.q: What are the first-line treatments for PTSD?

cards.a: Sertraline and paroxetine are the SSRIs with FDA approval for PTSD. They reduce intrusive symptoms, hyperarousal and avoidance, and they also treat comorbid depression. They take 4 to 6 weeks, and the dose needed is often higher than for depression.
cards.q: Which drugs are FDA-approved for PTSD, and what do they help?

cards.a: Prazosin, an alpha-1 blocker, at bedtime. It reduces trauma-related nightmares and improves sleep by blocking the noradrenaline surge that drives nightmares. Check blood pressure, because it can cause dizziness and low blood pressure on standing.
cards.q: A patient with PTSD has severe recurrent nightmares that do not improve on sertraline. What drug is added?

cards.a: Do not give a benzodiazepine. Benzodiazepines worsen PTSD outcomes, increase the risk of dependence, interfere with the processing needed in trauma-focused therapy, and increase the risk of aggression and suicide. Use an SSRI and trauma-focused therapy instead.
cards.q: A patient with PTSD asks for a sleeping pill because of nightmares and anxiety. Which drug class must be avoided?

cards.a: Acute stress disorder: symptoms identical to PTSD (intrusion, avoidance, negative mood, arousal, plus dissociation) but lasting 3 days to 1 month after the trauma. PTSD is diagnosed only when symptoms last more than 1 month.
cards.q: What is the difference between acute stress disorder and PTSD?

cards.a: Dissociation: feeling detached from oneself (depersonalisation), feeling the world is unreal (derealisation), or being unable to recall key parts of the trauma. It is common in acute stress disorder and in the dissociative subtype of PTSD, and it predicts a more severe course.
cards.q: What is dissociation in the context of trauma, and why does it matter?

cards.a: Psychological debriefing (forcing the person to relive the event in detail immediately afterwards) is not recommended and may worsen outcomes. The correct approach is psychological first aid: safety, practical support, calm reassurance, and monitoring, with trauma-focused therapy only if symptoms persist beyond a month.
cards.q: A patient is seen 2 days after a car crash with acute stress symptoms. What intervention should be avoided?

cards.a: Most people recover naturally within a month; about a third develop PTSD. The best predictor of PTSD is the severity and persistence of symptoms in the first month, especially dissociation and avoidance. Follow up at 1 month and start trauma-focused therapy if symptoms persist.
cards.q: A patient has acute stress disorder after an assault. What is the likely course, and what is the next step?

cards.a: Prolonged exposure: the patient repeatedly recounts the traumatic memory in detail in a safe setting, and gradually confronts avoided places and situations in real life. It works because the memory is processed rather than avoided, so the fear response extinguishes and the memory stops feeling dangerous.
cards.q: What is prolonged exposure therapy for PTSD, and why does it work?

cards.a: Yes, PTSD can be diagnosed from witnessing a trauma happening to others, learning a close family member or friend experienced a violent or accidental trauma, or repeated exposure to distressing details (for example first responders). Directly experiencing it is not required.
cards.q: Can PTSD develop in someone who only witnessed a trauma, without being harmed themselves?

cards.a: EMDR uses bilateral stimulation (usually guided eye movements) while the patient recalls the traumatic memory. It is as effective as trauma-focused CBT for many patients and is preferred by some who find prolonged reliving too distressing. The exact mechanism is debated, but the memory is processed and loses its emotional charge.
cards.q: What is EMDR, and when is it used in PTSD?

cards.a: Cognitive processing therapy: a structured CBT that targets the distorted beliefs after trauma, such as self-blame (it was my fault) and beliefs that the world is entirely unsafe. The patient writes about the trauma and learns to reframe these stuck points, which reduces guilt, shame and avoidance.
cards.q: What is cognitive processing therapy for PTSD?

cards.a: Screen for depression, alcohol and substance use, traumatic brain injury, and suicide risk, because these are common after trauma and change management. Also ask about sleep, pain and functioning. Treat comorbid depression with the same SSRI and refer for substance-use support where needed.
cards.q: A veteran with PTSD also has low mood and drinks heavily. What else must be assessed?

cards.a: Delayed-expression PTSD: symptoms begin or worsen more than 6 months after the trauma. Some patients cope initially and develop full PTSD later, often after a new stressor or reminder. Ask about the original trauma even if it was years ago.
cards.q: A patient develops full PTSD symptoms 9 months after a serious accident, having seemed fine at first. What is this called?

cards.a: Obsessions are recurrent, intrusive, unwanted thoughts, images or urges that cause anxiety (for example fear of contamination or harming someone). Compulsions are repetitive behaviours or mental acts done to reduce that anxiety (hand-washing, checking, counting). The person knows they are excessive but feels unable to stop.
cards.q: What is the difference between an obsession and a compulsion in OCD?

cards.a: Obsessive-compulsive disorder: obsessions or compulsions that take more than 1 hour a day or cause significant distress or impairment. Common themes are contamination, symmetry, harm, forbidden sexual or religious thoughts, and needing things just right.
cards.q: What defines OCD, and what are its common themes?

cards.a: CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP): the patient is exposed to the feared trigger and prevented from doing the compulsion, so they learn the anxiety fades on its own. It is first-line and more effective long-term than drugs alone.
cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for OCD?

cards.a: An SSRI at a higher dose than for depression, for example fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, sertraline or paroxetine, for at least 8 to 12 weeks before judging response. OCD responds more slowly and needs higher doses, so do not declare failure after 4 weeks at a low dose.
cards.q: Which drugs are used for OCD, and how does dosing differ from depression?

cards.a: Clomipramine, a tricyclic antidepressant that strongly blocks serotonin reuptake. It is very effective for OCD but is second-line because of side effects: sedation, dry mouth, constipation, weight gain, low blood pressure on standing, and risk of seizures and heart rhythm problems in overdose.
cards.q: A patient with OCD does not respond to two SSRIs. Which drug is next, and why is it second-line?

cards.a: It is not reassurance-seeking done to relieve anxiety, it is a compulsion. Giving reassurance briefly helps but the doubt returns stronger, so the cycle continues. Treatment is ERP: the patient must tolerate the uncertainty without asking for reassurance, so the brain learns the feared outcome does not happen.
cards.q: A patient with OCD asks family members repeatedly whether the door is locked. Why does reassurance not help?

cards.a: Hoarding disorder is now a separate diagnosis: persistent difficulty discarding possessions, causing clutter that makes living spaces unusable, with distress at the thought of discarding. It is not simply collecting, and it is treated with CBT focused on sorting and discarding, not with an SSRI alone.
cards.q: How is hoarding disorder distinguished from OCD?

cards.a: Body dysmorphic disorder: preoccupation with a perceived flaw in appearance that others do not see or see as minor, with repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking or seeking reassurance, and significant distress or impairment. Treat with an SSRI and CBT with exposure, not with cosmetic surgery.
cards.q: A patient is convinced their nose is deformed, checks mirrors constantly and wants repeated surgery, though others see nothing wrong. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Do not offer cosmetic surgery: it does not fix body dysmorphic disorder, because the problem is the distorted perception, not the body part. Patients are usually dissatisfied after surgery and seek more procedures. The correct treatment is an SSRI plus CBT.
cards.q: A patient with body dysmorphic disorder requests cosmetic surgery. What is the next best step?

cards.a: Trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder) and excoriation (skin-picking) disorder. They involve recurrent pulling or picking despite attempts to stop, causing hair loss or skin lesions. Treatment is habit reversal training (a form of CBT) and sometimes an SSRI; they are related to OCD but are separate diagnoses.
cards.q: What are trichotillomania and excoriation disorder, and how are they treated?

cards.a: Tics are sudden, rapid, non-rhythmic movements or sounds that are not aimed at reducing anxiety, while compulsions are deliberate acts done to neutralise an obsession. OCD and tic disorders often occur together, especially in children, and both should be screened for.
cards.q: How is a tic distinguished from a compulsion in a child with OCD?

cards.a: PANDAS: paediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorders associated with streptococcal infections, where OCD or tics start abruptly after a strep throat infection. The onset is sudden and dramatic, unlike the gradual onset of typical OCD. Treat the infection and the OCD; the diagnosis is clinical and remains debated.
cards.q: A child develops severe OCD suddenly, days after a streptococcal throat infection. What is this called?

cards.a: CBT works by identifying distorted thoughts (catastrophising, overestimating danger, intolerance of uncertainty), testing them against evidence, and using behavioural experiments and exposure to learn new, realistic beliefs. It gives lasting skills, which is why its benefits persist after treatment ends, unlike drugs that work only while taken.
cards.q: How does CBT work for anxiety disorders?

cards.a: Exposure therapy: facing the feared situation, object or sensation in a graded, planned way until anxiety naturally falls (habituation) and the person learns the feared outcome does not happen. Avoidance and safety behaviours must be dropped, or exposure will not work.
cards.q: What is exposure therapy, and why must safety behaviours be dropped during it?

cards.a: Cognitive restructuring: catching an automatic anxious thought, examining the evidence for and against it, and replacing it with a balanced thought. For example, a racing heart does not mean a heart attack, it is a normal adrenaline response that passes in minutes.
cards.q: What is cognitive restructuring in CBT for anxiety?

cards.a: SSRIs increase serotonin in the brain, which over weeks reduces the sensitivity of the fear circuits and the tendency to overreact to threat. They do not work immediately because the benefit comes from gradual changes in receptor sensitivity, not from the first dose.
cards.q: Why do SSRIs take weeks to work for anxiety?

cards.a: Sexual dysfunction (low libido, delayed orgasm, erectile problems), nausea, insomnia or drowsiness, weight gain, sweating and hyponatraemia. Explain these in advance, because many patients stop SSRIs silently due to sexual side effects; switching to another SSRI or adding bupropion can help.
cards.q: What are the most important side effects of SSRIs to counsel a patient about?

cards.a: Serotonin syndrome: agitation, confusion, sweating, tremor, clonus, hyperreflexia, fever and muscle rigidity, caused by too much serotonin, usually when an SSRI is combined with another serotonergic drug such as an MAOI, tramadol, triptans or St John's wort. It is a medical emergency: stop the drugs and give supportive care with benzodiazepines.
cards.q: What is serotonin syndrome, and which drug combinations cause it?

cards.a: Never combine an SSRI with an MAOI, and leave a washout period (at least 2 weeks, 5 weeks for fluoxetine) between them, because the combination can cause fatal serotonin syndrome. Also be cautious with tramadol, triptans, linezolid and St John's wort.
cards.q: Which drug combination must never be given with an SSRI?

cards.a: Discontinuation syndrome: dizziness, nausea, headache, electric-shock sensations, irritability and flu-like symptoms when an SSRI is stopped suddenly, especially paroxetine or venlafaxine, which have short half-lives. It is not addiction, but it is unpleasant, so taper slowly over weeks.
cards.q: A patient stops paroxetine suddenly and develops dizziness, nausea and electric-shock sensations. What is this?

cards.a: The combination is better than either alone for moderate to severe anxiety, especially panic disorder, social anxiety and OCD. The SSRI reduces symptoms while CBT teaches lasting skills and prevents relapse, so the patient can eventually stop the drug with a lower risk of relapse.
cards.q: Why is combined SSRI plus CBT often better than either alone for anxiety?

cards.a: Suicidal thoughts can increase in the first weeks of SSRI treatment, especially in adolescents and young adults. Warn the patient and family, arrange close follow-up in the first 2 weeks, and ask directly about suicidal thoughts at every visit.
cards.q: What safety warning must be given when starting an SSRI in a young adult with anxiety?

cards.a: Remission means minimal anxiety and normal functioning, not just feeling a bit better. Continue the SSRI for at least 12 months after remission in most anxiety disorders (longer in OCD), then taper slowly, because stopping early is the commonest cause of relapse.
cards.q: How long should an SSRI be continued after an anxiety disorder remits?

cards.a: Relapse prevention: the patient keeps a list of early warning signs, continues using CBT skills (exposure, cognitive restructuring), avoids alcohol and caffeine excess, keeps regular sleep and exercise, and knows to restart treatment early if symptoms return, rather than waiting until they are severe.
cards.q: What is relapse prevention planning for anxiety disorders?

cards.a: Benzodiazepines increase GABA activity, which calms the brain within minutes. They are useful for acute, short-term relief of severe anxiety or panic, for example while waiting for an SSRI to work, but they are never the long-term plan because of dependence.
cards.q: How do benzodiazepines work, and when are they appropriate?

cards.a: Tolerance, dependence, withdrawal (rebound anxiety, insomnia, tremor, seizures if stopped abruptly), sedation, impaired memory and falls, especially in the elderly, and worsening of depression and PTSD. They also blunt CBT, because the patient attributes safety to the pill, not to their own coping.
cards.q: What are the main risks of benzodiazepines?

cards.a: Short-acting benzodiazepines (alprazolam, lorazepam) wear off quickly, so withdrawal and rebound anxiety occur between doses and patients take them more often, raising dependence risk. Long-acting agents (diazepam, clonazepam) are smoother but accumulate, causing daytime sedation, especially in older adults.
cards.q: Why are short-acting benzodiazepines more dependence-forming than long-acting ones?

cards.a: Taper slowly over weeks to months, reducing by small steps, and never stop abruptly after more than a few weeks of use. Abrupt stopping can cause rebound anxiety, insomnia, tremor, seizures and delirium. Add CBT and an SSRI during the taper to manage the underlying anxiety.
cards.q: A patient has taken alprazolam daily for 6 months. How should it be stopped?

cards.a: Benzodiazepines are contraindicated in patients with a substance-use history, sleep apnoea, severe respiratory disease, myasthenia gravis, and in pregnancy (especially first trimester) because of sedation, respiratory depression and neonatal effects. Use CBT and SSRIs instead in these patients.
cards.q: In which patients are benzodiazepines contraindicated or best avoided?

cards.a: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist used to reverse benzodiazepine sedation in overdose or after procedures, but it can precipitate seizures and withdrawal in a patient who is benzodiazepine-dependent, so it is not given routinely in overdose in dependent patients.
cards.q: What is flumazenil, and why is it dangerous in a benzodiazepine-dependent patient?

cards.a: Z-drugs (zolpidem, zaleplon) and buspirone are alternatives for short-term anxiety or sleep, but they do not replace an SSRI for the underlying disorder. Hydroxyzine, an antihistamine, can help acute anxiety and insomnia without dependence, but it causes sedation and dry mouth. The long-term plan remains an SSRI plus CBT.
cards.q: A patient with anxiety cannot take a benzodiazepine. What short-term alternatives exist?

cards.a: Benzodiazepines plus opioids together cause profound sedation and respiratory depression, and the combination is a leading cause of overdose death. Avoid prescribing both together, and warn any patient on a benzodiazepine never to combine it with opioids or alcohol.
cards.q: Why is combining a benzodiazepine with an opioid dangerous?

cards.a: Because benzodiazepines impair memory, coordination and judgment, and cause next-day sedation. Counsel the patient not to drive, not to drink alcohol, and to avoid operating machinery, especially in the first days and after any dose increase.
cards.q: A patient started on lorazepam asks if they can drive to work. What do you advise?

cards.a: Check for benzodiazepine use first, because chronic benzodiazepine use worsens anxiety between doses and causes rebound anxiety on withdrawal, which can be mistaken for worsening GAD. The treatment is a slow taper plus an SSRI and CBT, not a higher benzodiazepine dose.
cards.q: A patient with GAD on long-term alprazolam reports worsening anxiety between doses. What is the likely cause?

cards.a: Propranolol blocks beta receptors, reducing the physical symptoms of anxiety: tremor, palpitations, sweating and a shaky voice. It does not reduce the mental worry itself, so it is used for performance anxiety (speaking, playing music, exams) rather than generalised anxiety.
cards.q: How does propranolol help performance anxiety?

cards.a: Take propranolol 30 to 60 minutes before the performance, at a low dose, and try it once beforehand at home to check for side effects. Do not take it daily, because daily use is not needed for situational anxiety and causes fatigue, low mood and low blood pressure.
cards.q: When and how should propranolol be taken for performance anxiety?

cards.a: Asthma or COPD (risk of bronchospasm), bradycardia or heart block, decompensated heart failure, and diabetes (it can mask the warning signs of low blood sugar, such as tremor and palpitations). Always ask about asthma and check the pulse and blood pressure before prescribing.
cards.q: What are the contraindications to propranolol for performance anxiety?

cards.a: A beta-blocker is wrong here: beta-blockers help only the physical symptoms of a single feared performance, not the persistent fear of judgment in many social situations. Generalised social anxiety needs an SSRI plus CBT with exposure, which treats the underlying fear.
cards.q: A patient with social anxiety in most situations is prescribed daily propranolol. Why is this the wrong choice?

cards.a: Atenolol is a beta-1 selective blocker sometimes used for performance anxiety, but propranolol is preferred because it crosses into the brain and blocks both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors, reducing tremor more effectively. Atenolol is safer in asthma because it is more selective, but it is less effective for tremor.
cards.q: What is the difference between propranolol and atenolol for performance anxiety?

cards.a: Separation anxiety disorder: excessive fear of separation from attachment figures, with distress, worry about harm to the figure, refusal to go to school, nightmares about separation, and physical symptoms such as stomach aches. It is normal in toddlers but a disorder when it is severe, persistent and impairs functioning in an older child.
cards.q: What is separation anxiety disorder in children?

cards.a: School refusal due to separation anxiety: the child stays home because of fear of separation, not because they dislike school. Treat with CBT, graded return to school, parent training, and sometimes an SSRI. Do not let the child stay home indefinitely, because avoidance strengthens the anxiety.
cards.q: A 9-year-old refuses to go to school, crying and clinging to their mother every morning. What is the management?

cards.a: CBT adapted for children, with parent involvement, graded exposure, and relaxation training. SSRIs (sertraline or fluoxetine) are added for moderate to severe anxiety. Benzodiazepines are avoided in children because of sedation, disinhibition and dependence.
cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for anxiety disorders in children?

cards.a: Ask about bullying, school pressure, family stress, parental anxiety, and trauma, and screen for depression, ADHD and autism, which often coexist with anxiety in children. Also ask about sleep, appetite and somatic complaints, because children often present with stomach aches and headaches rather than saying they are anxious.
cards.q: A child presents with recurrent stomach aches and school avoidance. What else must be assessed?

cards.a: Anxiety in the elderly often presents as somatic complaints, insomnia, worry about health and falls, and avoidance, and it is often missed because it is attributed to ageing or medical illness. It is also commonly comorbid with depression and dementia, so screen for both, and review medications that can cause anxiety.
cards.q: How does anxiety present differently in older adults?

cards.a: SSRIs are preferred in the elderly because benzodiazepines cause falls, confusion, memory problems and hip fractures. Use a low starting dose, increase slowly, and monitor for hyponatraemia and falls. CBT is also effective and has no drug side effects.
cards.q: A 78-year-old with GAD asks for a sleeping pill. Why is an SSRI preferred over a benzodiazepine?

cards.a: Buspirone or an SSRI, plus CBT, are safer choices in the elderly. If a benzodiazepine is unavoidable, use the lowest dose for the shortest time, choose a short-acting agent, and stop as soon as possible, with a falls-risk review.
cards.q: An older adult with anxiety cannot tolerate an SSRI. What is a safer alternative to a benzodiazepine?

cards.a: Selective mutism and social anxiety are more common in children, separation anxiety peaks in childhood, and GAD and panic are common in adolescents. Early treatment matters, because untreated childhood anxiety predicts adult anxiety, depression and substance use.
cards.q: Which anxiety disorders are most common in children, and why does early treatment matter?

cards.a: Hyperthyroidism causes anxiety, palpitations, tremor, sweating, weight loss and heat intolerance. Check TSH and free T4 in any patient with new anxiety plus these features, because treating the thyroid cures the anxiety, and an SSRI alone will not.
cards.q: A patient with new anxiety has palpitations, tremor, weight loss and heat intolerance. What test is needed and why?

cards.a: Pheochromocytoma: a tumour of the adrenal medulla that releases bursts of adrenaline, causing episodic severe hypertension, headache, palpitations, sweating and panic-like attacks. Check plasma or urine metanephrines, especially if attacks occur with very high blood pressure.
cards.q: A patient has panic-like attacks with severe headaches, sweating and blood pressure of 200 over 120 during attacks. What diagnosis must be ruled out?

cards.a: Supraventricular tachycardia or other arrhythmias can cause sudden palpitations, chest discomfort and a feeling of doom that mimics panic. Check an ECG during symptoms, or a Holter monitor if episodes are frequent, because treating the arrhythmia stops the attacks.
cards.q: A patient has sudden episodes of palpitations and fear that last minutes and stop abruptly. What medical cause must be excluded?

cards.a: Hypoglycaemia causes shakiness, sweating, palpitations and anxiety, especially in patients on insulin or sulfonylureas. Check glucose during an episode. Caffeine excess, cocaine, amphetamines and alcohol withdrawal also mimic panic and must be asked about in the history.
cards.q: What metabolic and substance causes mimic panic attacks?

cards.a: Asthma, COPD and pulmonary embolism cause breathlessness and panic-like fear. Always check oxygen saturation, listen to the chest, and consider a chest X-ray or CT if there are risk factors, because a missed pulmonary embolism is fatal while panic is not.
cards.q: A patient with sudden breathlessness and panic is thought to have a panic attack. What must be checked first?

cards.a: Mitral valve prolapse is associated with panic disorder, but it does not cause it, and treating the prolapse does not cure the panic. The association is a reminder to check the heart, not a reason to dismiss the panic as cardiac. Treat the panic disorder with an SSRI and CBT.
cards.q: A patient with panic disorder is found to have mitral valve prolapse. Does this explain the panic?

cards.a: Caffeine: advise the patient to cut down gradually, because excess caffeine causes jitteriness, palpitations and insomnia that worsen anxiety, and stopping suddenly causes headaches and fatigue. Also review over-the-counter decongestants, energy drinks and thyroid medication.
cards.q: A patient with GAD drinks 6 cups of coffee a day. What advice is given?

cards.a: Alcohol withdrawal causes tremor, sweating, anxiety and panic, and in severe cases seizures and delirium tremens. Ask every anxious patient about alcohol use, because the anxiety may be withdrawal, and the treatment is a medically supervised detox with benzodiazepines, not an SSRI alone.
cards.q: A heavy drinker presents with severe anxiety, tremor and sweating the morning after drinking. What is the likely cause?

cards.a: Adjustment disorder: emotional or behavioural symptoms (anxiety, low mood, or both) in response to an identifiable stressor, starting within 3 months of the stressor and resolving within 6 months of the stressor ending. The distress is out of proportion to the stressor and impairs functioning, but it does not meet criteria for another disorder.
cards.q: What is adjustment disorder?

cards.a: Adjustment disorder resolves when the stressor ends or the person adapts, usually within 6 months. GAD is chronic worry for 6 months or more without a single identifiable trigger, and major depression needs persistent low mood or loss of interest for 2 weeks with other depressive symptoms.
cards.q: How is adjustment disorder distinguished from GAD and major depression?

cards.a: Supportive psychotherapy and CBT are first-line, focusing on coping skills, problem-solving and reducing avoidance. Drugs are not first-line, but a short course of an SSRI or a brief benzodiazepine may be used if anxiety or insomnia is severe, alongside therapy.
cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for adjustment disorder?

cards.a: Adjustment disorder with disturbance of conduct: the patient reacts to a stressor with rule-breaking, aggression or reckless behaviour rather than anxiety or low mood. It is common in adolescents after a family breakdown or school change, and it is treated with therapy and family support, not with punishment alone.
cards.q: A teenager starts skipping school and fighting after their parents divorce. What subtype of adjustment disorder is this?

cards.a: Screen for suicide risk, because adjustment disorder carries a real risk of self-harm, especially in adolescents and in patients with a recent loss or relationship breakdown. Ask directly about suicidal thoughts and plans, involve family, and arrange close follow-up and safety planning.
cards.q: Why must suicide risk be assessed in adjustment disorder, even though it is often called a mild diagnosis?

cards.a: At least 6 months of continuous disturbance, including at least 1 month of active psychotic symptoms such as delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech. The 6-month period includes prodromal and residual phases. Shorter illness is schizophreniform disorder or brief psychotic disorder, not schizophrenia.
cards.q: What duration of symptoms is required to diagnose schizophrenia?

cards.a: At least 2 of: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior, and negative symptoms, with at least 1 being delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech. There must also be a marked decline in work, relationships, or self-care, and mood or substance or medical causes must be excluded.
cards.q: What are the two core symptom criteria needed for schizophrenia, and what else must be present?

cards.a: Weeks to months of social withdrawal, odd beliefs, poor hygiene, declining school or work performance, and mild perceptual changes before frank psychosis. Recognizing it matters because early treatment shortens untreated psychosis and improves outcome, and it helps distinguish schizophrenia from a sudden brief psychotic episode.
cards.q: What is the prodrome of schizophrenia and why does it matter on Step 3?

cards.a: Schizophrenia. The age, persistent delusions and hallucinations for more than 6 months, and functional decline fit schizophrenia. The next step is a medical and substance workup, then start a second-generation antipsychotic plus psychosocial support, not watchful waiting.
cards.q: A 22-year-old man has had paranoid delusions and auditory hallucinations for 8 months with job loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?

cards.a: When psychosis occurs without a major mood episode, or persists for at least 2 weeks when mood symptoms are absent. In mood disorders with psychotic features, psychosis occurs only during depression or mania. That 2-week psychosis-without-mood window points toward schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder.
cards.q: When should you suspect schizophrenia rather than a mood disorder with psychotic features?

cards.a: Men usually present in late teens to early 20s, women in late 20s to early 30s. Earlier onset in men is linked to more negative symptoms and worse outcome. Late onset after age 45 should prompt a search for medical, neurologic, or substance causes before calling it schizophrenia.
cards.q: What is the typical age of onset of schizophrenia in men versus women?

cards.a: History, mental status exam, vital signs, CBC, metabolic panel, thyroid function, B12, urine drug screen, pregnancy test when relevant, and HIV and syphilis testing when indicated. Brain imaging is done if there are focal neurologic signs, seizures, head injury, or atypical features. Do not label it primary psychosis until medical and substance causes are excluded.
cards.q: What medical workup is required before diagnosing first-episode psychosis as schizophrenia?

cards.a: Thyroid disease, vitamin B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis, HIV, brain tumor, temporal lobe epilepsy, autoimmune encephalitis, Wilson disease, and delirium. They can cause hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking. Treating the underlying medical cause is the priority, and an antipsychotic alone will not fix it.
cards.q: Which medical conditions can mimic schizophrenia and must be ruled out first?

cards.a: Because psychosis alone is not enough; schizophrenia is defined by loss of functioning in work, school, relationships, or self-care compared with before the illness. A person with intact functioning and a fixed false belief is more likely to have delusional disorder. Functional decline also predicts need for rehabilitation and supported employment.
cards.q: Why is functional decline part of the schizophrenia diagnosis?

cards.a: Speech that jumps between unrelated topics, gives tangential or incoherent answers, or uses invented words, reflecting disorganized thought. Ask open-ended questions and listen for derailment and loose associations. It is a core criterion and a reason to assess safety and ability to care for oneself.
cards.q: What is disorganized speech in schizophrenia and how is it tested?

cards.a: Behavior that is purposeless, bizarre, or unable to meet basic needs, such as wearing heavy clothes in summer, hoarding, public agitation without a trigger, or inability to prepare food or keep hygiene. It signals loss of goal-directed behavior and often means the patient needs supervision, hospitalization, or intensive support.
cards.q: What is grossly disorganized behavior in schizophrenia?

cards.a: Because the total duration is under 6 months. At 1 to under 6 months the diagnosis is schizophreniform disorder, a provisional label. If symptoms persist beyond 6 months it becomes schizophrenia; if they resolve within 6 months it was schizophreniform. Do not rush the schizophrenia label before the time criterion is met.
cards.q: A patient has 4 months of delusions and hallucinations with good prior functioning. Why is schizophrenia not yet the diagnosis?

cards.a: Added experiences that should not be there: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, and disorganized behavior. Auditory hallucinations, often commenting or commanding voices, are the most common. Positive symptoms respond best to dopamine-blocking antipsychotics.
cards.q: What are positive symptoms of schizophrenia?

cards.a: Loss of normal function: flat affect, alogia or poverty of speech, avolition or lack of motivation, anhedonia or loss of pleasure, and asociality or social withdrawal. They are harder to treat, respond poorly to antipsychotics, and predict worse long-term functioning than positive symptoms.
cards.q: What are negative symptoms of schizophrenia?

cards.a: Flat affect is reduced emotional expression, monotone voice, and limited gestures without necessarily feeling sad. Depression involves low mood, guilt, hopelessness, and often suicidal thoughts. Ask directly about mood and suicidal ideation, because depression in schizophrenia is common and treatable and raises suicide risk.
cards.q: How do you distinguish flat affect from depression in schizophrenia?

cards.a: Negative symptoms. Persistent avolition, flat affect, and social withdrawal predict poor work and social outcome even when hallucinations improve. Positive symptoms fluctuate and often improve with medication, while negative and cognitive symptoms drive long-term disability and need rehabilitation.
cards.q: Which symptom cluster predicts worse prognosis in schizophrenia: positive or negative?

cards.a: No, hallucinations alone are only one criterion; at least one more criterion is needed, plus 6 months duration and functional decline. Isolated hallucinations should also prompt a workup for substance use, medical illness, mood disorder, and hearing loss. Do not diagnose schizophrenia on a single symptom.
cards.q: A patient hears voices saying he is worthless but has no delusions. Is this enough for schizophrenia?

cards.a: Problems with attention, working memory, processing speed, and executive function. They persist even when psychosis is controlled and limit school, work, and daily living. Management includes cognitive remediation, supported employment, and choosing antipsychotics that do not worsen sedation or anticholinergic burden.
cards.q: What are cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia and why do they matter for management?

cards.a: Positive symptoms are linked to excess dopamine signaling in the mesolimbic pathway, which D2 blockade reduces. Negative and cognitive symptoms involve other pathways and brain regions, so dopamine blockade alone does not fix them. That is why psychosocial rehabilitation is essential even when hallucinations resolve.
cards.q: Why do antipsychotics help positive symptoms more than negative symptoms?

cards.a: A delusion is a fixed false belief that does not change with evidence, such as believing one is being followed. A hallucination is a false perception without an external stimulus, such as hearing voices when no one is speaking. Both are positive symptoms, but they are assessed and described differently.
cards.q: What is the difference between a delusion and a hallucination?

cards.a: An uninterrupted illness with a major mood episode, either depressive or bipolar type, plus psychotic symptoms, where delusions or hallucinations occur for at least 2 weeks without mood symptoms. That 2-week psychosis-without-mood period separates it from a mood disorder with psychotic features, where psychosis occurs only during mood episodes.
cards.q: What defines schizoaffective disorder?

cards.a: In schizoaffective disorder, major mood episodes are present for most of the illness. In schizophrenia, mood episodes are brief relative to the total illness. Ask about sustained periods of depression or mania, not just a few days of low mood during psychosis.
cards.q: How do you distinguish schizoaffective disorder from schizophrenia?

cards.a: In bipolar disorder with psychotic features, psychosis occurs only during mania or depression. In schizoaffective disorder, psychosis persists for at least 2 weeks after mood symptoms resolve. That persistent psychosis outside mood episodes is the key distinguishing feature.
cards.q: How do you distinguish schizoaffective disorder from bipolar disorder with psychotic features?

cards.a: An antipsychotic plus a mood stabilizer such as lithium or valproate. The antipsychotic treats psychosis and the mood stabilizer treats mania and prevents relapse. Monotherapy with either alone usually leaves one part of the illness untreated, so combination therapy is the standard next step.
cards.q: What is the treatment for schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type?

cards.a: An antipsychotic plus an antidepressant. The antipsychotic targets psychosis and the antidepressant targets the depressive episode. Monitor for worsening depression and suicide risk, and avoid using an antidepressant alone because it will not control psychosis.
cards.q: What is the treatment for schizoaffective disorder, depressive type?

cards.a: Intermediate. It is generally better than schizophrenia but worse than a pure mood disorder. Mood symptoms and response to mood stabilizers improve outlook, while persistent psychosis and negative symptoms worsen it. Long-term maintenance treatment and psychosocial support are usually needed.
cards.q: What is the prognosis of schizoaffective disorder compared with schizophrenia and mood disorders?

cards.a: Schizoaffective disorder. The psychosis lasting more than 2 weeks without mood symptoms rules out bipolar disorder with psychotic features. The next step is maintenance with an antipsychotic plus a mood stabilizer, with monitoring for relapse of either mood or psychosis.
cards.q: A patient has psychosis during mania, then continues to hear voices for 3 weeks after mood normalizes. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Because the diagnosis depends on the longitudinal pattern of mood and psychosis over time, especially the 2 weeks of psychosis without mood. A single visit cannot show that pattern. Take a detailed timeline, collateral history, and prior records before committing to the label.
cards.q: Why should you not diagnose schizoaffective disorder on a single cross-sectional visit?

cards.a: Sudden onset of delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, or grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior lasting at least 1 day but less than 1 month, with full return to baseline functioning. It is often triggered by a major stressor or postpartum period. If it lasts longer, reconsider schizophreniform disorder.
