cards.a: Treat for herniation with hyperosmolar therapy, ensure oxygenation and blood pressure, and get urgent neurosurgical review and CT. A blown pupil suggests the brain is herniating and needs immediate pressure relief.
cards.q: What is the next step if a head-injured patient develops a dilated unreactive pupil?

cards.a: Because they do not improve outcome and increase mortality. They are avoided in head injury despite their use in other brain conditions.
cards.q: Why are steroids not used in traumatic brain injury?

cards.a: High-energy blunt trauma, such as a motor vehicle crash or fall from height. The pelvis is a strong ring, so it takes major force to break it.
cards.q: What is the most common cause of pelvic fracture?

cards.a: Massive haemorrhage from pelvic veins and arteries into the retroperitoneum. The pelvis can hold a large volume of blood, so bleeding can be life-threatening before it is obvious externally.
cards.q: What is the main danger of a pelvic fracture?

cards.a: Apply a pelvic binder or sheet to close the pelvic ring. Closing the ring reduces the space for bleeding and helps tamponade venous bleeding.
cards.q: What is the first step in managing a suspected pelvic fracture with hypotension?

cards.a: Because that is where it best closes the pelvic ring. Placing it too high on the abdomen does not compress the pelvis effectively and can worsen bleeding.
cards.q: Why is a pelvic binder applied at the level of the greater trochanters?

cards.a: Angioembolisation or surgical packing, depending on the source and local resources. Arterial bleeding often needs embolisation, while venous bleeding may need packing.
cards.q: What is the next step if bleeding continues despite a pelvic binder?

cards.a: Because movement can disrupt clots and worsen bleeding. The pelvis is kept stable until the fracture is assessed and bleeding is controlled.
cards.q: Why should a pelvic fracture patient not be log-rolled unnecessarily?

cards.a: Bladder and urethral injury. The bladder sits in the pelvis, so a fracture can tear it, causing blood in the urine and inability to pass urine.
cards.q: What associated injury is common with pelvic fractures?

cards.a: Blood in the urine, inability to pass urine, and lower abdominal pain. A CT cystogram is used to confirm bladder rupture.
cards.q: What suggests bladder injury in a pelvic fracture patient?

cards.a: Extraperitoneal rupture leaks urine into the pelvis and is usually managed with a catheter, while intraperitoneal rupture leaks into the abdomen and needs surgical repair. The location determines treatment.
cards.q: What is the difference between extraperitoneal and intraperitoneal bladder rupture?

cards.a: Urgent resuscitation, antibiotics, wound care, and surgical control of bleeding, often with external fixation. Open fractures are contaminated and bleed heavily, so they need multidisciplinary care.
cards.q: What is the management of an open pelvic fracture?

cards.a: A fracture where the front of the pelvis opens outward like a book, usually from anteroposterior compression. It increases pelvic volume and bleeding risk, so a binder is especially important.
cards.q: What is an open-book pelvic fracture?

cards.a: A fracture from side impact that compresses the pelvis inward. It is often stable but can injure the bladder and internal organs on the side of impact.
cards.q: What is a lateral compression pelvic fracture?

cards.a: A fracture where one side of the pelvis is displaced upward, usually from a fall. It is unstable and often associated with major bleeding and nerve injury.
cards.q: What is a vertical shear pelvic fracture?

cards.a: When the pelvis is unstable and needs temporary stabilisation to control bleeding. It holds the ring closed while definitive fixation is planned.
cards.q: When is external fixation used for a pelvic fracture?

cards.a: Acute appendicitis. Early pain is visceral and felt around the umbilicus because the appendix shares midgut innervation; once inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum over McBurney point, pain localises to the right lower quadrant and becomes sharp. Anorexia with migratory pain is a classic Step 3 clue.
cards.q: A 22-year-old man has periumbilical pain that moved to the right lower quadrant over 12 hours, with anorexia, nausea and low-grade fever. What is the most likely diagnosis and why does the pain move?

cards.a: McBurney point is one-third of the distance from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus on the right. Tenderness there suggests appendicitis, because it overlies the base of the appendix; localised peritoneal irritation there makes the diagnosis much more likely.
cards.q: What is McBurney point and what does tenderness there suggest?

cards.a: Rovsing sign. Pressing the left side stretches the peritoneum and shifts bowel gas toward the inflamed appendix on the right, reproducing right-sided pain. It supports appendicitis but is not specific enough to confirm it alone.
cards.q: A patient with suspected appendicitis has pain in the right lower quadrant when you press the left lower quadrant. What is this sign called and what does it mean?

cards.a: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis. It is the most accurate test, shows an enlarged appendix over 6 mm, wall thickening, fat stranding and complications such as perforation or abscess, and it also rules out mimics such as ureteric stone or ovarian pathology.
cards.q: What is the best initial imaging test for suspected appendicitis in a non-pregnant adult, and why?

cards.a: Ultrasound first in both, because it avoids radiation. In children it often shows a non-compressible enlarged appendix; in pregnancy it also checks the uterus and ovaries. If ultrasound is inconclusive and suspicion remains high, MRI is next in pregnancy and CT is considered in children.
cards.q: A 9-year-old child and a pregnant woman both have suspected appendicitis. What imaging should be done first in each, and why?

cards.a: Laparoscopic appendicectomy. Antibiotics alone can settle uncomplicated appendicitis in some patients but carry a substantial recurrence risk within a year, whereas appendicectomy removes the source and is curative, so surgery remains the standard Step 3 answer.
cards.q: A healthy adult has uncomplicated acute appendicitis confirmed on CT. What is the definitive treatment, and why is surgery preferred over antibiotics alone?

cards.a: In selected uncomplicated cases when the patient prefers to avoid surgery, is a poor surgical candidate, or surgery is not immediately available. The patient must understand the recurrence risk and the need to return promptly if pain worsens, because delayed surgery after failed antibiotics can mean perforation.
cards.q: A patient with appendicitis is treated with antibiotics only and is doing well. When is this approach reasonable?

cards.a: Perforated appendicitis with an appendiceal abscess or phlegmon. The next step is IV antibiotics plus percutaneous drainage of the abscess, with interval appendicectomy in about 6 to 8 weeks, because operating immediately through inflamed, friable tissue risks bowel injury and a larger resection.
cards.q: A patient presents 5 days after appendicitis began, with a palpable right lower quadrant mass, fever and a walled-off collection on CT. What is the diagnosis and the next best step?

cards.a: Because the inflamed appendix is stuck to surrounding bowel and omentum, so dissection is difficult and the risk of caecal injury, bowel resection and postoperative complications is high. Draining the abscess and giving antibiotics lets inflammation settle first.
cards.q: Why is immediate appendicectomy usually avoided when a well-formed appendiceal abscess is present?

cards.a: Prompt surgical evaluation and laparoscopic appendicectomy if appendicitis is confirmed or highly suspected. Delay increases the risk of perforation, which raises the risk of fetal loss, whereas appendicectomy in pregnancy is safe; imaging should not delay a clear surgical abdomen.
cards.q: A pregnant woman at 20 weeks has right lower quadrant pain and suspected appendicitis. What is the management, and why should surgery not be delayed?

cards.a: Because the enlarging uterus displaces the appendix upward and laterally, so pain may be in the right flank rather than McBurney point, and normal pregnancy changes such as a raised white cell count and nausea can mask the usual clues.
cards.q: Why can appendicitis be harder to diagnose in pregnancy?

cards.a: Postoperative intra-abdominal abscess, usually from a perforated appendix at surgery. It is managed with broad-spectrum antibiotics and percutaneous drainage if the collection is accessible, because drainage removes the infected source that antibiotics alone cannot clear.
cards.q: After appendicectomy a patient develops fever, right lower quadrant pain and a fluid collection on CT on postoperative day 5. What is the most likely complication and its management?

cards.a: Pelvic inflammatory disease usually causes bilateral lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness and vaginal discharge, and pain often starts in the pelvis rather than migrating from the umbilicus. A pelvic examination, pregnancy test, sexually transmitted infection testing and pelvic ultrasound help separate the two, because missing either diagnosis has serious consequences.
cards.q: A 30-year-old woman has right lower quadrant pain, fever and vaginal discharge. How do you distinguish pelvic inflammatory disease from appendicitis?

cards.a: Because older adults often have a blunted inflammatory response and less obvious peritoneal signs, so appendicitis can be present with subtle findings. A higher index of suspicion and CT imaging are needed, since perforation is more common when diagnosis is delayed in this group.
cards.q: An elderly patient has right lower quadrant pain but minimal tenderness and a normal white cell count. Why can appendicitis still be present?

cards.a: Simple appendicectomy is usually curative for a small carcinoid under 2 cm confined to the tip, because these tumours rarely metastasise. Larger tumours, involvement of the base, or invasion into the mesoappendix require right hemicolectomy, so histology and size decide the operation.
cards.q: During appendicectomy the surgeon finds a small carcinoid tumour at the tip of the appendix. What is the usual next step and why?

cards.a: Biliary colic is episodic right upper quadrant pain lasting under 6 hours from a gallstone temporarily blocking the cystic duct, without fever or a raised white cell count. Acute cholecystitis is persistent pain over 6 hours with fever, leucocytosis and gallbladder wall inflammation, because the blockage persists; cholecystitis needs admission and cholecystectomy, while colic is usually managed electively.
cards.q: What is the difference between biliary colic and acute cholecystitis, and why does it matter?

cards.a: Pain and a catch in breathing when you press under the right costal margin as the patient breathes in, because the inflamed gallbladder descends onto your hand. It supports acute cholecystitis, especially when combined with fever and leucocytosis.
cards.q: A patient has right upper quadrant pain, fever and a positive Murphy sign. What does a positive Murphy sign mean?

cards.a: Right upper quadrant ultrasound. It shows gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening over 3 mm, pericholecystic fluid and a sonographic Murphy sign. Ultrasound is quick, radiation-free and highly sensitive for gallstones, which is why it comes before CT or HIDA scan.
cards.q: What is the first-line imaging test for suspected acute cholecystitis, and what findings support the diagnosis?

cards.a: HIDA scan. A tracer that should fill the gallbladder will not enter it if the cystic duct is obstructed, so non-visualisation of the gallbladder confirms acute cholecystitis with high accuracy when ultrasound is inconclusive.
cards.q: Ultrasound is equivocal in a patient with suspected acute cholecystitis. What is the next best test and why?

cards.a: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 72 hours of symptom onset, or during the same admission. Early surgery is safer because inflammation has not yet organised into dense adhesions, and it prevents recurrence, gangrene and perforation that occur when surgery is delayed.
cards.q: A patient with acute cholecystitis is stable with no perforation. When should cholecystectomy be done, and why?

cards.a: During the same admission once the pancreatitis has settled, usually within a few days. Removing the gallbladder prevents another stone passing into the common bile duct and causing recurrent pancreatitis or cholangitis, which is why discharge without cholecystectomy is not the plan.
cards.q: A patient develops gallstone pancreatitis. When should cholecystectomy be performed, and why?

cards.a: Choledocholithiasis, a stone in the common bile duct. MRCP is the next best test when the patient is stable, because it visualises the bile duct non-invasively and confirms the stone before ERCP, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic but carries procedural risk.
cards.q: A patient with gallstones has jaundice, a dilated common bile duct and a raised alkaline phosphatase. What is the likely diagnosis and the next best test?

cards.a: Right upper quadrant pain, fever and jaundice. It points to acute cholangitis, infection of an obstructed biliary tree, usually from a common bile duct stone. The triad reflects obstruction plus infection, so it demands urgent antibiotics and biliary decompression.
cards.q: What is Charcot triad, and what diagnosis does it point to?

cards.a: Charcot triad plus hypotension and confusion. It indicates severe suppurative cholangitis with sepsis, so mortality is high without rapid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics and urgent biliary decompression, usually by ERCP.
cards.q: What is Reynolds pentad, and why is it a surgical emergency?

cards.a: Antibiotics plus urgent biliary decompression, usually ERCP with stone removal or stenting. Antibiotics cannot clear pus behind a blocked duct, so the obstruction must be relieved to drain infected bile and prevent septic shock.
cards.q: A patient has cholangitis from a common bile duct stone. What is the definitive management, and why are antibiotics alone not enough?

cards.a: Acalculous cholecystitis. In critically ill patients, fasting, hypotension and prolonged parenteral nutrition cause gallbladder stasis and ischaemia of the gallbladder wall, leading to inflammation without stones. It is managed with antibiotics and percutaneous cholecystostomy or cholecystectomy, because it can progress rapidly to gangrene.
cards.q: A critically ill ICU patient on a ventilator develops right upper quadrant pain, fever and a thickened gallbladder wall on ultrasound, but has no gallstones. What is the diagnosis and why does it occur?

cards.a: Emphysematous cholecystitis, a gas-forming infection of the gallbladder wall that occurs mainly in diabetics and carries a high risk of gangrene and perforation. It needs emergency cholecystectomy plus broad-spectrum antibiotics, because antibiotics alone cannot control this rapidly necrotising infection.
cards.q: A diabetic man has severe right upper quadrant pain, fever, crepitus on examination and gas in the gallbladder wall on CT. What is the diagnosis and the next step?

cards.a: A gallstone impacted in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck compresses the common hepatic duct, causing jaundice and mimicking a bile duct stone. Surgery is difficult because the anatomy is distorted and the bile duct is at high risk of injury, so it often needs an experienced hepatobiliary surgeon and preoperative MRCP.
cards.q: What is Mirizzi syndrome, and why does it make cholecystectomy difficult?

cards.a: Bile leak, usually from the cystic duct stump or an accessory duct. Small leaks often settle with percutaneous drainage and ERCP with stenting to lower pressure in the bile duct, because reducing duct pressure lets the leak seal; a major duct injury needs surgical repair.
cards.q: After laparoscopic cholecystectomy a patient develops abdominal pain, fever and a bile collection on imaging. What is the most likely cause and its management?

cards.a: Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic cholelithiasis. Biliary colic recurs and can progress to cholecystitis, pancreatitis or choledocholithiasis, so removing the gallbladder prevents those complications; asymptomatic gallstones, by contrast, are usually left alone.
cards.q: A patient with gallstones has episodic right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals, normal liver tests and no fever. What is the management?

cards.a: Adhesions. Scar tissue bands from prior surgery tether loops of bowel and kink them, blocking passage of contents. Adhesions account for most small bowel obstructions in operated abdomens, which is why a surgical history is a key Step 3 clue.
cards.q: What is the most common cause of small bowel obstruction in a patient with previous abdominal surgery, and why?

cards.a: Small bowel obstruction. Initial management is nil by mouth, IV fluids, nasogastric tube decompression, correction of electrolytes and analgesia, because decompression relieves vomiting and distension while resuscitation corrects the dehydration and electrolyte losses from vomiting and third-space fluid shifts.
cards.q: A patient has crampy central abdominal pain, vomiting, distension and high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds. What is the diagnosis and the initial management?

cards.a: Fever, tachycardia, constant severe pain, peritoneal signs, leucocytosis, lactic acidosis and CT showing bowel wall thickening, pneumatosis or portal venous gas. These suggest the bowel blood supply is compromised, so emergency surgery is needed before the bowel infarcts and perforates.
cards.q: What findings on examination and imaging suggest strangulation in small bowel obstruction, and why is this an emergency?

cards.a: Mechanical obstruction causes crampy pain, vomiting, distension and a transition point on CT with dilated bowel proximally and collapsed bowel distally. Ileus causes diffuse distension with absent bowel sounds and dilated bowel throughout without a transition point, because it is a paralysis of bowel motility rather than a physical blockage.
cards.q: How do you distinguish mechanical small bowel obstruction from postoperative ileus?

cards.a: A segment of bowel is blocked at two points, so gas and fluid cannot escape in either direction. Pressure rises rapidly, the blood supply is cut off early and strangulation can occur within hours, so closed-loop obstruction needs urgent surgery even without overt peritonitis.
cards.q: What is a closed-loop obstruction, and why is it dangerous?

cards.a: It localises the site of obstruction: bowel is dilated upstream of the blockage and collapsed downstream. Finding the transition point helps identify the cause, such as adhesions or a hernia, and guides whether surgery or conservative management is appropriate.
cards.q: A patient with small bowel obstruction has a CT showing dilated loops, air-fluid levels and a transition point at the terminal ileum. What does the transition point tell you?

cards.a: Oral water-soluble contrast such as Gastrografin is given and its passage is followed on X-ray. If contrast reaches the colon within 24 hours, the obstruction is likely to resolve without surgery, because passage proves the blockage is partial; if it does not pass, surgery is usually needed.
cards.q: A patient with adhesive small bowel obstruction is stable with no strangulation signs. What is the role of a water-soluble contrast challenge, and why is it used?

cards.a: Colorectal cancer, diverticular stricture and volvulus. Large bowel obstruction causes more marked distension, less vomiting early on because the ileocaecal valve often stays competent, and constipation with failure to pass flatus; small bowel obstruction causes earlier profuse vomiting.
cards.q: What are the most common causes of large bowel obstruction, and how does its presentation differ from small bowel obstruction?

cards.a: Sigmoid volvulus, twisting of the sigmoid colon on its mesentery, which creates the coffee-bean appearance of a hugely dilated loop. Initial treatment is endoscopic detorsion with a rectal tube if there is no peritonitis, because untwisting relieves the obstruction, followed by elective sigmoid resection since recurrence is common.
cards.q: An elderly man has massive abdominal distension, constipation and a coffee-bean sign on abdominal X-ray. What is the diagnosis and the initial treatment?

cards.a: Because the redundant sigmoid colon that twisted once is very likely to twist again, and recurrent volvulus can strangulate. Elective resection during the same admission removes the redundant loop and prevents recurrence.
cards.q: Why is elective sigmoid resection recommended after successful endoscopic detorsion of a sigmoid volvulus?

cards.a: Caecal volvulus usually needs emergency surgery rather than endoscopic detorsion, because the caecum is mobile, endoscopic untwisting is often unsuccessful and the risk of ischaemia is high. Resection or caecopexy is performed depending on bowel viability.
cards.q: How does caecal volvulus differ from sigmoid volvulus in management, and why?

cards.a: An umbilical hernia in an adult is a protrusion through the umbilicus, often linked to raised intra-abdominal pressure from obesity, pregnancy or ascites. Small asymptomatic ones can be watched, but large, painful or incarcerated ones need repair, because strangulation can occur.
cards.q: What is an umbilical hernia in an adult, and when does it need repair?

cards.a: Richter hernia, where only part of the bowel wall is trapped in the hernial sac. It can strangulate without causing complete bowel obstruction, so the patient may have pain at the hernia site but still pass flatus, which makes it easy to miss.
cards.q: What is a Richter hernia, and why can it be missed?

cards.a: Mesh infection, recurrence, chronic groin pain and, rarely, bowel injury. Mesh infection usually needs removal of the infected mesh plus antibiotics, because bacteria form a biofilm on mesh that antibiotics cannot clear.
cards.q: What are the complications of mesh hernia repair, and why is mesh infection hard to treat with antibiotics alone?

cards.a: A hernia in a cirrhotic patient with ascites is at high risk of rupture, incarceration and poor wound healing, so elective repair is often deferred until ascites is controlled and nutrition and liver function are optimised. Emergency repair is still needed if it strangulates.
cards.q: Why is elective hernia repair often deferred in a patient with cirrhosis and ascites?

cards.a: A sliding hernia is one where part of the wall of the hernial sac is formed by an organ itself, such as the bladder or caecum, rather than just peritoneum. It matters at surgery because the organ can be injured if the surgeon does not recognise it as part of the sac wall.
cards.q: What is a sliding hernia, and why does it matter at operation?

cards.a: Acute mesenteric ischaemia, where the blood supply to the bowel is cut off. The classic clue is severe abdominal pain that seems out of proportion to the examination findings, because the bowel is ischaemic before it becomes infarcted and tender; early recognition saves bowel.
cards.q: A patient with atrial fibrillation has sudden severe abdominal pain but a soft abdomen with minimal tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis, and why is the pain out of proportion?

cards.a: An embolus from the heart, usually in atrial fibrillation, a thrombus on pre-existing atherosclerosis of the superior mesenteric artery, non-occlusive ischaemia from low blood pressure, and mesenteric venous thrombosis. Distinguishing them matters because embolic disease needs embolectomy, thrombotic disease needs revascularisation, and venous thrombosis is treated mainly with anticoagulation.
cards.q: What are the four main causes of acute mesenteric ischaemia?

cards.a: CT angiography of the abdomen. It shows the site and cause of the arterial or venous blockage and whether bowel is already infarcted, and it is fast and non-invasive, which is why it has replaced conventional angiography as the first test when mesenteric ischaemia is suspected.
cards.q: What is the gold standard imaging test for suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia, and why?

cards.a: No. Lactate rises only after bowel has already infarcted and tissue is dying, so a normal lactate does not exclude early mesenteric ischaemia. Relying on lactate delays diagnosis and loses bowel, which is why CT angiography is done on clinical suspicion.
cards.q: Can a normal lactate exclude acute mesenteric ischaemia? Why not?

cards.a: Resuscitation with IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, heparin anticoagulation and urgent surgical or vascular consultation for revascularisation, usually embolectomy or bypass, with laparotomy to assess bowel viability. Restoring blood flow early saves bowel; dead bowel must be resected.
cards.q: What is the initial management of acute embolic mesenteric ischaemia?

cards.a: A second-look laparotomy 24 to 48 hours after the first operation. Bowel that looked borderline at the first operation may declare itself dead or recover after revascularisation, so a planned re-exploration lets the surgeon resect only what is truly non-viable and preserve as much bowel as possible.
cards.q: Why is a second-look laparotomy planned after surgery for mesenteric ischaemia?

cards.a: Chronic mesenteric ischaemia from atherosclerotic narrowing of the mesenteric arteries. It causes postprandial pain as the gut demands more blood after eating, food fear and weight loss, because the narrowed arteries cannot meet the increased demand; it is treated with revascularisation, usually stenting or bypass.
cards.q: A patient has abdominal pain 30 minutes after eating, avoids food and has lost weight over months. What is the likely diagnosis and its cause?

cards.a: Mesenteric venous thrombosis, clotting in the mesenteric veins, often in a hypercoagulable state such as a thrombophilia, malignancy or recent surgery. It causes gradual abdominal pain, often with bowel wall thickening on CT, and is treated mainly with anticoagulation unless the bowel is infarcted.
cards.q: A young patient with a known thrombophilia develops gradual abdominal pain over days and CT shows bowel wall thickening and a clot in the superior mesenteric vein. What is the diagnosis and the main treatment?

cards.a: Non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia, where severe hypotension or vasopressor use reduces blood flow to the gut without a clot. Management is restoring blood pressure and cardiac output, stopping vasoconstrictors where possible, and giving vasodilators into the mesenteric circulation if needed, because the problem is low flow rather than a blockage.
cards.q: A critically ill ICU patient on high-dose vasopressors develops abdominal pain and rising lactate with no clot on CT angiography. What is the diagnosis and its management?

cards.a: Ischaemic colitis, usually affecting the watershed areas of the colon such as the splenic flexure, which have the poorest collateral blood supply. It presents with crampy left-sided pain and bloody diarrhoea after a hypotensive episode, and is usually managed supportively with fluids and bowel rest unless there is infarction or perforation.
cards.q: An elderly patient develops bloody diarrhoea and left-sided abdominal pain after a period of low blood pressure. What is the likely diagnosis, and why is the splenic flexure involved?

cards.a: Signs of bowel infarction include worsening constant pain, peritoneal signs, fever, leucocytosis, metabolic acidosis and pneumatosis on CT. Infarcted bowel must be resected urgently, because leaving dead bowel causes perforation, peritonitis and sepsis.
cards.q: What findings suggest the bowel has infarcted in mesenteric ischaemia, and what is the next step?

cards.a: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding, usually from a peptic ulcer or varices. Initial management is airway protection if needed, large-bore IV access, resuscitation with IV fluids and blood, a restrictive transfusion threshold around 7 g per dL in a stable patient, and urgent endoscopy once resuscitated.
cards.q: A patient vomits blood and passes black tarry stools. What is the likely source, and what is the initial management?

cards.a: A restrictive strategy, transfusing when haemoglobin falls below about 7 g per dL in a haemodynamically stable patient without cardiac disease. Over-transfusion raises portal pressure and can worsen bleeding, especially in variceal bleeding, while a restrictive approach has better outcomes.
cards.q: What transfusion threshold is used in acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding, and why is a restrictive strategy preferred?

cards.a: High-dose IV proton pump inhibitor, resuscitation and endoscopy within 24 hours. Endoscopy can stop bleeding with clips, injection or thermal therapy, and the appearance of the ulcer, known as the Forrest classification, guides whether endoscopic therapy is needed and the risk of rebleeding.
cards.q: A patient has a bleeding duodenal ulcer. What is the medical and endoscopic management?

cards.a: A visible vessel or active bleeding at endoscopy carries a high risk of rebleeding, so endoscopic therapy such as clipping or thermal coagulation is needed. A clean-based ulcer has a low rebleeding risk and needs no endoscopic therapy, which is why the Forrest classification changes management.
cards.q: Why does the endoscopic appearance of a bleeding ulcer change management?

cards.a: Oesophageal varices from portal hypertension in cirrhosis. Management is resuscitation, IV antibiotics, a vasoactive drug such as octreotide to lower portal pressure, and urgent endoscopic band ligation; a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt is reserved for bleeding that cannot be controlled endoscopically.
cards.q: A cirrhotic patient vomits large amounts of blood. What is the most likely cause and the management?

cards.a: Band ligation places rubber bands around the varix to strangulate it, while sclerotherapy injects a sclerosant. Band ligation is preferred because it has fewer complications such as ulceration and stricture, and better control of bleeding.
cards.q: Why is band ligation preferred over sclerotherapy for oesophageal varices?

cards.a: Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt, a stent placed between the portal and hepatic veins to decompress the portal system. It is used when variceal bleeding cannot be controlled by endoscopy and drugs, because lowering portal pressure stops the bleeding at its source.
cards.q: When is a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt used in variceal bleeding, and why?

cards.a: A Mallory-Weiss tear, a mucosal tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction from forceful vomiting or retching. It usually stops bleeding on its own, so most patients need only supportive care and observation, with endoscopic therapy reserved for ongoing bleeding.
cards.q: A patient vomits bright red blood after repeated forceful vomiting following heavy drinking. What is the most likely diagnosis and its usual course?

cards.a: A Dieulafoy lesion, an abnormally large submucosal artery that erodes through the mucosa and bleeds briskly. It is diagnosed and treated at endoscopy with clipping or banding, because the bleeding comes from a single large vessel that needs mechanical haemostasis.
cards.q: A patient has sudden massive haematemesis with no ulcer or varices seen on endoscopy, but a small mucosal defect with a spurting vessel. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Diverticular bleeding, the commonest cause of lower gastrointestinal bleeding in older adults. Management is resuscitation, then colonoscopy after bowel preparation if the patient is stable; CT angiography is used if bleeding is brisk and the patient is unstable, because it localises the bleeding site.
cards.q: An elderly patient has painless bright red blood per rectum. What is the most likely cause, and what is the next step if the patient is stable?

cards.a: CT angiography. In brisk lower gastrointestinal bleeding it can localise the source if the bleeding rate is fast enough, and it can guide embolisation; colonoscopy is difficult and unsafe in an unstable, unprepared patient with active bleeding.
cards.q: A patient with lower gastrointestinal bleeding is unstable with ongoing brisk bleeding. What imaging is done next, and why not colonoscopy?

cards.a: Angiodysplasia, dilated tortuous blood vessels in the caecum and ascending colon, common in older patients and in aortic stenosis. It causes intermittent painless bleeding and is treated endoscopically with argon plasma coagulation, because the lesions are superficial vascular malformations.
cards.q: An elderly patient with aortic stenosis has recurrent painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding. Colonoscopy shows dilated tortuous vessels in the caecum. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Surgery is needed when endoscopic therapy fails, bleeding is massive and uncontrollable, or the source is a tumour or a lesion that cannot be reached endoscopically. The operation is usually a segmental resection of the bleeding segment, because removing the source is the only way to stop the bleeding when other methods fail.
cards.q: When is surgery indicated for gastrointestinal bleeding?

cards.a: An aortoenteric fistula, an abnormal connection between the aorta, often an aortic graft, and the bowel. It classically causes a small herald bleed followed by massive haemorrhage, and it is a surgical emergency needing urgent vascular surgery, because endoscopy cannot fix an aortic fistula.
cards.q: A patient with a previous aortic graft has a small bleed per rectum, then suddenly collapses with massive haematemesis and melaena. What is the diagnosis and the next step?

cards.a: Meckel diverticulum, a remnant of the vitelline duct containing ectopic gastric mucosa that ulcerates and bleeds. It is the commonest cause of painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding in children, and a technetium scan detects the ectopic gastric mucosa, guiding surgical resection.
cards.q: A child has painless bright red blood per rectum. What is the most likely cause, and what test confirms it?

cards.a: The anticoagulant should be held, and reversal given only if bleeding is life-threatening or surgery is needed, because reversing anticoagulation risks thrombosis. Most gastrointestinal bleeding in anticoagulated patients is managed with resuscitation and endoscopy first, with the decision to restart anticoagulation made once bleeding is controlled.
cards.q: A patient on warfarin has a gastrointestinal bleed. How do you manage the anticoagulation, and why?

cards.a: Capsule endoscopy, a swallowable camera that images the small bowel. It is used for obscure gastrointestinal bleeding when upper and lower endoscopy are normal, because the small bowel is beyond the reach of standard endoscopes and capsule endoscopy can find angiodysplasia, tumours or ulcers there.
cards.q: Upper and lower endoscopy are both normal in a patient with recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding and iron deficiency anaemia. What is the next test, and why?

cards.a: Rebleeding after failed endoscopic therapy is an indication for surgery, usually resection of the bleeding segment, because repeated endoscopy has a falling chance of success and ongoing bleeding causes transfusion dependence and haemodynamic instability. Angiographic embolisation is an alternative in high-risk surgical patients.
cards.q: A patient with a bleeding duodenal ulcer rebleeds after two attempts at endoscopic therapy. What is the next best step?

cards.a: The Alvarado score combines migratory pain, anorexia, nausea, right lower quadrant tenderness, rebound, fever and leucocytosis to stratify the likelihood of appendicitis. A low score supports discharge with safety-netting, while a high score supports imaging or surgical review, because it makes clinical judgement more consistent.
cards.q: What is the Alvarado score used for in suspected appendicitis?

cards.a: Mesenteric adenitis, inflammation of lymph nodes in the right lower quadrant, often after a viral illness in children. It mimics appendicitis with right lower quadrant pain and fever, but pain is usually less localised, there is often a recent sore throat or viral illness, and ultrasound shows enlarged lymph nodes with a normal appendix.
cards.q: A child has right lower quadrant pain, fever and a recent viral illness, but ultrasound shows a normal appendix and enlarged lymph nodes. What is the likely diagnosis?

cards.a: Wound infection, more common after perforated appendicitis or open surgery. It presents with wound erythema, pain and discharge a few days after surgery and is managed with wound opening, drainage and antibiotics, because infected wounds need drainage rather than antibiotics alone.
cards.q: A patient develops wound redness, pain and discharge 4 days after open appendicectomy for perforated appendicitis. What is the most likely complication and its management?

cards.a: Admit for observation, serial abdominal examinations and repeat imaging or diagnostic laparoscopy if pain persists or worsens. A normal CT does not completely exclude early appendicitis, and clinical deterioration is more important than a single negative scan.
cards.q: CT is normal but a patient still has convincing right lower quadrant pain and tenderness. What is the next step, and why?

cards.a: Gallstone ileus, where a large gallstone erodes through the gallbladder into the duodenum and blocks the small bowel, usually at the terminal ileum. CT shows a gallstone, pneumobilia and small bowel obstruction, known as Rigler triad, and treatment is surgery to remove the stone, with cholecystectomy often deferred.
cards.q: An elderly woman with gallstones develops small bowel obstruction, and CT shows a large gallstone in the ileum and air in the biliary tree. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Recurrent biliary colic is not an emergency, but the gallbladder should be removed electively because attacks recur and can progress to cholecystitis or pancreatitis; there is no need for emergency surgery between attacks.
cards.q: A patient has recurrent biliary colic with normal liver tests and no fever. What is the management?

cards.a: Cholangitis in older adults can present subtly with confusion, hypotension or vague abdominal pain rather than the full Charcot triad, because the immune response is blunted. A low threshold for liver tests, blood cultures and imaging is needed, since delayed decompression carries high mortality.
cards.q: Why can cholangitis be easy to miss in an elderly patient?

cards.a: Gallbladder empyema, pus filling the gallbladder, or gallbladder perforation. Both cause worsening right upper quadrant pain, fever and peritoneal signs, and need urgent cholecystectomy or percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics, because pus under pressure can perforate and cause peritonitis.
cards.q: A patient with acute cholecystitis worsens with severe right upper quadrant pain, high fever and peritoneal signs. What complication should you suspect?

cards.a: Conservative management is usually tried for 48 to 72 hours in adhesive small bowel obstruction without strangulation, using nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression and IV fluids. If the obstruction does not resolve, or the patient deteriorates, surgery is needed, because prolonged obstruction risks bowel ischaemia and the bowel wall becomes oedematous and harder to operate on.
cards.q: How long is conservative management usually tried for adhesive small bowel obstruction, and when is surgery indicated?

cards.a: A malignant large bowel obstruction, usually from colorectal cancer, may be treated with a self-expanding metal stent as a bridge to surgery or as palliation, because stenting decompresses the bowel and allows bowel preparation and staging before elective resection. Emergency surgery is still needed if there is perforation or ischaemia.
cards.q: A patient has a large bowel obstruction from a sigmoid cancer with no peritonitis. What is the role of a colonic stent?

cards.a: Endoscopic detorsion is contraindicated if there is peritonitis, perforation or ischaemia, because untwisting dead bowel can release bacteria and toxins into the circulation and delay the surgery that is needed. Emergency laparotomy with resection is the correct step instead.
cards.q: When is endoscopic detorsion contraindicated in sigmoid volvulus, and what should be done instead?

cards.a: Toxic megacolon, a severe complication of ulcerative colitis or infective colitis where the colon dilates massively and the wall becomes thin. It presents with abdominal distension, fever, tachycardia and systemic toxicity, and needs urgent medical treatment with IV steroids and antibiotics, with colectomy if there is perforation or failure to improve.
cards.q: A patient with ulcerative colitis develops massive colonic dilatation, fever, tachycardia and abdominal pain. What is the diagnosis and the management?

cards.a: Hinchey stage IV, faecal peritonitis from a free perforation of a diverticulum. It needs emergency surgery, usually Hartmann procedure, because faecal contamination causes overwhelming sepsis and must be controlled at source.
cards.q: What does Hinchey stage IV diverticulitis mean, and what is the management?

cards.a: A diverticular stricture, narrowing of the colon from repeated episodes of inflammation and fibrosis. It can cause a large bowel obstruction and can be hard to distinguish from colon cancer, so CT and colonoscopy after the acute phase are needed to exclude malignancy.
cards.q: A patient with a history of diverticulitis develops progressive constipation and a narrowed sigmoid colon on imaging. What complication is this?

cards.a: Pneumoperitoneum can occur without perforation after recent abdominal surgery, peritoneal dialysis, or prolonged mechanical ventilation, because air can enter the peritoneal cavity through these routes. The key is whether the patient has peritonitis; free air with a soft abdomen and no peritoneal signs can be observed, while free air with peritonitis needs surgery.
cards.q: Can free air under the diaphragm occur without a perforated viscus? Give examples and explain how management differs.

cards.a: A perforated gastric ulcer should raise suspicion of malignancy, unlike most duodenal ulcers. Biopsies of the ulcer edge should be taken at surgery and the ulcer should be sent for histology, because a gastric cancer can present as a perforation and needs different follow-up and treatment.
cards.q: Why should a perforated gastric ulcer be biopsied, and how does it differ from a perforated duodenal ulcer?

cards.a: Boerhaave syndrome is managed with resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, nil by mouth and urgent surgical repair or, in selected stable patients with a contained leak, endoscopic stenting. Early treatment matters because mediastinal contamination causes rapid sepsis and high mortality.
cards.q: What is the management of Boerhaave syndrome, and why is early treatment important?

cards.a: Resuscitation with IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics within the first hour, source control, and monitoring in intensive care. Peritonitis causes sepsis with fluid loss into the abdomen and third spacing, so early antibiotics and fluids reduce mortality while surgery removes the source.
cards.q: A patient has generalised peritonitis and septic shock. What is the initial management and why is timing important?

cards.a: Watchful waiting is reasonable for a minimally symptomatic inguinal hernia in an older man with significant comorbidities, because the risk of strangulation is low and surgery carries risk. Any hernia that becomes painful, irreducible or strangulated needs prompt surgery.
cards.q: When is watchful waiting reasonable for an inguinal hernia, and when is surgery needed?

cards.a: Because atrial fibrillation causes emboli that lodge in the superior mesenteric artery, cutting off blood flow to the midgut. Patients with new atrial fibrillation and acute abdominal pain should be assessed urgently for mesenteric ischaemia, and heparin should be started early to prevent clot extension while revascularisation is arranged.
cards.q: Why is new atrial fibrillation a risk factor for acute mesenteric ischaemia, and what should be started early?

cards.a: Mesenteric venous thrombosis is treated with anticoagulation for at least 3 to 6 months, and longer if there is an ongoing thrombophilia or malignancy. A thrombophilia workup is done after the acute phase, because finding the underlying cause determines how long anticoagulation should continue.
cards.q: How long is anticoagulation given for mesenteric venous thrombosis, and what workup follows?

cards.a: Chronic mesenteric ischaemia is treated with revascularisation, usually endovascular stenting of the superior mesenteric artery, or surgical bypass if stenting is not suitable. Restoring blood flow relieves postprandial pain and allows the patient to eat and gain weight, which is why medical treatment alone is not enough.
cards.q: What is the definitive treatment of chronic mesenteric ischaemia, and why?

cards.a: Testing for and eradicating Helicobacter pylori after a peptic ulcer bleed, because the infection is a major cause of ulcer recurrence and rebleeding. Eradication plus a proton pump inhibitor reduces the risk of another bleed, which is why it is part of standard follow-up.
cards.q: Why should Helicobacter pylori be tested for and treated after a peptic ulcer bleed?

cards.a: Gastric varices are treated with endoscopic injection of tissue glue such as cyanoacrylate, rather than band ligation, because gastric varices are larger and deeper and bands often fail to control bleeding. A transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt is used if glue injection fails.
cards.q: How are bleeding gastric varices treated differently from oesophageal varices, and why?

cards.a: Colonoscopy for lower gastrointestinal bleeding is usually done after bowel preparation once the patient is stable and resuscitated, ideally within 24 hours. Preparation is needed to see the mucosa clearly, and doing it too early in an unstable patient risks missing the source and worsening the situation.
cards.q: When should colonoscopy be done in lower gastrointestinal bleeding, and why is bowel preparation needed?

cards.a: Double-balloon enteroscopy, an endoscope that can reach deep into the small bowel. It is used when capsule endoscopy finds a bleeding lesion in the small bowel, because it allows both diagnosis and treatment such as clipping or coagulation of the lesion.
cards.q: Capsule endoscopy finds a bleeding angiodysplasia in the small bowel. What is the next step, and why?

cards.a: An incidental Meckel diverticulum found at surgery in an adult is usually left alone if it is narrow-based and has no complications, because the risk of future problems is low and resection adds risk. A wide-based or inflamed diverticulum, or one with a palpable mass, is usually resected.
cards.q: A Meckel diverticulum is found incidentally during surgery in an adult with no symptoms from it. Should it be removed, and why?

cards.a: Antibiotics are given in acute variceal bleeding in cirrhosis, because they reduce the risk of infection and rebleeding and improve survival. Infection is common in cirrhotic patients with bleeding and worsens outcomes, so antibiotics are part of standard care, not just for confirmed infection.
cards.q: Why are antibiotics given in acute variceal bleeding in cirrhosis?

cards.a: Balanced massive transfusion with red cells, plasma and platelets in roughly equal ratios, guided by blood tests and clinical response. In massive gastrointestinal bleeding, replacing clotting factors alongside red cells prevents coagulopathy, which is why giving red cells alone is not enough.
cards.q: What transfusion approach is used in massive gastrointestinal bleeding, and why?

cards.a: Appendicitis in children progresses to perforation more quickly than in adults, partly because the omentum is less developed and cannot wall off the inflamed appendix. Early diagnosis and prompt surgery matter more in children for this reason, and a low threshold for imaging is needed.
cards.q: Why does appendicitis perforate more quickly in children?

cards.a: Sepsis from an intra-abdominal source needs early antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, lactate measurement and urgent source control, because each hour of delay in source control increases mortality. This is why a patient with peritonitis and septic shock goes to theatre promptly rather than waiting for prolonged optimisation.
cards.q: A patient with peritonitis has septic shock. Why is urgent source control more important than prolonged preoperative optimisation?

cards.a: The ileocaecal valve often stays competent in large bowel obstruction, so gas and fluid cannot decompress backwards into the small bowel and the caecum distends most, because it has the largest diameter. A caecum over about 10 to 12 cm is at high risk of perforation, which is why caecal diameter is watched on imaging.
cards.q: Why is the caecum at highest risk of perforation in large bowel obstruction?
A 65-year-old man has left lower quadrant pain, fever and a raised white cell count for 3 days. What is the most likely diagnosis?
cards.a: Diverticulitis, inflammation of a colonic diverticulum, usually in the sigmoid colon. It presents with left lower quadrant pain, fever, a raised white cell count and change in bowel habit, because faecal matter obstructs a diverticulum and bacteria invade its wall.

cards.q: What is the best imaging test for suspected acute diverticulitis, and why is colonoscopy avoided during the acute episode?
cards.a: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast. It confirms colonic wall thickening, fat stranding and diverticula, and shows complications such as abscess, perforation or fistula that change management, which is why it is preferred over colonoscopy during an acute episode, when the inflamed colon risks perforation.

cards.q: When can acute diverticulitis be managed as an outpatient, and when does it need admission?
cards.a: Uncomplicated diverticulitis without abscess or perforation, in a stable patient who can tolerate oral intake, can be managed as an outpatient with a clear liquid diet and close follow-up, with or without antibiotics, because uncomplicated inflammation often settles on its own. Admission is needed with fever, leucocytosis, immunosuppression or inability to take fluids.

cards.q: A patient with diverticulitis has a 5 cm pericolic abscess on CT. What is the management, and why is drainage needed?
cards.a: Percutaneous drainage plus IV antibiotics. An abscess larger than about 3 to 4 cm is too large for antibiotics to penetrate reliably, so draining it removes the infected collection, while smaller abscesses often settle with antibiotics alone.

cards.q: A patient with diverticulitis develops severe generalised abdominal pain, rigidity, hypotension and free air on imaging. What is the diagnosis and the next best step?
cards.a: Perforated diverticulitis with generalised peritonitis. This is a surgical emergency needing resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics and emergency surgery, usually Hartmann procedure with a colostomy, because faecal contamination of the peritoneum causes sepsis and must be controlled at source.

cards.q: After an episode of acute diverticulitis, when should colonoscopy be done, and why is it delayed?
cards.a: Colonoscopy is deferred until about 6 to 8 weeks after the acute episode settles. The colon wall is inflamed and friable during acute diverticulitis, so colonoscopy risks perforation; waiting lets inflammation resolve and allows a safe check for an underlying cancer that can mimic diverticulitis.

cards.q: What does free air under the diaphragm on an erect chest X-ray suggest, and why?
cards.a: Free air under the diaphragm on an erect chest X-ray suggests a perforated viscus, from gas escaping through a hole in a hollow organ into the peritoneal cavity. It is the classic sign of a perforated viscus and, with peritonitis, is an indication for urgent surgery.

cards.q: A patient develops sudden severe epigastric pain, a rigid abdomen and free air under the diaphragm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
cards.a: Perforated peptic ulcer, usually duodenal. Sudden severe epigastric pain, board-like rigidity, tachycardia and free air under the diaphragm suggest a hole in the stomach or duodenum, often linked to NSAIDs or Helicobacter pylori, and it needs urgent resuscitation and surgery.

cards.q: What operation is most commonly done for a perforated duodenal ulcer, and why?
cards.a: Graham patch, an omental patch sewn over the perforation to seal it. It closes the hole without resecting stomach, preserves gastric function and is quick in a sick patient; definitive ulcer surgery such as vagotomy is rarely done now because proton pump inhibitors and Helicobacter pylori eradication control acid afterwards.

cards.q: Why do NSAIDs increase the risk of peptic ulcer perforation?
cards.a: NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin production, which reduces the protective mucus and bicarbonate layer of the stomach and duodenum, leaving the mucosa exposed to acid. This can cause ulceration and perforation, often without much warning pain, especially in older patients and those on steroids or anticoagulants.

cards.q: How do you distinguish secondary peritonitis from spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and why does it matter?
cards.a: Secondary peritonitis comes from a hole in a hollow organ and needs surgery to close it, whereas spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is infection of ascitic fluid in cirrhosis without a perforation and is treated with antibiotics and albumin, not surgery. Distinguishing them matters because operating on spontaneous bacterial peritonitis worsens outcomes.

cards.q: A patient is unwell with fever, tachycardia and abdominal pain 5 days after bowel resection. What complication should you suspect, and why?
cards.a: Anastomotic leak, where the join between two pieces of bowel fails and bowel contents leak into the abdomen. It presents with fever, tachycardia, abdominal pain and rising inflammatory markers a few days after surgery, and needs imaging, antibiotics, drainage and often reoperation, because ongoing leakage causes sepsis.

cards.q: What is the difference between an incarcerated and a strangulated hernia?
cards.a: Incarcerated means the hernia cannot be pushed back but the bowel blood supply is still intact; strangulated means the blood supply is cut off, causing ischaemia, severe constant pain, a tense tender irreducible lump and often signs of obstruction or sepsis. Strangulation is a surgical emergency, while incarceration still needs urgent surgery but is less immediately life-threatening.

An abdominal aortic aneurysm is a dilatation of the abdominal aorta to 3 cm or more, or more than 50 percent wider than normal. It is most often infrarenal, below the renal arteries, because that segment has less supporting tissue and more atherosclerosis, so screening and repair decisions focus there.
cards.q: What size defines an abdominal aortic aneurysm, and where is it most often found?

cards.a: Screen men aged 65 to 75 who have ever smoked, with a one-time abdominal ultrasound. Smoking is the strongest risk factor, and ultrasound is cheap, non-invasive and accurate for size, so a single screen catches most aneurysms before they rupture.
cards.q: Who should be screened once for abdominal aortic aneurysm, and with what test?

cards.a: Older age, male sex, smoking, hypertension, atherosclerosis, family history, and connective tissue disease. Smoking matters most because it damages the aortic wall and speeds expansion, which is why cessation is part of every management plan.
cards.q: What are the main risk factors for abdominal aortic aneurysm?

cards.a: Surveillance with repeat ultrasound, smoking cessation, blood pressure and cholesterol control, and no surgery yet. Small aneurysms rupture rarely, so the risk of repair outweighs the benefit until the aneurysm reaches the repair threshold or grows fast.
cards.q: A 68-year-old man has a 4.2 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm found on ultrasound. What is the next step?

cards.a: Repeat imaging every 6 to 12 months, usually ultrasound, sooner if symptoms appear. This size is close enough to the repair threshold that regular checks catch rapid growth before rupture, without exposing the patient to repeated CT radiation.
cards.q: How often should a 4.0 to 4.9 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm be followed?

cards.a: 5.5 cm or larger. Above this size the yearly rupture risk rises steeply and exceeds the operative risk of repair, so elective repair becomes the safer choice.
cards.q: What size abdominal aortic aneurysm usually triggers elective repair in a man?

cards.a: 5.0 cm or larger. Women rupture at smaller diameters than men, so the threshold is lower, because waiting to 5.5 cm would leave a higher rupture risk untreated.
cards.q: What size abdominal aortic aneurysm usually triggers elective repair in a woman?

cards.a: Growth of 0.5 cm or more in 6 months, or 1 cm or more in one year. Rapid growth signals an unstable wall and a rising rupture risk, so size alone should not delay repair.
cards.q: What growth rate of an abdominal aortic aneurysm is an indication for repair even if it is below 5.5 cm?

cards.a: Treat it as symptomatic or impending rupture and arrange urgent surgical evaluation, with CT angiography only if the patient is stable enough. Pain and tenderness mean the wall is stretching or leaking, so the size threshold no longer applies.
cards.q: A patient with a 4.8 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm has new severe back pain and a tender pulsatile mass. What is the next step?

cards.a: Severe abdominal or back pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile abdominal mass. The triad is present in only a minority of cases, so do not wait for all three before acting when rupture is suspected.
cards.q: What is the classic triad of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm?

cards.a: Resuscitate with blood products, allow permissive hypotension, and go straight to the operating room or endovascular suite without delaying for CT. Imaging in an unstable patient wastes time and increases mortality, because the diagnosis is clinical and the treatment is bleeding control.
cards.q: A hypotensive patient has a suspected ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. What is the immediate management?

cards.a: CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis. It confirms rupture, shows the anatomy for endovascular versus open repair, and is fast, which is why it is the test of choice when the patient can safely tolerate the scan.
cards.q: A haemodynamically stable patient has suspected rupture of an abdominal aortic aneurysm. What imaging is best?

cards.a: Open repair replaces the aneurysm with a graft through a laparotomy and lasts longer, while EVAR places a stent-graft from inside the artery through the groins with a quicker recovery but a need for lifelong surveillance. The choice depends on anatomy, age, and operative fitness.
cards.q: What is the difference between open repair and endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) for abdominal aortic aneurysm?

cards.a: A short, angulated, or heavily calcified aortic neck, or iliac arteries too narrow or tortuous for the device. EVAR needs a good seal zone above and below the aneurysm, so poor anatomy risks a leak and makes open repair safer.
cards.q: What anatomical feature makes a patient unsuitable for EVAR?

cards.a: To detect endoleak, graft migration, and sac growth, which can lead to late rupture even after a successful repair. EVAR does not remove the aneurysm sac, so surveillance, usually with CT or ultrasound, is part of the treatment.
cards.q: Why does a patient need lifelong imaging after EVAR?

cards.a: An endoleak is persistent blood flow into the aneurysm sac outside the stent-graft. Type I and type III leaks come from a poor seal or a graft defect and carry a high rupture risk, so they need prompt repair, while type II leaks from branch vessels are often watched.
cards.q: What is an endoleak after EVAR, and which type is most concerning?

cards.a: Smoking cessation, a statin, blood pressure control, and an antiplatelet agent if there is other atherosclerotic disease. These slow expansion and reduce heart attack and stroke risk, which are the commonest causes of death in these patients.
cards.q: What medical therapy should every patient with an abdominal aortic aneurysm receive?

cards.a: An aortoenteric fistula, a connection between the graft and the bowel, often heralded by a small sentinel bleed. It is life-threatening and needs urgent CT angiography and surgical evaluation, because endoscopy often misses it.
cards.q: A patient with an abdominal aortic aneurysm has a gastrointestinal bleed months after open repair. What must be suspected?

cards.a: Cardiac events, especially myocardial infarction. These patients have widespread atherosclerosis, so pre-operative cardiac risk assessment and peri-operative statin and beta-blocker management matter as much as the aneurysm itself.
cards.q: What is the most common cause of death after elective abdominal aortic aneurysm repair?

cards.a: Saccular aneurysms bulge on one side of the wall and rupture at smaller sizes than fusiform aneurysms, which involve the whole circumference. Their shape concentrates wall stress, so the repair threshold is lower.
cards.q: A saccular abdominal aortic aneurysm measures 4.5 cm. Why might it be repaired earlier than a fusiform aneurysm of the same size?

cards.a: The ankle-brachial index is the ankle systolic pressure divided by the brachial systolic pressure. A value below 0.90 diagnoses peripheral arterial disease, because a pressure drop across the leg means a flow-limiting stenosis is present.
cards.q: What is the ankle-brachial index, and what value diagnoses peripheral arterial disease?

cards.a: Intermittent claudication, cramping calf pain on walking that is relieved within minutes by rest. Exercise raises muscle oxygen demand beyond what the narrowed artery can supply, and rest lowers demand, which is why the pain follows this pattern.
cards.q: What is the classic symptom of peripheral arterial disease, and what relieves it?

cards.a: Supervised exercise therapy, smoking cessation, and risk-factor control, before any procedure. Walking training builds collateral vessels and improves walking distance, and revascularisation alone does not fix the underlying atherosclerosis.
cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for intermittent claudication?

cards.a: That the patient does not have heart failure. Cilostazol is contraindicated in heart failure because it is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor with a similar concern to other drugs in that class, and it can worsen heart failure.
cards.q: A patient with claudication is started on cilostazol. What must be checked first?

cards.a: An antiplatelet agent, a high-intensity statin, blood pressure control, smoking cessation, and diabetes control. Peripheral arterial disease is a marker of systemic atherosclerosis, so the main goal is preventing heart attack, stroke, and death, not just leg symptoms.
cards.q: What medical therapy should every patient with peripheral arterial disease receive?

cards.a: Rest pain for more than two weeks, a non-healing ulcer, or gangrene, with an ankle pressure below 50 mmHg or a toe pressure below 30 mmHg. These mean the leg is not getting enough blood even at rest, so without revascularisation the limb is at high risk of amputation.
cards.q: What findings define critical limb ischaemia?

cards.a: Medial calcification makes the ankle arteries stiff and non-compressible, so the cuff pressure reads falsely high. In that situation use the toe-brachial index or toe pressures, because toe arteries calcify less.
cards.q: Why can the ankle-brachial index be falsely normal or high in a diabetic patient with peripheral arterial disease?

cards.a: It confirms flow-limiting peripheral arterial disease that is worse under stress. Exercise increases leg blood flow demand, so a stenosis that is borderline at rest causes a bigger pressure drop after walking.
cards.q: A patient with peripheral arterial disease has an ankle-brachial index of 0.85 at rest that falls after exercise. What does this mean?

cards.a: Aortoiliac occlusive disease causing the triad of bilateral buttock and thigh claudication, erectile dysfunction, and absent femoral pulses. It reflects blockage at the aortic bifurcation, so the symptoms are proximal and bilateral rather than in one calf.
cards.q: What is Leriche syndrome?

cards.a: For critical limb ischaemia, or for lifestyle-limiting claudication that has not improved with exercise and medical therapy. Revascularisation restores flow when the limb is threatened or symptoms limit daily life despite conservative treatment.
cards.q: When is revascularisation indicated for peripheral arterial disease?

cards.a: The anatomy and length of the blockage, the quality of the vein for a bypass conduit, the patient's operative risk, and the availability of a good outflow vessel. Short focal lesions favour angioplasty and stenting, while long occlusions with a good saphenous vein often favour bypass.
cards.q: What determines whether a patient with critical limb ischaemia gets endovascular treatment or bypass surgery?

cards.a: Thromboangiitis obliterans, or Buerger disease, an inflammatory vasculitis of small and medium vessels in young smokers. The key treatment is complete smoking cessation, because continued smoking drives progression to amputation.
cards.q: A young heavy smoker has painful finger and toe ulcers, Raynaud phenomenon, and normal pulses proximally. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome, where the popliteal artery is compressed by muscle or fibrous bands during exercise. It affects young active people without risk factors, so the diagnosis is missed if only atherosclerosis is considered.
cards.q: A young athlete has calf claudication and a normal ankle-brachial index at rest that falls after exercise, with no atherosclerosis. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Offloading pressure from the ulcer, plus wound care, infection control, glycaemic control, and revascularisation if there is critical ischaemia. Pressure keeps the wound open, so no dressing or antibiotic will heal it until the foot is offloaded.
cards.q: What is the most important step in managing a diabetic foot ulcer with peripheral arterial disease?

cards.a: Chronic mesenteric ischaemia from atherosclerotic stenosis of the mesenteric arteries. Eating increases gut blood demand that the narrowed arteries cannot meet, causing pain after meals and avoidance of food.
cards.q: A patient has postprandial abdominal pain, food fear, and weight loss. What vascular diagnosis is suspected?

cards.a: Stenosis of the subclavian artery proximal to the vertebral artery, causing blood to flow backwards down the vertebral artery to supply the arm, which can cause dizziness and arm claudication. It matters most when the arm is exercised or when the vertebral artery is needed for brain perfusion.
cards.q: What is subclavian steal syndrome?

cards.a: Coronary artery disease, because peripheral arterial disease is systemic atherosclerosis and many of these patients have silent coronary disease. Their cardiac risk is high, which is why statin, antiplatelet, and blood pressure treatment are central.
cards.q: A patient with peripheral arterial disease also needs screening for what other condition?

cards.a: For resistant hypertension, flash pulmonary oedema, or progressive kidney failure with a significant stenosis and a viable kidney. Most renal artery stenosis is managed medically, and stenting is reserved for these high-risk presentations.
cards.q: When is revascularisation considered for renal artery stenosis?

cards.a: Carotid duplex ultrasound. It is non-invasive, quick, and measures flow velocity to grade stenosis, so it is the standard first test before CT or MR angiography.
cards.q: What is the first test for suspected carotid artery stenosis after a transient ischaemic attack?

cards.a: Carotid endarterectomy within two weeks, plus antiplatelet therapy, a statin, and risk-factor control. The stroke risk is highest in the first days after a transient ischaemic attack, so early surgery prevents the next, often disabling, stroke.
cards.q: A patient had a transient ischaemic attack and duplex shows 70 to 99 percent ipsilateral carotid stenosis. What is the management?

cards.a: Consider carotid endarterectomy in selected patients, especially men with recent hemispheric symptoms, and otherwise treat medically. The benefit of surgery is smaller at this degree of stenosis, so patient selection matters.
cards.q: A patient had a transient ischaemic attack and duplex shows 50 to 69 percent ipsilateral carotid stenosis. What is the management?

cards.a: Medical therapy only, with an antiplatelet agent, a statin, blood pressure control, and smoking cessation. Surgery does not reduce stroke risk at this degree of stenosis, so the risks of operation outweigh any benefit.
cards.q: A patient had a transient ischaemic attack and duplex shows less than 50 percent ipsilateral carotid stenosis. What is the management?

cards.a: For 70 to 99 percent stenosis in a patient with a long life expectancy and a low peri-operative stroke and death risk, usually under 3 percent. The benefit is small and takes years to appear, so it only helps if the surgical risk is very low.
cards.q: When is carotid endarterectomy considered for asymptomatic carotid stenosis?

cards.a: Less than 6 percent. If the surgeon's or centre's rate is higher, the operation causes more strokes than it prevents, so medical therapy becomes the safer choice.
cards.q: What is the maximum acceptable peri-operative stroke and death rate for carotid endarterectomy in symptomatic patients?

cards.a: A bruit can be heard with mild stenosis, with turbulent flow from another cause, or be absent with a near-occlusion where flow is too low to make sound. Duplex ultrasound measures velocity directly, so it grades stenosis far more accurately.
cards.q: Why is a carotid bruit not a reliable test for carotid stenosis?

cards.a: Endarterectomy removes the plaque surgically through a neck incision, while stenting places a stent from inside the artery through the groin or arm. Endarterectomy is preferred in most symptomatic older patients, while stenting is considered when surgery is high risk or the anatomy is unfavourable.
cards.q: What is the difference between carotid endarterectomy and carotid artery stenting?

cards.a: Patients with a high neck, prior neck surgery or radiation, a lesion too high to reach surgically, or severe cardiac or lung disease making general anaesthesia risky. Stenting avoids a neck operation, so it helps when the surgical approach itself is the problem.
cards.q: Which patients are better suited to carotid artery stenting than endarterectomy?

cards.a: Repeated transient ischaemic attacks over hours to days with increasing frequency. It signals an unstable carotid plaque at high risk of a completed stroke, so it needs urgent admission, imaging, and expedited carotid revascularisation.
cards.q: What is crescendo transient ischaemic attack, and what is the next step?

cards.a: Headache, seizures, confusion, or brain haemorrhage days after surgery from sudden restoration of blood flow to a brain that had adapted to low flow. It is more likely with severe stenosis and poor collaterals, and strict blood pressure control after surgery reduces the risk.
cards.q: What is cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome after carotid endarterectomy?

cards.a: The hypoglossal nerve, causing tongue deviation toward the operated side. It runs close to the carotid bifurcation, so retraction or dissection can stretch it, and most injuries are temporary.
cards.q: What cranial nerve is most commonly injured during carotid endarterectomy?

cards.a: The symptomatic side first. It carries the immediate stroke risk, while the asymptomatic side can be assessed later, because treating the wrong side first leaves the dangerous lesion untreated.
cards.q: A patient has bilateral carotid stenosis, one side symptomatic and one side asymptomatic. Which side is treated first?

cards.a: Operating too soon risks turning an infarct haemorrhagic from restored blood flow into damaged brain. Surgery is delayed until the infarct has stabilised, usually by at least a few days to weeks depending on size, while medical therapy continues.
cards.q: Why is carotid endarterectomy usually delayed after a large completed stroke?

cards.a: Carotid artery dissection, a tear in the vessel wall that can cause a stroke in young people without atherosclerosis. It is diagnosed with CT or MR angiography and usually treated with anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy.
cards.q: A young patient has a stroke after neck trauma or sudden neck movement. What vascular diagnosis is suspected?

cards.a: An antiplatelet agent, a high-intensity statin, blood pressure control, and smoking cessation, plus duplex surveillance. Surgery removes the plaque but not the underlying atherosclerosis, so medical therapy prevents stroke from other vessels and restenosis.
cards.q: What medical therapy should a patient receive after carotid endarterectomy?

cards.a: Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, and poikilothermia, meaning a cold limb. They describe an acutely threatened limb, and paraesthesia and paralysis are the most worrying because they signal nerve and muscle damage.
cards.q: What are the six Ps of acute limb ischaemia?

cards.a: It grades limb viability from viable, to threatened but salvageable, to irreversible, based on pain, sensory loss, motor loss, and Doppler signals. It guides how urgently revascularisation is needed and whether amputation is the only option.
cards.q: What is the Rutherford classification of acute limb ischaemia used for?

cards.a: Atrial fibrillation, with clot forming in the left atrium and travelling to a leg artery. The embolus usually lodges at a bifurcation in a previously normal artery, so the onset is sudden and the other leg is often normal.
cards.q: What is the most common cause of acute limb ischaemia from an embolus?

cards.a: Thrombosis occurs on top of pre-existing atherosclerosis, so the onset is often less sudden and there is a history of claudication, while embolism is sudden in a previously healthy leg. The distinction matters because thrombosis often needs bypass or thrombolysis rather than simple embolectomy.
cards.q: How does acute arterial thrombosis differ from embolism as a cause of acute limb ischaemia?

cards.a: Give intravenous unfractionated heparin, provide analgesia, keep the limb at heart level, and arrange urgent vascular surgery review. Heparin prevents the clot from extending while the plan is made, and delay increases the risk of irreversible damage.
cards.q: What is the immediate management of suspected acute limb ischaemia?

cards.a: Because muscle and nerve die within hours, and the priority is restoring blood flow. CT angiography is useful when the diagnosis is uncertain or the limb is viable, but a threatened limb needs the operating room, not a prolonged work-up.
cards.q: Why should imaging not delay treatment in a patient with a clearly threatened limb?

cards.a: The limb is threatened but still salvageable, because veins are still draining while arterial inflow is lost. Loss of both arterial and venous signals suggests irreversible ischaemia, so this distinction helps decide urgency.
cards.q: What does a venous Doppler signal with no arterial Doppler signal mean in acute limb ischaemia?

cards.a: Fixed mottling, muscle rigor, profound sensory and motor loss, and absent arterial and venous Doppler signals. These mean the tissue is already dead, so revascularisation will not save the limb and amputation is needed.
cards.q: What signs indicate irreversible acute limb ischaemia?

cards.a: As soon as possible, ideally within 6 hours of onset. Skeletal muscle tolerates ischaemia for only a few hours, so every hour of delay increases the risk of amputation and death.
cards.q: What is the time window for revascularisation in acute limb ischaemia?

cards.a: A surgical procedure where a balloon-tipped catheter is passed beyond a clot and inflated to pull the embolus out of the artery. It is the classic treatment for an embolic occlusion in a healthy artery, because it restores flow quickly without needing thrombolysis.
cards.q: What is a Fogarty embolectomy?

cards.a: For a viable or marginally threatened limb from thrombosis, especially with a long clot burden or an unclear source, when there is no immediate threat to the limb. It dissolves clot slowly over hours, so it is not suitable for an immediately threatened limb.
cards.q: When is catheter-directed thrombolysis preferred for acute limb ischaemia?

cards.a: Recent surgery, recent stroke, active bleeding, or a known bleeding disorder. Thrombolysis carries a major bleeding risk, so it must not be used when bleeding would be catastrophic.
cards.q: What is a contraindication to thrombolysis for acute limb ischaemia?

cards.a: Swelling of reperfused muscle inside a tight fascial compartment, causing severe pain, tense compartments, and loss of pulses. It is treated with urgent fasciotomy, because the pressure itself cuts off blood flow and will kill the muscle if not released.
cards.q: What is compartment syndrome after revascularisation of an ischaemic limb, and how is it treated?

cards.a: Release of potassium, acid, and muscle breakdown products into the blood, causing hyperkalaemia, acidosis, arrhythmia, and acute kidney injury. It happens because ischaemic tissue accumulates toxic metabolites that flood the circulation once flow returns, so electrolytes and kidney function must be monitored.
cards.q: What is reperfusion injury after restoring flow to an ischaemic limb?

cards.a: Cholesterol embolisation syndrome, where cholesterol crystals are dislodged from aortic plaque during a catheter procedure. It affects the skin, kidneys, and other organs, and the key is supportive care and avoiding further arterial procedures.
cards.q: A patient develops painful blue toes, livedo reticularis, and kidney failure after an angiogram. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Search for the embolic source, usually with an ECG, echocardiogram, and rhythm monitoring for atrial fibrillation, plus long-term anticoagulation. Removing the clot does not stop the next embolus, so the source must be found and treated.
cards.q: After an embolectomy for acute limb ischaemia, what work-up is needed?

cards.a: Because urgent surgery or angiography may be needed, and fluids support blood pressure and kidney function during reperfusion. It is preparation for a time-critical procedure, not just supportive care.
cards.q: Why is a patient with acute limb ischaemia kept nil by mouth and given intravenous fluids?

cards.a: It estimates the pre-test probability of deep vein thrombosis from clinical features such as calf swelling, tenderness, cancer, and immobility. It guides whether a D-dimer can safely rule out a clot or whether ultrasound is needed.
cards.q: What is the Wells score used for in suspected deep vein thrombosis?
