cards.q: A woman has greenish or milky discharge from both nipples. Is this concerning for cancer?
cards.a: Usually not. Discharge from multiple ducts in both breasts is more often hormonal or medication-related, for example from high prolactin. Single-duct, bloody, or spontaneous discharge from one breast is the pattern that needs workup for a papilloma or cancer.

cards.q: A woman has cyclical breast pain and lumpiness that worsens before her period. What is this and how is it managed?
cards.a: Fibrocystic change, a common benign condition where hormonal swings cause cysts and tender, lumpy tissue. Management is reassurance, a well-fitting bra, and pain relief; a new dominant lump that persists after the period still needs imaging and biopsy because cancer can hide in lumpy breasts.

cards.q: A woman has eczema-like scaling and crusting of the nipple that does not heal with steroid cream. What must be ruled out?
cards.a: Paget disease of the nipple, a cancer of the nipple skin that is almost always linked to an underlying ductal cancer in the breast. A punch biopsy of the nipple skin is needed, plus mammography; treatment is surgery for the underlying cancer, not more cream.

cards.q: A 45-year-old man has a painless lump under his nipple. What should be considered?
cards.a: Male breast cancer, which is uncommon but real, and gynecomastia, which is usually tender and bilateral. A unilateral hard lump in a man needs mammography and core needle biopsy just as in a woman, because male breast cancer is usually found late and is treated the same way.

cards.q: A woman with a breast lump has a biopsy showing atypical ductal hyperplasia. What does this mean?
cards.a: It is a precancerous change where duct cells look abnormal but not enough to call it cancer. It raises the future risk of breast cancer in both breasts, so management is close surveillance and discussion of risk-reducing endocrine therapy; surgery is only to remove the area if the biopsy may have missed cancer.

cards.q: A woman asks when to start breast cancer screening and how often. What is the standard advice?
cards.a: Average-risk women start yearly or every-other-year mammograms around age 40 to 50 and continue as long as they are healthy. Screening finds cancers before they can be felt, when treatment is simpler and survival is better; the exact start age is a shared decision with her doctor.

cards.q: A woman with a strong family history of breast cancer has a normal mammogram but dense breasts. What additional screening is considered?
cards.a: Breast MRI, which is more sensitive than mammography in dense tissue and in high-risk women. MRI is used alongside mammography, not instead of it, because MRI finds more cancers but also more false positives that need biopsy.

cards.q: A patient has a breast mass and the biopsy result is fat necrosis. What caused it and what is the management?
cards.a: Fat necrosis follows trauma or surgery to the breast, where damaged fat forms a firm lump that can look like cancer on exam and mammogram. Once biopsy proves it is benign, no treatment is needed beyond reassurance, though a lump that keeps changing still needs re-evaluation.

cards.q: A woman has a large, rapidly growing breast mass and the biopsy shows a phyllodes tumor. How is it treated?
cards.a: Surgical removal with wide clear margins, because phyllodes tumors can grow back locally and occasionally spread. Unlike ordinary breast cancer, lymph node removal is usually not needed because spread is through the blood, not the lymph nodes.

cards.q: A woman has nipple inversion that is new in one breast. What is the concern and next step?
cards.a: An underlying cancer pulling the nipple inward, or a benign duct problem. New unilateral nipple retraction needs mammography, ultrasound, and biopsy of any underlying mass, because long-standing inversion on both sides is usually benign but a new change on one side is not.

cards.q: A dark, irregular mole on the back has changed in size and color over 6 months. What is the next step?
cards.a: Full-thickness excisional biopsy with a narrow margin of normal skin. A changing pigmented lesion must be removed whole for diagnosis, because a shave or punch biopsy can miss the depth of a melanoma, and depth decides the treatment. Do not watch a changing mole.

cards.q: What are the ABCDE features that raise concern for melanoma?
cards.a: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter larger than 6 mm (about a pencil eraser), and Evolving change over time. Any lesion with these features needs prompt biopsy; evolution, meaning any change, is the most important single warning sign.

cards.q: A biopsy confirms melanoma. What single feature most determines prognosis and further treatment?
cards.a: Breslow thickness, the depth of the tumor measured in millimeters from the skin surface. Thicker melanomas are more likely to have spread to lymph nodes and beyond, so thickness decides the width of the surgical margin and whether a sentinel lymph node biopsy is needed.

cards.q: A melanoma is 1.5 mm thick with no ulceration. What surgery is needed?
cards.a: Wide local excision with a 1 to 2 cm margin of normal skin around the melanoma, plus sentinel lymph node biopsy. The margin removes microscopic cancer cells around the visible tumor, and the sentinel node check stages the disease; thicker tumors need wider margins.

cards.q: A melanoma is 0.5 mm thick. What is the management?
cards.a: Wide local excision with a 1 cm margin and no sentinel lymph node biopsy. Very thin melanomas have a very low risk of lymph node spread, so node surgery adds risk without benefit, and the prognosis after complete excision is excellent.

cards.q: A patient with melanoma has a positive sentinel lymph node. What happens next?
cards.a: Staging is completed with imaging, and discussion of further treatment such as completion lymph node dissection or, more often now, adjuvant immunotherapy or targeted therapy. A positive node means stage III disease with a higher risk of recurrence, so systemic treatment is considered even though the visible tumor was removed.

cards.q: A patient with metastatic melanoma has a BRAF V600E mutation. What treatment does this allow?
cards.a: BRAF and MEK inhibitor combination therapy, which blocks the mutated signaling pathway that drives the tumor. Targeted therapy can shrink tumors quickly, while immunotherapy is the alternative; the choice depends on how fast the disease is growing and the patient's other conditions.

cards.q: A patient with advanced melanoma without a BRAF mutation is offered immunotherapy. How does it work and what must be watched for?
cards.a: Checkpoint inhibitors such as anti-PD-1 drugs release the brakes on the immune system so it can attack the melanoma. They can cause immune side effects in any organ — colitis, hepatitis, pneumonitis, thyroid problems, and skin rash — so new diarrhea, cough, or rash during treatment must be reported and investigated urgently.

cards.q: A fair-skinned man has a pearly, translucent bump with visible blood vessels on his nose that bleeds easily. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
cards.a: Basal cell carcinoma, the most common skin cancer, which grows slowly and almost never spreads to other organs but invades local tissue. Treatment is surgical excision with clear margins, or Mohs surgery on the face, because complete removal prevents local destruction.

cards.q: Why is Mohs micrographic surgery preferred for a basal cell carcinoma on the nose or eyelid?
cards.a: Because Mohs removes the cancer layer by layer, checking each layer under the microscope during the operation until the margins are clear, which gives the highest cure rate while sparing the most normal tissue. This matters most on the face, where tissue is precious and cosmetic and functional outcomes matter.

cards.q: A man has a scaly, crusted, tender lesion on the back of his hand that does not heal. What is the likely diagnosis and how is it treated?
cards.a: Squamous cell carcinoma, a skin cancer linked to sun exposure that can spread to lymph nodes, unlike basal cell carcinoma. Treatment is excision with clear margins, and larger or high-risk tumors may need lymph node assessment; a lesion that does not heal in a sun-exposed area should always be biopsied.

cards.q: What is actinic keratosis and why does it matter?
cards.a: A rough, scaly patch on sun-exposed skin caused by chronic sun damage, which is a precancerous lesion. A small proportion progress to squamous cell carcinoma, so actinic keratoses are treated with cryotherapy or topical therapy and the patient is advised about sun protection and regular skin checks.

cards.q: A patient had a kidney transplant and is on immunosuppressants. Why is he at high risk for skin cancer and what should be done?
cards.a: Immunosuppression weakens the immune surveillance that normally removes early skin cancers, so squamous cell carcinoma in particular becomes much more common and more aggressive. He needs regular full skin exams, prompt biopsy of any new or non-healing lesion, and strict sun protection.

cards.q: A patient has a rapidly growing, painless, reddish-purple nodule on sun-exposed skin. What rare aggressive skin cancer should be considered?
cards.a: Merkel cell carcinoma, a neuroendocrine skin cancer that grows fast and spreads early to lymph nodes. It needs prompt wide excision, sentinel lymph node biopsy, and staging, because delay worsens the prognosis; it is most common in older, immunosuppressed, or fair-skinned patients.

cards.q: A patient with a skin lesion has a biopsy showing squamous cell carcinoma with perineural invasion. Why does this change management?
cards.a: Perineural invasion means cancer is tracking along nerves, which raises the risk of local recurrence and spread, so wider excision, lymph node evaluation, and often radiation are needed. It also explains why the lesion may be painful or numb.

cards.q: A patient has a new dark spot under a fingernail that does not grow out with the nail. What must be considered?
cards.a: Acral lentiginous melanoma, a melanoma of the palms, soles, or under the nails that occurs in all skin types and is often diagnosed late because it is hidden. A pigmented nail streak needs referral and biopsy of the nail matrix, because a bruise grows out but a melanoma does not.

cards.q: A lesion on the cheek is diagnosed as lentigo maligna (melanoma in situ). How is it treated?
cards.a: Surgical excision with clear margins, often with Mohs surgery on the face. Melanoma in situ is confined to the top layer of skin and has not invaded, so it cannot spread, but it must be fully removed because it can become invasive melanoma if left alone.

cards.q: A patient had a melanoma removed 2 years ago and now has a firm lump under the skin near the scar. What is the concern and next step?
cards.a: Local recurrence or an in-transit metastasis, where cancer cells spread through lymph vessels between the original site and the lymph nodes. The next step is biopsy of the lump and staging, because recurrence changes the prognosis and usually means systemic therapy is needed.

cards.q: A man has a red, hot, swollen lower leg with fever after a small cut. What is the diagnosis and first treatment?
cards.a: Cellulitis, a skin and soft tissue infection usually caused by Streptococcus or Staphylococcus. Treatment is antibiotics covering both, elevation of the leg, and marking the edge of the redness to track spread. If the redness spreads rapidly, pain becomes severe, or blisters appear, a deeper infection must be considered.

cards.q: A patient with cellulitis is treated with antibiotics but the redness keeps spreading and the pain becomes severe and out of proportion to the exam. What is the next step?
cards.a: Urgent surgical evaluation for necrotising fasciitis. Pain out of proportion is a classic early warning sign of deep tissue death, and the infection can kill within hours; imaging must not delay the operating room when this is suspected.

cards.q: A diabetic man has a foot wound with foul-smelling discharge, gas on X-ray, and rapidly spreading redness. What is the diagnosis and immediate management?
cards.a: Necrotising soft tissue infection, most likely necrotising fasciitis. Immediate management is broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics plus emergency surgical debridement of all dead tissue, because antibiotics cannot reach dead tissue and the infection spreads along fascia planes. Delay is often fatal.

cards.q: Which patients are at highest risk for necrotising fasciitis?
cards.a: People with diabetes, immunosuppression, chronic kidney disease, alcohol use, peripheral vascular disease, or recent surgery or trauma, including minor cuts. These conditions impair healing and immune defense, so even a small break in the skin can let bacteria invade deep tissue.

cards.q: A patient with suspected necrotising fasciitis has normal-looking skin over the area but severe pain and a high white blood cell count. Why can the skin look normal early on?
cards.a: Because the infection spreads along the deep fascia first, under the skin, so the surface can look deceptively normal while muscle and fascia are dying underneath. This is why pain out of proportion, systemic illness, and risk factors matter more than the skin appearance, and why surgical exploration is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

cards.q: What organisms most commonly cause necrotising fasciitis and what antibiotics are started?
cards.a: It is usually polymicrobial (mixed aerobes and anaerobes) in diabetics and after abdominal surgery, or group A Streptococcus alone after minor trauma. Empiric treatment is broad-spectrum coverage for Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and anaerobic bacteria, often including clindamycin to shut down toxin production in streptococcal infection, plus urgent surgery.

cards.q: A patient has a painful, red, swollen area in the armpit with a central collection of pus. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
cards.a: A skin abscess, a walled-off collection of pus usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Treatment is incision and drainage, which is the key step; antibiotics alone cannot clear a walled-off abscess. Antibiotics are added if there is spreading cellulitis, fever, or immune compromise.

cards.q: A patient has recurrent painful boils in the groin and armpits that form tunnels under the skin. What is this condition?
cards.a: Hidradenitis suppurativa, a chronic inflammatory disease of the hair follicles in skin folds that causes painful nodules, abscesses, and sinus tracts. It is not a simple infection, so management includes smoking cessation, weight management, antibiotics for flares, and referral for long-term therapy or surgery for severe disease.

cards.q: A man has a carbuncle on the back of his neck with fever. How is it treated and why is it different from a simple boil?
cards.a: A carbuncle is a cluster of connected furuncles with multiple draining points and deeper tissue involvement, so it needs incision and drainage plus antibiotics, and diabetes should be checked. A single small boil may drain on its own, but a carbuncle is larger, more painful, and more likely to cause systemic infection.

cards.q: A patient is bitten by a dog and the wound is on the hand. What is the immediate management?
cards.a: Thorough wound cleaning, irrigation, tetanus update, and antibiotics covering Pasteurella, Staphylococcus, and anaerobes, usually amoxicillin-clavulanate. Hand bites are high risk because infection can spread quickly in the tight spaces of the hand, so early antibiotics and close follow-up are essential.

cards.q: A patient has a human bite to the hand after punching someone in the mouth. Why is this especially dangerous?
cards.a: A clenched-fist injury drives oral bacteria, including Eikenella, deep into the joint and tendon sheaths of the hand, where infection spreads fast and can destroy the joint. It needs urgent wound exploration, irrigation, antibiotics, and often admission, not just a simple dressing.

cards.q: A patient has a red, painful streak running up the arm from a wound. What is this and what does it mean?
cards.a: Lymphangitis, inflammation of the lymph vessels carrying infection toward the lymph nodes. It means the infection is spreading and needs prompt antibiotics and treatment of the source wound; if fever or rapid spread develops, admission for intravenous antibiotics is needed.

cards.q: A child has impetigo with honey-colored crusts around the mouth. What causes it and how is it treated?
cards.a: Impetigo, a superficial skin infection usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, which spreads easily between children. Treatment is topical antibiotics for limited disease or oral antibiotics for widespread disease, plus keeping the area clean and avoiding scratching to prevent spread.

cards.q: A patient has a large, tense blister with surrounding redness on the leg and the skin peels away with light pressure. What dangerous infection is this?
cards.a: This suggests a toxin-mediated or necrotising infection, such as staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome or a deep soft tissue infection. Blistering and skin that shears off easily mean the skin layers are separating from tissue damage, and this needs urgent evaluation, antibiotics, and often surgical consultation.

cards.q: A patient with a leg wound has crepitus (a crackling feeling) under the skin. What does this mean and what is the next step?
cards.a: Gas in the soft tissues, which suggests a gas-forming infection such as necrotising fasciitis or clostridial myonecrosis (gas gangrene). This is a surgical emergency: broad-spectrum antibiotics and immediate operating room exploration, because gas-forming infections destroy muscle rapidly and are often fatal without surgery.

cards.q: A patient develops gas gangrene after a deep crush injury to the leg. What is the cause and treatment?
cards.a: Clostridium perfringens, an anaerobic bacterium from soil that grows in dead, oxygen-poor muscle and produces gas and toxins. Treatment is emergency surgical removal of all dead muscle, high-dose penicillin plus clindamycin, and intensive care; amputation may be needed to save the patient's life.

cards.q: A patient has a pilonidal sinus at the top of the buttock crease with recurrent discharge. What is it and how is it treated?
cards.a: A pilonidal sinus is a tract under the skin near the tailbone, often containing hair, that becomes infected and forms an abscess. An acute abscess needs incision and drainage, and definitive treatment is surgical removal of the sinus tract to prevent recurrence, along with hair removal and hygiene.

cards.q: A patient has an infected sebaceous cyst on the back. What is the treatment?
cards.a: Incision and drainage if it is acutely infected and painful, followed by later removal of the whole cyst wall once the infection settles. Simply draining the pus without removing the cyst wall leaves it likely to refill and become infected again.

cards.q: A patient has a wound that is red and swollen 3 days after surgery, with pus draining from the incision. What is the diagnosis and management?
cards.a: Surgical site infection. Management is opening the wound, draining pus, sending a culture, and antibiotics if there is spreading cellulitis or fever. The wound is usually left open to heal from the inside rather than stitched closed again over infection.

cards.q: A patient has a diabetic foot ulcer with exposed bone visible in the wound. What test confirms bone infection and what is the treatment?
cards.a: A probe-to-bone test at the bedside, confirmed by MRI or bone biopsy, suggests osteomyelitis. Treatment is prolonged antibiotics, often 6 weeks, plus surgical removal of infected bone if needed, along with offloading the foot and good blood sugar control.

cards.q: A patient has a foot ulcer and the ankle-brachial index is 0.5. What does this mean for wound healing?
cards.a: Significant peripheral arterial disease with poor blood flow to the foot, which means the ulcer is unlikely to heal without restoring blood flow. The patient needs vascular referral for possible revascularization; debridement alone will not heal an ischemic ulcer.

cards.q: A diabetic patient has a foot ulcer that is painless and on the sole under a pressure point. Why is it painless and what is the key treatment?
cards.a: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy has destroyed the protective pain sensation, so the patient keeps walking on an injured foot without noticing. The key treatment is offloading — keeping all pressure off the ulcer with a total contact cast or special boot — because continued pressure prevents healing no matter what dressing is used.

cards.q: A diabetic patient has a red, hot, swollen foot with no wound and a normal white blood cell count. What must be ruled out?
cards.a: Charcot neuroarthropathy, a destructive joint process from neuropathy where the bones of the foot fracture and collapse without pain, and also acute infection. The foot must be offloaded and imaged urgently; walking on a Charcot foot causes permanent deformity, and missing an infection can cost the limb.

cards.q: A diabetic patient has a foot ulcer with a foul smell and black tissue at the edges. What does the black tissue mean?
cards.a: Necrotic, dead tissue, which must be removed by debridement because it harbors bacteria and blocks healing. Black tissue in a diabetic foot also raises concern for poor blood flow, so pulses and vascular supply must be checked before aggressive debridement.

cards.q: A patient with diabetes has a foot ulcer and an HbA1c of 11 percent. Why does blood sugar control matter for the ulcer?
cards.a: High blood sugar impairs white blood cell function, collagen formation, and small blood vessel flow, all of which slow wound healing and raise infection risk. Improving glucose control is part of ulcer treatment, along with offloading, debridement, and treating infection.

cards.q: A diabetic foot ulcer is clean, well-perfused, and not infected but is not healing after 4 weeks of good care. What is the next step?
cards.a: Reassess for hidden problems: check blood flow again, look for bone infection, review offloading, and consider advanced wound therapies or referral to a wound care specialist. A non-healing ulcer despite good basic care means something is being missed, and the risk of amputation rises with time.

cards.q: A patient has a pressure ulcer over the sacrum after a long hospital stay. What is the most important preventive measure?
cards.a: Regular repositioning at least every 2 hours and pressure-relieving surfaces, because pressure cuts off blood flow to the skin over bony areas and causes tissue death. Prevention is far more effective than treating an established ulcer, and it starts with turning the patient and keeping the skin dry.

cards.q: A bedbound patient has a red area over the heel that does not turn white when pressed. What stage is this pressure injury and what should be done?
cards.a: Stage 1 pressure injury: intact skin with non-blanchable redness over a bony prominence, meaning the tissue underneath is already damaged from pressure. The pressure must be relieved immediately by repositioning and offloading the heel, and the area monitored closely, because it will worsen if pressure continues.

cards.q: A pressure ulcer shows partial-thickness skin loss with a shallow open blister. What stage is this?
cards.a: Stage 2 pressure injury, where the top layers of skin are lost and the wound is shallow with a pink-red bed. It is treated with pressure relief, keeping the wound moist and clean, and protecting it from further injury; it usually heals without surgery if pressure is removed.

cards.q: A pressure ulcer has full-thickness skin loss with fat visible but no bone, tendon, or muscle exposed. What stage is this?
cards.a: Stage 3 pressure injury. Fat is visible but deeper structures are not, and the wound may have undermining or tunneling. Treatment is pressure relief, debridement of dead tissue, moist wound care, and good nutrition; surgery is considered if it does not heal.

cards.q: A pressure ulcer has full-thickness loss with bone visible at the base. What stage is this and what complication must be ruled out?
cards.a: Stage 4 pressure injury, the deepest stage, with bone, tendon, or muscle exposed. Bone infection (osteomyelitis) must be ruled out, and these ulcers usually need surgical closure such as a flap, because they will not heal on their own.

cards.q: A pressure ulcer is covered with thick black eschar so the depth cannot be seen. How is it classified?
cards.a: Unstageable pressure injury, because the true depth is hidden by the dead tissue covering it. The eschar must be removed (unless it is a stable, dry eschar on the heel with poor blood flow) before the wound can be staged and treated properly.

cards.q: A patient has a deep purple area of intact skin over the sacrum that is painful and feels different from surrounding skin. What is this?
cards.a: Suspected deep tissue pressure injury, where damage has occurred in the muscle and tissue under intact skin. The skin may later break down into a deep ulcer even though it looks intact now, so the area must be offloaded immediately and watched closely.

cards.q: A patient with a stage 3 sacral pressure ulcer is malnourished with a low albumin. Why does nutrition matter and what should be given?
cards.a: Wound healing needs protein, calories, vitamin C, and zinc to build collagen and new tissue, and malnutrition is one of the main reasons pressure ulcers fail to heal. A high-protein diet and nutritional supplements are part of treatment, along with pressure relief and wound care.

cards.q: A pressure ulcer has yellow slough and a foul smell but no surrounding redness or fever. What is the next step?
cards.a: Debridement to remove the dead slough, because dead tissue blocks healing and feeds bacteria, plus wound cultures if infection is suspected. A foul smell alone does not prove deep infection, but the wound cannot heal until the dead tissue is cleared and the wound bed is clean.

cards.q: A paraplegic patient has a large stage 4 ischial pressure ulcer that has not healed after months of wound care. What is the definitive treatment?
cards.a: Surgical flap closure, where healthy muscle and skin are moved over the wound to fill the defect and provide padding over the bone. Conservative care rarely closes a stage 4 ulcer, but surgery only works if pressure relief, nutrition, and infection control are also addressed, or the flap will break down.

cards.q: A patient in the intensive care unit is at high risk for pressure ulcers. What is the single most effective prevention strategy?
cards.a: Frequent repositioning and pressure redistribution, turning the patient at least every 2 hours and using a pressure-relieving mattress. No dressing or cream prevents ulcers if pressure is not relieved, because sustained pressure is what starves the tissue of blood.

cards.q: A patient has a pressure ulcer and the wound edges are rolled and the base is pale. What does this suggest?
cards.a: A chronic, non-healing wound where the edge has stopped advancing and blood flow or nutrition may be poor. Rolled edges and a pale base mean the wound is stuck, so the cause must be found — ongoing pressure, poor circulation, infection, or malnutrition — rather than just changing the dressing.

cards.q: A heel pressure ulcer in a patient with severe peripheral arterial disease is covered with dry, stable black eschar and is not painful. Should the eschar be removed?
cards.a: No, a dry, stable eschar on the heel in a patient with poor blood flow should be left alone and kept dry. Removing it in an ischemic foot can create an open wound that cannot heal and may lead to infection and amputation; the eschar acts as a natural protective cover.

cards.q: A patient has a pressure ulcer with spreading redness, fever, and a high white blood cell count. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
cards.a: Cellulitis or deeper infection of the pressure ulcer, which needs antibiotics, wound cultures, and debridement of dead tissue. Infection in a pressure ulcer can spread to the bone or bloodstream, so systemic signs mean it is no longer a local wound problem.

cards.q: A patient has a diabetic foot ulcer and an infected toe that is black and dry. What is this and what is the management?
cards.a: Dry gangrene of the toe from poor blood flow, where the tissue has died from lack of oxygen. The patient needs urgent vascular evaluation, and the dead toe usually requires amputation, because gangrenous tissue cannot recover and can become infected and threaten the leg and the patient's life.

cards.q: A patient has a wet, swollen, foul-smelling gangrenous foot with fever. How is this different from dry gangrene and what is the urgency?
cards.a: Wet gangrene is infected dead tissue with spreading infection and is a surgical emergency, while dry gangrene is sterile tissue death from poor blood flow without infection. Wet gangrene needs immediate antibiotics, surgical removal of dead tissue or amputation, and intensive care, because the infection can cause sepsis within hours.

cards.q: A diabetic patient had a toe amputated for gangrene. What is the most important step to prevent another amputation?
cards.a: Daily foot inspection, protective footwear, blood sugar control, smoking cessation, and regular foot exams, because the same neuropathy and poor circulation that caused the first amputation still threaten the rest of the foot. Most diabetic amputations are preventable with foot care and early treatment of new ulcers.

cards.q: A patient has a venous leg ulcer above the ankle with hemosiderin staining and swelling. How is it distinguished from an arterial ulcer and what is the treatment?
cards.a: Venous ulcers are shallow, occur above the ankle, and come with swelling and brown staining from chronic venous pressure, while arterial ulcers are painful, deep, and on the toes or pressure points with poor pulses. Venous ulcers are treated with compression therapy and leg elevation, which only works if arterial flow is adequate.

cards.q: A patient has an arterial leg ulcer and the ankle-brachial index is 0.4. Why must compression therapy NOT be used?
cards.a: Because compression would further reduce the already poor blood flow to the leg and worsen the ischemia, potentially causing more tissue death. Compression is for venous disease with adequate arterial flow; an ischemic leg needs vascular revascularization first.

cards.q: A patient has a wound that has been open for 3 months with no sign of healing despite good wound care. What malignancy should be considered?
cards.a: Marjolin ulcer, a squamous cell carcinoma that arises in a chronic wound or old burn scar. Any long-standing non-healing wound, especially one with raised or irregular edges, needs a biopsy, because cancer in a chronic wound is often missed until it is advanced.

cards.q: A patient has a large burn scar from childhood and now has a growing ulcer in the scar. What is the concern?
cards.a: Marjolin ulcer, a squamous cell carcinoma developing in the old burn scar, which is more aggressive than ordinary skin cancer and can spread to lymph nodes. It needs biopsy and wide excision with lymph node assessment.

cards.q: A patient has a soft tissue wound with maggots in it. Is this harmful or helpful?
cards.a: Maggots in a wound are usually medical maggots used deliberately or fly larvae that eat only dead tissue and can actually clean a wound, a treatment called maggot debridement therapy. However, an uncontrolled infestation in a neglected wound needs cleaning and evaluation for deeper infection, and it often signals poor wound care or neglect.

cards.q: A patient has a breast abscess that keeps coming back in the same spot despite drainage. What underlying problem should be considered?
cards.a: A periductal fistula or an underlying mass, or an unrecognized cause such as diabetes, smoking, or an inflammatory condition. Recurrent abscesses in the same location need imaging and sometimes biopsy, because a cancer or a chronic duct problem can present as a recurring abscess.

cards.q: A patient with a skin abscess is found to have MRSA on culture. What antibiotic is used and what else matters?
cards.a: An antibiotic that covers MRSA, such as trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, doxycycline, or clindamycin depending on susceptibility, but drainage remains the most important treatment. The patient should also be advised about hygiene and not sharing towels or razors, because MRSA spreads easily by skin contact.

cards.q: A patient has a rapidly enlarging, painful, red nodule on the leg after a thorn prick while gardening. What infection is suspected?
cards.a: Sporotrichosis, a fungal infection from soil and plants that enters through a small prick and causes nodules that spread along the lymph vessels. It is treated with antifungal therapy, usually itraconazole, and needs to be distinguished from bacterial cellulitis, which would not follow this pattern.

cards.q: A patient has a painful, red, swollen finger with a small blister after cleaning a fish tank. What organism is likely?
cards.a: Mycobacterium marinum, a slow-growing bacterium from water and fish tanks that causes skin infection after minor cuts. It grows slowly over weeks, does not respond to ordinary antibiotics, and needs specific antibiotics such as clarithromycin, so the water exposure history is the key clue.

cards.q: A patient has a skin lesion that is a firm, dome-shaped, pink nodule that bleeds when bumped. What benign tumor is this and when is it removed?
cards.a: A pyogenic granuloma, a benign overgrowth of blood vessels that bleeds easily and grows quickly after minor trauma. It is removed by excision or cautery because it bleeds repeatedly and can look like a melanoma or other cancer, so tissue should always be sent for pathology.

cards.q: A patient has multiple soft, fleshy skin tags in the armpits and neck. Are these dangerous?
cards.a: No, skin tags (acrochordons) are benign outgrowths of skin that are harmless, though they can be irritated by clothing. They are associated with obesity, diabetes, and friction, so their presence is a reason to check blood sugar, but the tags themselves need removal only if they are painful or bothersome.

cards.q: A patient has a lipoma, a soft, mobile, painless lump under the skin on the shoulder. When should it be removed?
cards.a: Only if it is painful, growing quickly, compressing nearby structures, or the diagnosis is uncertain. Most lipomas are benign fatty tumors that need no treatment, but a deep, large, or fast-growing mass needs imaging and possibly biopsy to rule out a liposarcoma.

cards.q: A patient has a large, deep soft tissue mass in the thigh that is growing and painful. What is the next step?
cards.a: MRI of the thigh followed by referral to a sarcoma center for biopsy. A deep, large, growing soft tissue mass in an adult must be treated as a possible sarcoma until proven otherwise, and biopsy should be planned by the sarcoma team so it does not spoil the chance of complete removal.

cards.q: A patient had a sarcoma removed from the leg and the margins were positive. What is the next step?
cards.a: Re-excision to achieve clear margins, often with radiation. Positive margins mean cancer cells were left behind and the tumor will likely come back, so leaving a positive margin is not acceptable when the limb can be saved with further surgery.

cards.q: A 68-year-old smoker has a 2.5 cm peripheral lung nodule and no lymph node enlargement on CT. What is the next best step in staging before surgery?
cards.a: Get a PET-CT scan, because it looks for hidden spread to lymph nodes or distant sites that CT alone can miss, and finding spread changes whether surgery is the right plan.

cards.q: Why is PET-CT done before lung cancer surgery even when the chest CT looks resectable?
cards.a: PET-CT finds metabolically active cancer in nodes or distant organs that look normal on CT, so it prevents an operation that would not cure the patient because the cancer has already spread.

cards.q: A patient with suspected lung cancer has an enlarged mediastinal lymph node on CT. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Sample the node with EBUS-guided biopsy, because treatment depends on whether cancer is in the mediastinal nodes, and tissue confirmation is needed before deciding between surgery and chemoradiation.

cards.q: What does a positive N2 mediastinal lymph node mean for a patient being considered for lung cancer surgery?
cards.a: It means cancer has spread to lymph nodes on the same side of the chest centre, which usually makes upfront surgery less suitable, so chemoradiation or neoadjuvant therapy is usually discussed first.

cards.q: Why is mediastinoscopy or EBUS preferred over going straight to surgery when mediastinal nodes look abnormal?
cards.a: Because operating on N2 disease without knowing it leads to incomplete treatment, while confirming nodal disease first lets the team choose chemoradiation or induction therapy that treats the whole chest.

cards.q: A 70-year-old with a 1.8 cm lung adenocarcinoma needs surgery. What operation is preferred and why?
cards.a: Lobectomy with lymph node sampling, because removing the whole lobe plus nodes gives the best chance of cure and accurate staging, while a smaller wedge resection leaves more risk of the cancer coming back in that lobe.

cards.q: When is a wedge resection acceptable instead of lobectomy for lung cancer?
cards.a: When the patient cannot tolerate a lobectomy because of poor lung function or other illness, because a smaller resection is safer for them even though the risk of local recurrence is higher.

cards.q: What lung function test must be checked before lung resection surgery?
cards.a: Spirometry with FEV1 and DLCO, because they predict whether the patient can breathe well enough after part of the lung is removed, and poor values mean a higher risk of breathing failure after surgery.

cards.q: A patient planned for lobectomy has a predicted postoperative FEV1 below 40 percent. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Do a cardiopulmonary exercise test with VO2 max, because it measures overall fitness for surgery better than spirometry alone and helps decide if surgery is safe or if a smaller resection or non-surgical treatment is better.

cards.q: Why is a predicted postoperative FEV1 calculated instead of using the preoperative FEV1 alone?
cards.a: Because removing lung tissue lowers breathing capacity, so the predicted value after surgery is what matters for whether the patient will cope, not how well they breathe with the whole lung still there.

cards.q: A patient with stage I non-small cell lung cancer cannot have surgery because of severe COPD. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Offer stereotactic body radiotherapy, because it delivers a focused high dose to a small tumour and can cure early lung cancer without removing lung tissue in patients unfit for surgery.

cards.q: What is the most important difference between small cell and non-small cell lung cancer in management?
cards.a: Small cell lung cancer spreads early and is rarely treated with surgery, so chemotherapy with or without radiotherapy is the main treatment, while early non-small cell lung cancer is often cured by surgery.

cards.q: A patient has limited-stage small cell lung cancer. What is the next best treatment?
cards.a: Concurrent chemotherapy and chest radiotherapy, because small cell cancer responds well to both together, and combined treatment controls the chest disease better than chemotherapy alone.

cards.q: Why is prophylactic cranial irradiation considered in small cell lung cancer after a good response to treatment?
cards.a: Because small cell lung cancer commonly spreads to the brain, and preventive brain radiotherapy lowers that risk, though the decision must weigh memory and thinking side effects.

cards.q: A 55-year-old has a lung mass and a pleural effusion. What test best determines if the effusion is malignant?
cards.a: Thoracentesis with cytology, because finding cancer cells in the fluid proves stage IV disease, which changes management from surgery to systemic therapy.

cards.q: Why does a malignant pleural effusion rule out curative lung surgery?
cards.a: Because cancer cells in the pleural space mean the cancer has spread beyond the lung, so removing the lung cannot remove all the disease and systemic treatment is needed instead.

cards.q: A patient with lung adenocarcinoma is found to have an EGFR mutation. What does this change in advanced disease?
cards.a: It means targeted therapy against EGFR is the first treatment, because the tumour depends on that pathway and targeted drugs work better and with fewer side effects than standard chemotherapy in these patients.

cards.q: Why is molecular testing done on advanced non-small cell lung cancer tissue?
cards.a: Because mutations such as EGFR and ALK rearrangements and PD-L1 level guide whether targeted therapy or immunotherapy will work, and giving the wrong first treatment wastes the best chance of control.

cards.q: A patient with stage III non-small cell lung cancer has completed chemoradiation without progression. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Give consolidation immunotherapy, because it helps the immune system keep the cancer controlled after chemoradiation and lowers the chance of the cancer coming back.

cards.q: What is the next best step for a patient with a solitary lung nodule under 8 mm and low risk for cancer?
cards.a: Watch it with repeat CT imaging, because most small nodules are benign and operating on every small nodule would harm many patients, while follow-up catches the few that grow.

cards.q: A smoker has a lung nodule that has grown on repeat CT. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Get tissue diagnosis or surgical resection, because growth in a smoker strongly suggests cancer, and waiting longer risks spread while the tumour is still curable.

cards.q: Why is a chest CT with contrast preferred over chest X-ray for staging lung cancer?
cards.a: CT shows the tumour size, lymph nodes, chest wall and vessels in detail that X-ray misses, so it stages the cancer accurately and shows whether surgery is technically possible.

cards.q: A patient with lung cancer has hoarseness. What does this suggest and why does it matter?
cards.a: It suggests the recurrent laryngeal nerve is involved by tumour or nodes, which usually means locally advanced disease, so surgery alone is unlikely to cure it and staging must be completed.

cards.q: A patient with lung cancer has a new Horner syndrome with shoulder pain. What is the likely diagnosis?
cards.a: A Pancoast tumour at the top of the lung, because it invades the sympathetic chain causing Horner syndrome and the brachial plexus causing shoulder and arm pain, and it needs chemoradiation before surgery.

cards.q: Why is a Pancoast tumour treated with chemoradiation before surgery rather than surgery first?
cards.a: Because the tumour invades the chest wall and nerves, so shrinking it first makes a complete resection more likely and treats microscopic spread around the tumour.

cards.q: A patient is found to have lung cancer with a brain metastasis and a resectable lung tumour. What is the management principle?
cards.a: Treat both sites, often with brain treatment first followed by lung resection or systemic therapy, because a single brain metastasis does not always mean incurable disease if both sites can be controlled.

cards.q: What is the role of adjuvant chemotherapy after complete resection of stage II non-small cell lung cancer?
cards.a: It kills microscopic cancer cells left behind after surgery, because even a complete resection can leave invisible spread, and chemotherapy lowers the chance of recurrence.

cards.q: Why is adjuvant chemotherapy usually not given for stage IA non-small cell lung cancer after complete resection?
cards.a: Because the risk of recurrence is low and the side effects of chemotherapy outweigh the small benefit, so surgery alone is enough.

cards.q: A patient after lobectomy develops a persistent air leak. What is the most likely cause and next step?
cards.a: A leak from the lung staple line, because air escapes from the cut lung surface, and most leaks close with chest tube drainage and time, while a large persistent leak may need reoperation.

cards.q: A patient with lung cancer has superior vena cava syndrome with facial swelling. What is the urgent next step?
cards.a: Get urgent imaging and start treatment of the underlying cancer, often with radiotherapy or stenting, because the vein is blocked by tumour and relieving the blockage prevents airway and brain swelling.

cards.q: A 65-year-old with progressive difficulty swallowing solids then liquids and weight loss has a mid-oesophageal mass. What is the next best diagnostic step?
cards.a: Upper endoscopy with biopsy, because it sees the tumour directly and provides tissue to confirm cancer type, which is needed before staging and treatment planning.

cards.q: Why is endoscopic ultrasound done after oesophageal cancer is diagnosed?
cards.a: It shows how deep the tumour goes into the oesophageal wall and whether nearby lymph nodes are involved, which determines if the cancer is resectable and whether chemotherapy before surgery is needed.

cards.q: A patient with oesophageal cancer has a CT showing no distant spread. What additional staging test is most useful?
cards.a: PET-CT, because it detects distant metastases and involved nodes outside the chest that CT can miss, and finding them changes the plan from surgery to systemic treatment.

cards.q: What is the difference in management between early mucosal oesophageal cancer and deeper invasive cancer?
cards.a: Very early mucosal cancer can sometimes be removed endoscopically, while deeper cancer needs chemotherapy or chemoradiation followed by surgery, because deeper invasion carries a higher risk of lymph node spread.

cards.q: A patient has locally advanced oesophageal adenocarcinoma with no distant spread. What is the standard treatment sequence?
cards.a: Chemoradiation or chemotherapy first, then oesophagectomy, because shrinking the tumour before surgery improves the chance of a complete resection and treats microscopic spread.

cards.q: Why is surgery alone usually not enough for locally advanced oesophageal cancer?
cards.a: Because the cancer often has microscopic spread to nodes or beyond the wall even when scans look clear, so treatment before surgery improves cure rates compared with surgery alone.

cards.q: A patient with oesophageal squamous cell cancer has a complete response to chemoradiation. What is the next decision to discuss?
cards.a: Whether to proceed to surgery or watch closely, because squamous cancers can respond fully to chemoradiation, but surgery still offers the best chance of removing any remaining cancer, and the choice weighs surgical risk.

cards.q: What is the most common serious complication after oesophagectomy that the team watches for in the first days?
cards.a: Anastomotic leak where the stomach is joined to the remaining oesophagus, because leakage causes infection in the chest, so fever, chest pain and rising inflammatory signs after surgery must be investigated urgently.

cards.q: Why are patients counselled about eating small frequent meals after oesophagectomy?
cards.a: Because the stomach is pulled up into the chest and is smaller, so large meals cause early fullness, reflux and dumping symptoms, while small frequent meals are better tolerated.

cards.q: A patient with oesophageal cancer develops dysphagia again after treatment and a stent is considered. When is stenting preferred over surgery?
cards.a: When the cancer is unresectable or metastatic and the goal is to relieve swallowing, because a stent opens the blocked oesophagus quickly for palliation without the risks of major surgery.

cards.q: What is Barrett oesophagus and why does it matter for oesophageal cancer risk?
cards.a: It is a change in the oesophageal lining caused by long-term acid reflux, and it raises the risk of adenocarcinoma, so patients need surveillance endoscopy to catch dysplasia or early cancer.

cards.q: A patient with oesophageal cancer has severe weight loss before treatment. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Start nutritional support with a dietitian, because malnutrition worsens surgical outcomes and tolerance of chemotherapy, and improving nutrition before treatment improves recovery.

cards.q: Why is a feeding jejunostomy sometimes placed during oesophagectomy?
cards.a: Because patients often cannot eat enough by mouth in the early weeks after surgery, and a jejunostomy allows safe feeding while the new join heals.

cards.q: A patient with metastatic oesophageal cancer has difficulty swallowing. What is the main goal of treatment?
cards.a: Palliation of swallowing and quality of life, because metastatic disease cannot be cured by surgery, so treatment focuses on relieving symptoms with stenting, radiotherapy or systemic therapy.

cards.q: What symptom suggests oesophageal cancer has spread to the liver or lungs?
cards.a: New right upper abdominal pain, jaundice, or worsening breathlessness, because these suggest liver or lung metastases, and staging scans are needed to confirm spread and change the treatment plan.

cards.q: A 60-year-old with early satiety, weight loss and a gastric mass on endoscopy has a biopsy showing adenocarcinoma. What is the next best staging step?
cards.a: CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis plus endoscopic ultrasound, because they show depth of invasion, nodal spread and distant metastases, which decide if surgery with curative intent is possible.

cards.q: Why is staging laparoscopy sometimes done before gastric cancer surgery?
cards.a: Because small peritoneal metastases are often invisible on CT, and finding them at laparoscopy avoids a large operation that would not cure the patient.

cards.q: A patient has resectable gastric adenocarcinoma with no distant spread. What is the standard treatment?
cards.a: Perioperative chemotherapy plus gastrectomy, because chemotherapy before and after surgery shrinks the tumour, treats microscopic spread and improves cure rates compared with surgery alone.

cards.q: What operation is done for a distal gastric cancer that is resectable?
cards.a: Subtotal gastrectomy with lymph node dissection, because removing the lower stomach with clear margins and nodes cures early distal cancer while preserving part of the stomach for eating.

cards.q: When is total gastrectomy needed instead of subtotal gastrectomy?
cards.a: When the tumour is proximal, large, or involves most of the stomach, because a clear margin cannot be obtained with a partial resection, so the whole stomach must be removed.

cards.q: Why is a D2 lymph node dissection done during gastric cancer surgery?
cards.a: Because gastric cancer spreads early to regional nodes, and removing a wider group of nodes improves staging accuracy and lowers recurrence, so it is part of curative surgery.

cards.q: A patient after gastrectomy develops dumping syndrome with sweating and palpitations after meals. What is the explanation?
cards.a: Food passes too quickly into the small bowel without the stomach to slow it, causing rapid fluid shifts and hormone release, so small low-sugar meals and avoiding liquids with meals help.

cards.q: Why do patients after total gastrectomy need lifelong vitamin B12 replacement?
cards.a: Because B12 is absorbed with intrinsic factor made in the stomach, and without a stomach they cannot absorb B12, so deficiency causes anaemia and nerve damage unless replaced by injection.

cards.q: A patient with gastric cancer has a positive HER2 test. What does this change in advanced disease?
cards.a: It means adding HER2-targeted therapy to chemotherapy, because HER2-positive tumours are driven by that receptor and targeted treatment improves response in advanced disease.

cards.q: What is linitis plastica of the stomach and why is its prognosis poor?
cards.a: It is diffuse gastric cancer that thickens and stiffens the whole stomach wall, and it spreads early through the wall and peritoneum, so it is often advanced at diagnosis and hard to resect completely.

cards.q: A patient with gastric outlet obstruction from gastric cancer cannot eat. What is the next best step if the cancer is unresectable?
cards.a: Place a stent or consider a bypass, because relieving the blockage allows eating and improves quality of life, while surgery to remove the tumour is not possible.

cards.q: Why is endoscopy with biopsy preferred over CT alone to diagnose gastric cancer?
cards.a: Because CT can show a mass but cannot prove it is cancer or its type, while biopsy gives a tissue diagnosis that guides treatment and excludes benign causes such as ulcer or lymphoma.

cards.q: A patient with early gastric cancer confined to the mucosa is offered endoscopic resection. Why is this possible?
cards.a: Because mucosal cancer has a very low risk of lymph node spread, so removing it endoscopically can cure it without major stomach surgery.

cards.q: What is the role of adjuvant chemoradiation after gastric cancer surgery when chemotherapy was not given before surgery?
cards.a: It treats microscopic cancer left in the stomach bed and nodes, because surgery alone leaves a high risk of local recurrence, and chemoradiation after surgery lowers that risk.

cards.q: A patient with gastric cancer has iron deficiency anaemia and melaena. What is the first priority?
cards.a: Stabilise bleeding and transfuse if needed, then endoscopy, because chronic blood loss from the tumour causes anaemia, and active bleeding must be controlled before staging and definitive treatment.

cards.q: A 65-year-old with painless jaundice, weight loss and a pancreatic head mass on CT has a dilated bile duct. What is the next best diagnostic step?
cards.a: Endoscopic ultrasound with fine needle biopsy, because it confirms pancreatic cancer and stages local invasion, while tissue diagnosis is needed before treatment.

cards.q: Why is a pancreatic head cancer causing painless jaundice a surgical emergency in terms of timing but not an operation the same day?
cards.a: Because the bile duct is blocked by the tumour, so jaundice needs relief and staging must be completed first, and rushing to surgery without staging risks operating on cancer that has already spread.

cards.q: What determines whether pancreatic cancer is resectable, borderline resectable, or unresectable?
cards.a: How much the tumour involves major vessels such as the superior mesenteric artery and vein and the portal vein, because vessel involvement decides if a complete resection with clear margins is technically possible.

cards.q: A patient has borderline resectable pancreatic cancer. What is the next best treatment?
cards.a: Give neoadjuvant chemotherapy with or without radiotherapy first, because shrinking the tumour and treating microscopic spread improves the chance of a complete resection.

cards.q: What operation is done for resectable cancer of the pancreatic head?
cards.a: Pancreaticoduodenectomy, known as the Whipple procedure, because it removes the pancreatic head, duodenum, bile duct and gallbladder together with clear margins and lymph nodes.

cards.q: What operation is done for resectable cancer of the pancreatic tail?
cards.a: Distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy, because the tail is removed with the spleen when the tumour is close to splenic vessels, giving a clear margin.

cards.q: Why is adjuvant chemotherapy given after a Whipple procedure for pancreatic cancer even when margins are clear?
cards.a: Because pancreatic cancer almost always has microscopic spread beyond the pancreas, and chemotherapy after surgery lowers recurrence and improves survival.

cards.q: What is the most feared early complication after a Whipple procedure?
cards.a: Pancreatic leak from the join between pancreas and bowel, because leaked pancreatic fluid causes infection and bleeding, so drain output and fever after surgery must be checked urgently.

cards.q: A patient after Whipple develops delayed gastric emptying and cannot eat. What is the management?
cards.a: Supportive care with nasogastric decompression, anti-nausea drugs and nutritional support, because the stomach is slow to recover after surgery and most cases settle with time.

cards.q: Why do patients after Whipple need pancreatic enzyme replacement?
cards.a: Because much of the pancreas is removed and the remaining pancreas makes less enzyme, so food is not digested properly and patients develop fatty stools and weight loss without replacement.

cards.q: A patient with pancreatic cancer has new diabetes. Why does this happen?
cards.a: Because the tumour destroys insulin-producing cells and causes insulin resistance, so new diabetes in an older adult with weight loss should prompt a search for pancreatic cancer.

cards.q: What is Courvoisier sign in pancreatic cancer?
cards.a: A palpable non-tender gallbladder with jaundice, because the bile duct is blocked by a pancreatic head tumour and the gallbladder distends without inflammation, unlike gallstone blockage which is usually tender.

cards.q: A patient with unresectable pancreatic cancer has a blocked bile duct and jaundice. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Place a biliary stent by ERCP, because it drains bile, relieves jaundice and itching, and allows chemotherapy to be given safely.

cards.q: Why is a biliary stent preferred over surgical bypass for jaundice in unresectable pancreatic cancer?
cards.a: Because stenting is less invasive and relieves jaundice quickly, while bypass surgery carries major operative risk in a patient whose cancer cannot be cured.

cards.q: A patient with pancreatic cancer has severe back pain not relieved by opioids. What intervention is considered?
cards.a: Coeliac plexus block, because the nerves carrying pancreatic pain pass through the coeliac plexus, and blocking them can relieve pain when medicines are not enough.

cards.q: What tumour marker is followed in pancreatic cancer and what is its limitation?
cards.a: CA 19-9, because it often rises with pancreatic cancer and falls with successful treatment, but it can also rise with bile duct blockage and is absent in some patients, so it never replaces imaging or biopsy.

cards.q: A patient with pancreatic cancer has a blood clot in the leg. Why is this common?
cards.a: Because pancreatic cancer causes a hypercoagulable state, so clots are common and need anticoagulation, and a new clot can be a clue to hidden cancer.

cards.q: Why is staging laparoscopy sometimes done before planned pancreatic surgery?
cards.a: Because small liver or peritoneal metastases are missed on CT, and finding them avoids a Whipple operation that would not cure the patient.

cards.q: A patient with metastatic pancreatic cancer is offered chemotherapy. What is the main goal?
cards.a: To prolong life and control symptoms, because metastatic pancreatic cancer cannot be cured, so treatment aims to slow the cancer and improve quality of life.

cards.q: What is the role of genetic testing in pancreatic cancer?
cards.a: To look for inherited mutations such as BRCA, because they affect treatment choices and family screening, and some mutations make the tumour more sensitive to certain chemotherapy.

cards.q: A 58-year-old has a right-sided colon cancer with iron deficiency anaemia. What is the next best diagnostic step?
cards.a: Colonoscopy with biopsy, because it sees the whole colon, confirms the cancer with tissue, and finds other polyps or cancers that change the surgical plan.

cards.q: Why does right-sided colon cancer usually present with anaemia rather than bowel obstruction?
cards.a: Because the right colon is wide and stool is liquid, so tumours bleed slowly without blocking the bowel, while left-sided tumours grow in a narrower colon with solid stool and cause obstruction.

cards.q: A patient has left-sided colon cancer with change in bowel habit and blood in stool. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Colonoscopy with biopsy and staging CT, because tissue confirms cancer and CT looks for spread to liver and lungs, which decides if surgery can cure it.

cards.q: What is the standard curative treatment for localised colon cancer with no distant spread?
cards.a: Surgical resection with lymph node removal, because removing the tumour segment with clear margins and nodes cures early colon cancer and provides accurate staging.

cards.q: Why is at least 12 lymph nodes the target in colon cancer surgery?
cards.a: Because examining enough nodes makes staging accurate, and finding cancer in nodes changes the need for chemotherapy, so too few nodes risks missing nodal spread.

cards.q: A patient has stage III colon cancer after complete resection. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Give adjuvant chemotherapy, because cancer in lymph nodes means microscopic spread is likely, and chemotherapy lowers the chance of recurrence.

cards.q: Why is adjuvant chemotherapy usually not given for stage I colon cancer after complete resection?
cards.a: Because the risk of recurrence is very low, so the side effects of chemotherapy outweigh any benefit.

cards.q: A patient has rectal cancer 6 cm from the anal verge. What staging test is essential before treatment?
cards.a: Pelvic MRI, because it shows depth of invasion, nodal involvement and distance to the mesorectal fascia, which decides if chemoradiation before surgery is needed.

cards.q: Why is pelvic MRI preferred over CT for staging rectal cancer?
cards.a: Because MRI shows the layers of the rectal wall and the mesorectum in detail, while CT cannot distinguish these layers well enough to plan surgery or radiotherapy.

cards.q: A patient has locally advanced rectal cancer. What is the standard treatment sequence?
cards.a: Neoadjuvant chemoradiation followed by surgery, because shrinking the tumour improves the chance of a complete resection and lowers local recurrence.

cards.q: What operation is done for low rectal cancer that cannot be removed with a safe margin while preserving the sphincter?
cards.a: Abdominoperineal resection with a permanent colostomy, because the tumour is too low to save the anal sphincter, so removing the rectum and anus is needed for cure.

cards.q: What is total mesorectal excision and why is it important in rectal cancer surgery?
cards.a: It is removal of the rectum together with its surrounding fatty envelope containing lymph nodes, because cancer spreads within that envelope, and removing it intact lowers local recurrence.

cards.q: A patient with rectal cancer has a complete response to chemoradiation. What option may be discussed?
cards.a: Watch and wait with close surveillance instead of immediate surgery, because no tumour is detectable, but this needs strict follow-up as some cancers regrow and then need surgery.

cards.q: Why is a diverting ileostomy sometimes created during rectal cancer surgery?
cards.a: Because a low join in the pelvis is at high risk of leaking, and a temporary ileostomy diverts stool away so a leak is less dangerous while the join heals.

cards.q: A patient with colon cancer has a raised CEA after surgery. What does this suggest?
cards.a: It suggests recurrence, because CEA often rises when colorectal cancer returns, so a rising CEA prompts imaging to look for liver or lung metastases.

cards.q: What is the limitation of CEA as a screening test for colorectal cancer?
cards.a: It is not sensitive or specific enough, because CEA can be normal in early cancer and raised in smokers and benign disease, so it is used for follow-up after diagnosis, not screening.

cards.q: A patient with colon cancer presents with large bowel obstruction. What is the urgent management?
cards.a: Resuscitate, decompress and get urgent surgical review, because obstruction can lead to perforation, so relieving the blockage is urgent even before full staging is complete.

cards.q: Why is a stent sometimes used for malignant large bowel obstruction instead of emergency surgery?
cards.a: Because stenting can relieve the blockage and allow bowel preparation and staging, turning an emergency operation into a planned one with lower risk.

cards.q: A patient has colorectal cancer with a single liver metastasis. What is the management principle?
cards.a: Consider resection of both the primary tumour and the liver metastasis, because a single resectable liver metastasis can still be cured, unlike widespread metastatic disease.

cards.q: What screening test is recommended for average-risk adults for colorectal cancer?
cards.a: Colonoscopy, because it both detects cancer early and removes precancerous polyps, preventing cancer from developing.

cards.q: A patient with colorectal cancer has liver metastases on CT. What is the next best step to decide if liver surgery is possible?
cards.a: Get detailed liver imaging with MRI and review by a liver surgeon, because the number, size and position of metastases and the remaining liver volume decide if resection can cure the patient.

cards.q: Why is the future liver remnant volume important before liver resection for metastases?
cards.a: Because the liver left behind must be large enough to function, and removing too much liver causes liver failure, so volume is calculated before surgery.

cards.q: What makes a liver metastasis from colorectal cancer resectable?
cards.a: It can be removed with a clear margin while leaving enough healthy liver, because resectable metastases can be cured, while unresectable widespread disease is treated with chemotherapy.

cards.q: A patient has colorectal liver metastases that are initially unresectable. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Give systemic chemotherapy first, because shrinking the metastases can make them resectable, and response to chemotherapy also shows the cancer biology before major liver surgery.

cards.q: Why is portal vein embolisation sometimes done before major liver resection?
cards.a: Because blocking the vein to the part of liver to be removed makes the remaining liver grow, so the future remnant becomes large enough to function safely after surgery.

cards.q: What is the role of ablation for liver metastases?
cards.a: To destroy small metastases with heat or cold when surgery is not possible, because ablation can control small lesions, though surgery gives a better chance of cure when it is feasible.

cards.q: A patient with liver metastases has a rising bilirubin and jaundice. What does this suggest?
cards.a: It suggests extensive liver involvement or bile duct blockage, because the liver cannot clear bilirubin when it is replaced by tumour or bile flow is blocked, and this changes prognosis and treatment.

cards.q: Why are liver metastases from colorectal cancer treated differently from widespread lung and bone metastases?
cards.a: Because liver-only metastases can sometimes be removed for cure, while widespread metastases in many organs usually cannot be cured by surgery, so systemic therapy is the main treatment.

cards.q: What is the most common primary cancer causing liver metastases seen by surgeons?
cards.a: Colorectal cancer, because it drains through the portal vein to the liver, so the liver is the first site of spread and the most common site for resectable metastases.

cards.q: A patient after liver resection for metastases needs follow-up. What is the main purpose of surveillance imaging?
cards.a: To detect new liver or lung metastases early, because recurrence is common and early detection may allow another resection or ablation.

cards.q: A patient with advanced cancer has a malignant bowel obstruction and widespread metastases. What is the main goal of surgical decisions now?
cards.a: To relieve symptoms and improve quality of life, because the cancer cannot be cured, so any operation must be judged by whether it will make the patient feel better and not by removing the tumour.

cards.q: Why is major surgery often avoided in a patient with advanced cancer and poor performance status?
cards.a: Because the risks of surgery outweigh any benefit when the patient is frail and the cancer is incurable, and surgery can worsen quality of life and shorten the remaining time.

cards.q: A patient with terminal cancer asks for surgery to remove the tumour even though it cannot cure them. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Have an honest discussion about goals, risks and expected benefit, because surgery that cannot cure may still be right for symptom relief, but the patient must understand the risks and what surgery can and cannot achieve.

cards.q: What is the role of a venting gastrostomy in malignant bowel obstruction when surgery is not appropriate?
cards.a: To drain stomach contents and relieve nausea and vomiting, because it decompresses the stomach without major surgery and improves comfort in the final weeks.

cards.q: A patient with advanced oesophageal cancer cannot swallow and is not a candidate for surgery. What palliative option helps swallowing?
cards.a: Oesophageal stenting, because it holds the blocked oesophagus open so the patient can swallow liquids and soft food, improving comfort without major surgery.

cards.q: Why is early palliative care involvement recommended in advanced cancer, not only at the end of life?
cards.a: Because palliative care controls pain, nausea and breathlessness and helps with decisions, and starting it early improves quality of life alongside cancer treatment.

cards.q: A patient with advanced pancreatic cancer has severe pain, weight loss and jaundice. What is the priority in management?
cards.a: Control pain, relieve jaundice with a stent if needed, and support nutrition, because these symptoms affect quality of life most, and treating them matters more than trying to remove an unresectable tumour.

cards.q: What is the difference between curative and palliative surgery in cancer?
cards.a: Curative surgery aims to remove all cancer for cure, while palliative surgery aims to relieve a symptom such as obstruction or bleeding when cure is not possible.

cards.q: A patient with metastatic cancer develops bleeding from the tumour. What surgical principle applies?
cards.a: Consider the least invasive way to stop bleeding, such as endoscopy, embolisation or limited surgery, because the goal is to control bleeding and stabilise the patient, not to cure the cancer.

cards.q: Why is a multidisciplinary team discussion important before palliative surgery in advanced cancer?
cards.a: Because surgeons, oncologists, palliative care and anaesthetists together weigh whether surgery will help the patient, what the risks are, and whether a less invasive option would achieve the same relief with less harm.

Give a large-volume balanced crystalloid bolus, usually 30 mL/kg, right away. Sepsis causes vasodilation and leaky capillaries, so the circulation is effectively empty; restoring intravascular volume improves perfusion to the brain, kidneys, and gut before vasopressors are needed.
cards.q: A patient with suspected sepsis has a lactate of 4.5 mmol/L and low blood pressure. What is the first resuscitation step, and why?

cards.a: Start norepinephrine if hypotension persists after adequate fluids, and do not delay it while waiting for a central line. It is first-line because it raises blood pressure mainly by vasoconstriction with less tachycardia and arrhythmia than dopamine or epinephrine, and it preserves coronary and renal perfusion.
cards.q: In septic shock, when do you start norepinephrine, and why is it first-line?

cards.a: Add vasopressin as a second agent. It works through a different receptor, so it raises vascular tone without adding more catecholamine side effects such as tachycardia, and it helps reach the mean arterial pressure goal while limiting the norepinephrine dose.
cards.q: A septic patient remains hypotensive on norepinephrine. What is the next best step?

cards.a: Aim for a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg. Below this, autoregulation fails in the kidneys and brain, so organ perfusion falls sharply; higher targets have not shown better outcomes and increase vasopressor side effects.
cards.q: What mean arterial pressure target is used in septic shock, and why?

cards.a: Give broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour of recognizing septic shock, after cultures are drawn if that does not delay them. Every hour of delay allows bacterial load and the inflammatory response to grow, which worsens organ failure and mortality.
cards.q: When should antibiotics be given in septic shock?

cards.a: Draw two sets of blood cultures, plus cultures from the suspected source such as urine, sputum, or wound, and check lactate, CBC, metabolic panel, coagulation studies, and imaging of the suspected source. Cultures identify the organism and allow narrowing of antibiotics, but they must never delay the first antibiotic dose.
cards.q: What cultures and workup should be done before antibiotics in sepsis, without delaying treatment?

cards.a: Check hemoglobin, cardiac output, and oxygen delivery, and consider transfusion only if hemoglobin is below 7 g/dL, or dobutamine if there is clear cardiac dysfunction. Low venous oxygen saturation means tissues are extracting more oxygen than is being delivered, so the cause is either too little hemoglobin, too little flow, or a failing heart.
cards.q: A patient with septic shock has a low central venous oxygen saturation despite fluids and norepinephrine. What should you check next?

cards.a: Because transfusion above 7 g/dL in stable patients does not improve outcomes and adds risks such as transfusion reactions, lung injury, and infection. The exception is active bleeding, severe hypoxemia, or symptomatic cardiac ischemia, where a higher threshold may be reasonable.
cards.q: Why is a restrictive transfusion threshold of 7 g/dL used in most septic patients?

cards.a: Urgent source control with surgery, in addition to antibiotics and resuscitation. Antibiotics cannot sterilize a perforated viscus or an undrained abscess; the infected focus must be removed or drained, or sepsis will persist no matter how good the antibiotics are.
cards.q: A patient with intra-abdominal sepsis has free air on imaging. What is the key management principle?

cards.a: Sepsis is infection with organ dysfunction, such as altered mental status, low urine output, or high lactate. Septic shock is sepsis plus persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors and a lactate above 2 mmol/L despite fluids, meaning circulation has failed and mortality is much higher.
cards.q: What is the difference between sepsis and septic shock?

cards.a: Worsening tissue hypoperfusion, possibly from inadequate cardiac output, excessive vasoconstriction, or a new source such as bowel ischemia. Rising lactate means tissues are still starved of oxygen, so reassess volume status, cardiac function, and source control rather than simply increasing the vasopressor.
cards.q: A patient on vasopressors for septic shock develops cold, mottled skin and a rising lactate. What does this suggest?

cards.a: Large volumes of normal saline cause a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis and can worsen kidney injury. Balanced fluids such as lactated Ringer's or Plasma-Lyte more closely match plasma electrolytes, so they resuscitate without adding a large chloride load.
cards.q: Why are balanced crystalloids preferred over large volumes of normal saline in sepsis?

cards.a: Restore perfusion with fluids and vasopressors to a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg, and stop or avoid nephrotoxic drugs. Most sepsis-related kidney injury is from hypoperfusion and inflammation, so fixing perfusion protects the kidney; dialysis is reserved for refractory acidosis, hyperkalemia, volume overload, or uremic complications.
cards.q: A septic patient develops acute kidney injury with rising creatinine and low urine output. What is the most important initial step?

cards.a: Consider low-dose hydrocortisone only when hypotension persists despite adequate fluids and vasopressors. Steroids help restore vascular responsiveness to catecholamines in relative adrenal insufficiency, but they increase hyperglycemia and infection risk, so they are not routine first-line therapy.
cards.q: When should steroids be given in septic shock?

cards.a: Disseminated intravascular coagulation from sepsis. Treat the underlying infection and support perfusion; give platelets, fresh frozen plasma, or cryoprecipitate only for active bleeding or before an invasive procedure, because replacing factors without treating the trigger does not stop the process.
cards.q: A patient with sepsis has a platelet count falling and a rising INR with bleeding. What is the diagnosis and next step?

cards.a: Because the antibiotic choice and need for drainage or surgery depend on the source. Check lungs, urine, abdomen, skin and soft tissue, lines and catheters, and the central nervous system; a missed source such as an infected line or abscess will keep driving sepsis despite antibiotics.
cards.q: Why is early source identification important in sepsis, and what are common sources to check?

cards.a: Remove the line and send the tip for culture, and place a new line at a different site if access is still needed. An infected catheter is a continuous source of bacteria into the bloodstream, so antibiotics alone cannot clear it while the line remains.
cards.q: A central line is suspected as the source of sepsis. What is the next best step?

cards.a: Use low tidal volumes of about 6 mL/kg of predicted body weight and keep plateau pressure below 30 cm H2O. Large tidal volumes overstretch injured alveoli and worsen lung injury, while low volumes limit that damage even if carbon dioxide rises somewhat.
cards.q: A patient with septic shock is intubated and on high ventilator pressures. What ventilator strategy protects the lungs?

cards.a: It can help support the decision to stop antibiotics when it falls, but it should not delay starting antibiotics or replace clinical judgment. Procalcitonin rises with bacterial infection and falls as infection clears, so a falling level suggests the infection is controlled.
cards.q: What is the role of procalcitonin in sepsis management?

cards.a: Emergent surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics, without waiting for imaging or definitive cultures. This infection spreads rapidly along fascial planes and kills tissue by the hour; surgery is the only way to remove dead tissue and stop progression, and delay increases mortality.
cards.q: A patient with necrotizing soft tissue infection has severe pain out of proportion, bullae, and crepitus. What is the next best step?

cards.a: Narrowing to the organism found reduces resistance, Clostridioides difficile infection, drug toxicity, and cost. Broad coverage is needed up front when the organism is unknown, but continuing it after identification exposes the patient to unnecessary harm without benefit.
cards.q: Why is de-escalation of antibiotics important once cultures return in sepsis?

cards.a: Suspect infective endocarditis and obtain blood cultures and an echocardiogram, preferably transesophageal if the transthoracic study is negative. A heart valve infection continuously seeds the blood, so it needs prolonged antibiotics and often surgery, and it will not clear with a short course.
cards.q: A septic patient has a new heart murmur and persistent bacteremia despite antibiotics. What should you suspect and do?
