Cardiogenic shock after MI has a very high mortality, and only opening the artery plus circulatory support improves survival. Call cardiology and critical care immediately.
cards.q: A patient with STEMI has a blood pressure of 88/60 and signs of shock. What is the first management priority?

cards.a: Pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Start CPR and defibrillate immediately, then give adrenaline and amiodarone as per ACLS. Defibrillation is the only treatment that restores a normal rhythm; drugs alone will not convert pulseless VT.
cards.q: A patient is found pulseless with wide-complex tachycardia on the monitor. What is the rhythm and the immediate treatment?

cards.a: Monomorphic VT has identical QRS shapes and is usually from scar after MI; stable cases get amiodarone or procainamide, unstable cases get synchronised cardioversion. Polymorphic VT with a long QT is torsades: stop QT-prolonging drugs, give intravenous magnesium, correct low potassium, and overdrive pace or give isoproterenol to shorten the QT. Amiodarone can worsen torsades, so do not use it there.
cards.q: What is the difference between monomorphic VT and polymorphic VT (torsades de pointes) in management?

cards.a: Immediate synchronised cardioversion with sedation if possible. Hypotension and chest pain mean the VT is unstable and the heart cannot fill or perfuse the coronaries. Do not wait for drugs to work in an unstable patient; electricity is faster and more effective.
cards.q: A patient with a pulse has sustained VT at 180 beats per minute, blood pressure 70/40, and chest pain. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Intravenous amiodarone, with procainamide as an alternative. A stable patient with a pulse can be treated medically first, but keep the defibrillator nearby and prepare for cardioversion if the patient deteriorates. Always look for the cause, especially ischaemia and low potassium or magnesium.
cards.q: A patient with a pulse has VT at 170 beats per minute but is alert with a blood pressure of 118/70. What is the first drug treatment?

cards.a: Start high-quality CPR, defibrillate as soon as the defibrillator is ready, and resume CPR immediately after the shock. Early defibrillation is the strongest predictor of survival in VF. Give adrenaline after the second shock and amiodarone after the third if VF persists.
cards.q: A patient is in ventricular fibrillation. What is the sequence of the first three actions?

cards.a: Adrenaline constricts blood vessels and raises coronary perfusion pressure during CPR, improving the chance of return of spontaneous circulation. In VF or pulseless VT, give it after the second defibrillation attempt, then every 3 to 5 minutes. It does not replace defibrillation or good compressions.
cards.q: Why is adrenaline given in cardiac arrest, and what is its timing in a shockable rhythm?

cards.a: Give atropine 1 mg intravenously, repeated up to 3 mg. If atropine fails, start transcutaneous pacing or an infusion of dopamine or adrenaline, and call for transvenous pacing. Atropine blocks vagal slowing, but it often fails in heart block below the AV node, so pacing is the definitive treatment.
cards.q: A patient has symptomatic bradycardia at 38 beats per minute with hypotension and confusion. What is the first drug, and what if it fails?

cards.a: Complete heart block or Mobitz type II second-degree block, especially with a wide QRS, because the block is below the AV node and the escape rhythm is slow and unreliable. Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) is usually nodal, often benign and rarely needs pacing. Do not discharge a patient with Mobitz II or complete block without cardiology review.
cards.q: Which type of heart block is most likely to need a permanent pacemaker urgently?

cards.a: Immediate synchronised cardioversion. An unstable SVT with hypotension needs electricity, not drugs. If the patient were stable, vagal manoeuvres then adenosine would be first, but instability overrides that sequence.
cards.q: A patient with a heart rate of 190, narrow QRS, regular rhythm and no visible P waves has SVT and is hypotensive. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Try vagal manoeuvres such as a Valsalva manoeuvre or carotid sinus massage if there is no carotid bruit or recent stroke, then give adenosine 6 mg as a rapid intravenous bolus followed by a saline flush. Adenosine briefly blocks the AV node and breaks the re-entry circuit. Warn the patient about brief chest discomfort and a feeling of doom, which pass in seconds.
cards.q: A stable patient has SVT at 180 beats per minute. What are the first two steps before drugs?

cards.a: Adenosine has a half-life of seconds, so it must reach the heart quickly before it is broken down; a slow injection will not work. Avoid it in asthma because it can cause bronchospasm, and use caution with dipyridamole or carbamazepine which increase its effect, and with theophylline which blocks it.
cards.q: Why must adenosine be given as a rapid bolus with a flush, and what should you avoid giving with it?

cards.a: Stop amiodarone and all other QT-prolonging drugs immediately, give intravenous magnesium sulfate, and correct low potassium to above 4.5. Magnesium stabilises the heart even if the level is normal. If torsades is pulseless, defibrillate; if it recurs, overdrive pacing or isoproterenol to raise the heart rate shortens the QT.
cards.q: A patient on amiodarone develops torsades de pointes. What is the most urgent treatment, and what must be stopped?

cards.a: Immediate synchronised cardioversion. Rapid AF with hypotension or chest pain is unstable, and rate control drugs will be too slow and may worsen blood pressure. If the patient were stable, rate control with a beta blocker or diltiazem would be first, with anticoagulation decided by stroke risk.
cards.q: A patient has atrial fibrillation with a rapid rate of 160, chest pain and hypotension. What is the management?

cards.a: Yes, if the onset is clearly under 48 hours and there is no clot risk, immediate cardioversion is usually safe without prior anticoagulation. If the duration is over 48 hours or unknown, do a transoesophageal echo to exclude a left atrial clot or anticoagulate for 3 weeks before cardioversion, because cardioversion can dislodge a clot and cause a stroke.
cards.q: A patient has new atrial fibrillation for 6 hours, is stable, and has no anticoagulation. Can you cardiovert immediately?

cards.a: No. A score of 0 means a very low stroke risk, so the bleeding risk of anticoagulation outweighs the benefit. A score of 1 in a man needs discussion, and 2 or more needs anticoagulation. Always reassess the score as risk factors change.
cards.q: A patient with AF has a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 0. Does he need long-term anticoagulation?

cards.a: Giving a beta blocker, calcium channel blocker, digoxin or adenosine. These block the AV node and force conduction down the accessory pathway, which can conduct very fast and degenerate into VF. Treat wide-complex irregular AF in WPW with procainamide or cardioversion, and get cardiology help urgently.
cards.q: What is the most dangerous drug error in a patient with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome who develops AF?

cards.a: Treat it as VT until proven otherwise. VT is far more common and more dangerous, and treating SVT drugs in VT can cause collapse. If unstable, cardiovert; if stable, give amiodarone or procainamide and get cardiology review. Do not give verapamil to a wide-complex tachycardia.
cards.q: A patient with a wide-complex tachycardia is unsure if it is VT or SVT with aberrancy. How should you treat it in the emergency department?

cards.a: Give intravenous calcium, high-dose insulin with glucose, and glucagon, plus vasopressors and pacing if needed. Calcium improves contractility, insulin helps the heart use glucose for energy despite beta blockade, and glucagon bypasses the beta receptor. Atropine alone often fails in beta blocker overdose.
cards.q: A patient has a heart rate of 45 after a beta blocker overdose, with hypotension. What is the treatment beyond atropine?

cards.a: Intravenous calcium gluconate, high-dose insulin with glucose, and vasopressors, with pacing if needed. Calcium directly overcomes the channel blockade. Atropine may help briefly but is often insufficient, so do not rely on it alone.
cards.q: A patient has bradycardia and hypotension after a calcium channel blocker overdose. What is the specific antidote treatment?

cards.a: Atropine. Inferior MI often causes vagal slowing and AV block that responds to atropine because the block is nodal. If atropine fails or the block is below the node, pacing is needed.
cards.q: What is the first-line drug for a patient with symptomatic sinus bradycardia due to excess vagal tone after an inferior MI?

cards.a: Start transcutaneous pacing, check the pacemaker settings and battery, and look for causes such as high potassium, ischaemia or lead displacement. Do not assume the device is working; a failing pacemaker is a pacing emergency and needs cardiology and device team help immediately.
cards.q: A patient with a pacemaker has a heart rate of 30 and the pacemaker is not capturing. What is the immediate step?

cards.a: Hypertensive emergency with encephalopathy. Admit to intensive care and lower blood pressure with an intravenous drug such as labetalol or nicardipine, reducing mean arterial pressure by about 10 to 20 percent in the first hour and to around 160 over 100 over the next few hours. Do not drop the pressure to normal quickly, because the brain has adapted to high pressure and a sudden fall causes stroke.
cards.q: A patient arrives with a blood pressure of 220/130, headache, confusion and papilloedema. What is the diagnosis and the blood pressure target?

cards.a: Hypertensive emergency has acute target-organ damage such as encephalopathy, stroke, pulmonary oedema, aortic dissection, acute kidney injury or retinal haemorrhage. Hypertensive urgency has very high blood pressure but no acute organ damage. Emergency needs intravenous drugs and intensive care; urgency can be managed with oral drugs and close follow-up.
cards.q: What distinguishes hypertensive urgency from hypertensive emergency?

cards.a: This is hypertensive urgency. Do not lower the pressure rapidly in the emergency department. Start or adjust oral antihypertensives, arrange follow-up within days, and check for causes. Rapid lowering in an asymptomatic patient risks stroke and kidney injury without benefit.
cards.q: A patient has a blood pressure of 195/115, no symptoms and no organ damage. What is the correct management?

cards.a: Nitroglycerin or nitroprusside, because they reduce preload and afterload and relieve pulmonary congestion quickly. Labetalol is also used, but nitrates directly reduce the filling pressures that cause oedema. Avoid hydralazine as first choice because its effect is unpredictable and prolonged.
cards.q: Which intravenous drug is preferred for hypertensive emergency with acute pulmonary oedema, and why?

cards.a: An intravenous beta blocker such as esmolol first, then a vasodilator such as nitroprusside if needed. The beta blocker reduces heart rate and the force of contraction, lowering shear stress on the torn aorta. Giving a vasodilator alone first causes reflex tachycardia and increases shear stress, which can extend the dissection.
cards.q: A patient with hypertensive emergency and acute aortic dissection needs blood pressure control. What drug is given first and why?

cards.a: Systolic blood pressure 100 to 120 and heart rate under 60 beats per minute. These targets reduce shear stress on the aortic wall and limit extension of the dissection. Use an arterial line and intensive care monitoring to hold these targets.
cards.q: What blood pressure and heart rate targets are used in aortic dissection?

cards.a: No, continue controlled lowering but avoid an excessive fall. The kidney injury is caused by the severe hypertension itself, and a modest, controlled reduction improves perfusion over time. A sudden large drop can worsen kidney perfusion, so lower gradually and monitor urine output and creatinine.
cards.q: A patient with hypertensive emergency has acute kidney injury with a rising creatinine. Should you stop lowering blood pressure?

cards.a: Avoid aggressive lowering unless blood pressure is very high, generally above 220 systolic or 120 diastolic, or the patient is receiving thrombolysis where the target is below 185 over 110. Lowering too much reduces blood flow to the already ischaemic brain and enlarges the stroke. Nitroprusside is avoided because it can raise intracranial pressure.
cards.q: Which drug should be avoided in hypertensive emergency with acute stroke, and what is the blood pressure threshold for treatment?

cards.a: An alpha blocker such as phentolamine or phenoxybenzamine first. Blocking beta receptors alone leaves alpha vasoconstriction unopposed and can cause a dangerous further rise in blood pressure. Alpha blockade first, then beta blockade for heart rate control.
cards.q: A patient with phaeochromocytoma crisis has severe hypertension and tachycardia. What drug must be given before a beta blocker?

cards.a: Treat as hypertensive emergency with acute coronary syndrome. Admit to intensive care, give intravenous nitroglycerin or labetalol to lower pressure gradually, plus aspirin and anticoagulation for ACS, and involve cardiology. The high pressure increases heart oxygen demand and worsens ischaemia, so both problems must be treated together.
cards.q: A patient has a blood pressure of 230/140 and new chest pain with ST depression. What is the priority?

cards.a: Acute aortic dissection, likely Stanford type A involving the ascending aorta. The tearing pain, blood pressure difference between arms and new aortic regurgitation murmur are classic. Get an urgent CT angiogram of the aorta and involve cardiothoracic surgery immediately; do not delay for a chest X-ray alone.
cards.q: A 65-year-old man has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back, blood pressure 190/110 in the right arm and 150/90 in the left, and a new diastolic murmur. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Type A involves the ascending aorta and is a surgical emergency because it can rupture into the pericardium, cause tamponade or block the coronary arteries. Type B involves only the descending aorta and is usually managed medically with blood pressure and heart rate control, with surgery or stenting only if there is rupture, malperfusion or uncontrolled pain.
cards.q: What is the difference between Stanford type A and type B aortic dissection in management?

cards.a: CT angiography of the chest and abdomen is the first test in a stable patient because it is fast and highly accurate. If the patient is unstable or in the operating theatre, transoesophageal echo is preferred because it can be done at the bedside. Do not send an unstable patient to the CT scanner without resuscitation and monitoring.
cards.q: What is the first imaging test for suspected aortic dissection in a stable patient, and what if the patient is unstable?

cards.a: No. A normal chest X-ray does not exclude dissection; about one in ten patients has a normal film. If the history suggests dissection, proceed to CT angiography regardless of the X-ray. Relying on a normal X-ray is a dangerous error.
cards.q: A patient with aortic dissection has a widened mediastinum on chest X-ray. Does a normal chest X-ray rule out dissection?

cards.a: D-dimer can be normal early in dissection and is raised in many other conditions, so it is not reliable enough to exclude the diagnosis when the clinical suspicion is high. Use it only in low-risk patients as part of a validated score; high-risk patients need imaging regardless of D-dimer.
cards.q: Why is D-dimer not a safe rule-out test for aortic dissection in a high-risk patient?

cards.a: Cardiac tamponade from rupture of the dissection into the pericardium. Blood fills the pericardial sac and compresses the heart so it cannot fill. This is a surgical emergency; give fluids and vasopressors as a bridge, avoid pericardiocentesis if surgery is immediately available because draining can worsen bleeding, and call cardiothoracic surgery now.
cards.q: A patient with known aortic dissection suddenly becomes hypotensive with raised jugular venous pressure and muffled heart sounds. What has happened?

cards.a: Avoid anticoagulation and fibrinolytics. If the diagnosis is actually a dissection, anticoagulation can cause fatal bleeding or rupture. Do not give heparin for presumed ACS until dissection is excluded when the pain is tearing, radiates to the back, or there is a blood pressure difference between arms.
cards.q: What is the most important drug to avoid in suspected aortic dissection before imaging confirms it?

cards.a: Aortic dissection. Marfan syndrome weakens the aortic wall and greatly increases dissection risk, often at a younger age and with a dilated aortic root. Get urgent CT angiography and surgical review; do not attribute the pain to musculoskeletal causes in this patient.
cards.q: A patient with Marfan syndrome has sudden severe chest pain. What diagnosis must be excluded first?

cards.a: Malperfusion: the dissection flap is blocking blood flow to the leg and the gut. This is a complication that needs urgent surgical or endovascular repair, not just medical therapy. Check pulses in all limbs, urine output and lactate, and involve vascular and cardiothoracic surgery immediately.
cards.q: A patient with aortic dissection has absent pulses in the left leg and abdominal pain. What does this indicate?

cards.a: Lifelong beta blocker therapy to keep heart rate and blood pressure low and reduce shear stress, plus strict blood pressure control and regular imaging surveillance of the aorta. Stop smoking and avoid heavy lifting and strenuous exercise as advised. Without this, the aorta can dilate or dissect again.
cards.q: What is the long-term medical therapy after repair of an aortic dissection?

cards.a: Cardiogenic shock. The pump has failed, so the heart cannot push blood forward; that causes low blood pressure, cold clammy skin, low urine output and confusion, with signs of fluid backing up such as pulmonary oedema and raised jugular pressure. Treat the cause, usually a large MI, with urgent revascularisation plus fluids cautiously, vasopressors and inotropes, and intensive care support.
cards.q: A patient after a large MI has a blood pressure of 82/55, cold clammy skin, low urine output, confusion and pulmonary oedema. What type of shock is this and what is the cause?

cards.a: A fluid-filled pericardium compresses the heart so it cannot fill, so stroke volume falls despite a fast heart rate. Vasopressors alone cannot fix an empty, squeezed heart; fluids can help briefly by raising filling pressure, but the definitive treatment is to remove the fluid, usually by pericardiocentesis or surgery.
cards.q: Why do vasopressors alone fail in obstructive shock from cardiac tamponade?

cards.a: Massive pulmonary embolism is obstructive shock because a large clot blocks blood flow through the lungs, so the right ventricle fails and the left heart receives too little blood. Look for sudden breathlessness, chest pain, low oxygen, tachycardia, a raised jugular pressure and clear lungs. Give oxygen, anticoagulation if there is no contraindication, and thrombolysis or embolectomy if unstable.
cards.q: A patient suddenly becomes breathless, tachycardic and hypotensive with clear lungs and a raised jugular venous pressure. What type of shock and cause should you suspect?

cards.a: Tension pneumothorax is obstructive shock: air under pressure in the chest compresses the heart and great veins so blood cannot return to the heart. The classic signs are hypotension, a deviated trachea away from the affected side, absent breath sounds and a distended neck vein. Decompress immediately with a needle, then place a chest drain; do not wait for an X-ray.
cards.q: What is the emergency treatment for tension pneumothorax causing obstructive shock, and what signs point to it?

cards.a: Give intravenous fluids in small boluses with frequent reassessment, plus vasopressors such as noradrenaline if pressure stays low, and treat the cause. In cardiogenic shock the heart is weak, so large fluid boluses worsen pulmonary oedema; in obstructive shock fluids help fill the compressed heart, but the obstruction must still be relieved. Monitor lungs, oxygen and urine output closely.
cards.q: How does fluid management differ between cardiogenic shock and obstructive shock?

cards.a: Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor because it raises blood pressure with less tachycardia and arrhythmia than dopamine, and it preserves coronary perfusion. Dobutamine can be added if cardiac output remains low despite adequate pressure, because it improves contractility. Avoid phenylephrine alone in cardiogenic shock because it raises afterload without improving pump function.
cards.q: Which vasopressor is first-line in cardiogenic shock, and what inotrope is added if output stays low?

cards.a: Mechanical support such as an intra-aortic balloon pump or a ventricular assist device as a bridge to recovery or revascularisation. When drugs and fluids cannot maintain perfusion, the heart needs mechanical help to rest and recover. This needs urgent cardiology and critical care discussion, and the underlying cause must still be fixed.
cards.q: When drugs fail in cardiogenic shock after MI, what is the next level of support?

cards.a: Acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture after MI. The valve leaks badly, blood floods back into the lungs and forward flow falls, causing pulmonary oedema and shock. This is a surgical emergency; stabilise with oxygen, vasodilators if pressure allows, and urgent cardiology and cardiac surgery review.
cards.q: A patient days after MI develops sudden severe pulmonary oedema, a new murmur and shock. What complication should you suspect?

cards.a: A blocked coronary artery is the most common cause of cardiogenic shock, so get an ECG and troponin immediately and involve cardiology for urgent angiography. Other causes include severe myocarditis, end-stage heart failure, severe valve disease and arrhythmia. Finding and fixing the cause matters more than just raising the blood pressure.
cards.q: What is the most common cause of cardiogenic shock, and what is the first test?

cards.a: Give oxygen, sit the patient upright, and give intravenous furosemide to remove fluid, nitrates to reduce preload and afterload, and morphine cautiously if there is severe distress and anxiety. Non-invasive ventilation helps if oxygen stays low despite treatment. Treat the trigger such as ischaemia, arrhythmia or missed medication.
cards.q: A patient with acute pulmonary oedema is severely breathless with crackles to the top of both lungs and oxygen saturation 88 percent. What is the immediate treatment?

cards.a: Nitrates dilate veins and reduce the blood returning to the heart and the pressure the heart must pump against, so fluid moves out of the lungs and breathing improves. They work within minutes, which is why they are used alongside diuretics. Avoid them if blood pressure is low or the patient has taken a phosphodiesterase inhibitor such as sildenafil in the last 24 hours.
cards.q: Why are nitrates given in acute pulmonary oedema, and when should they be avoided?

cards.a: Sit the patient up, give high-flow oxygen, intravenous furosemide and nitrates if pressure allows, and start non-invasive positive pressure ventilation. CPAP keeps the airways open, pushes fluid out of the alveoli and reduces the work of breathing. Intubate if ventilation fails or the patient becomes exhausted or unresponsive.
cards.q: What is the role of non-invasive ventilation in acute pulmonary oedema, and when should you intubate instead?

cards.a: No, diuretics help remove fluid but they do not fix the underlying cause, which may be ischaemia, a fast arrhythmia, severe hypertension or a valve problem. Always look for and treat the trigger, otherwise the oedema will recur. In cardiogenic shock, diuretics can worsen low blood pressure, so use them cautiously there.
cards.q: A patient with pulmonary oedema improves with furosemide. Is diuretic therapy alone enough?

cards.a: Acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary oedema. The failing heart cannot pump blood forward, so pressure builds up behind it and fluid leaks into the lungs. The low blood pressure and poor urine output show the heart is also failing to perfuse the body, so this is a high-risk presentation needing admission and often intensive care.
cards.q: A patient with known heart failure has new severe breathlessness, a blood pressure of 95/60, low urine output and bilateral crackles. What is the diagnosis and the severity?

cards.a: Stop the offending drug, give oxygen and intravenous fluids cautiously, and treat the underlying cause. Beta blockers, calcium channel blockers and antiarrhythmics can all worsen acute heart failure by reducing contractility or heart rate. Do not restart the drug until cardiology reviews it.
cards.q: A patient with heart failure deteriorates after starting a new beta blocker. What is the most likely explanation and the first step?

cards.a: No, beta blockers are harmful in acute decompensated heart failure with shock or pulmonary oedema because they reduce contractility and heart rate when the heart is already failing. They are started only once the patient is stable and euvolaemic, when they improve long-term survival. Never start a beta blocker during an acute decompensation.
cards.q: Should a beta blocker be started during an acute heart failure decompensation?

cards.a: Digoxin slows the heart rate in atrial fibrillation and improves contractility slightly, but it has a narrow therapeutic window and toxicity causes nausea, visual changes, confusion and dangerous arrhythmias. Check potassium and magnesium, because low levels increase toxicity, and check kidney function because digoxin is cleared by the kidneys.
cards.q: What is the role of digoxin in acute heart failure with rapid atrial fibrillation, and what must be checked?

cards.a: Give oxygen, intravenous furosemide, nitrates if pressure allows, and treat the ischaemia urgently with cardiology. Ischaemia is a common trigger for pulmonary oedema, and the oedema will keep returning until blood flow to the heart is restored. Do not just diurese and discharge without checking for ACS.
cards.q: A patient with acute pulmonary oedema has new ST depression and a raised troponin. What is the priority?

cards.a: Yes, if blood pressure is low and there is shock, vasopressors and inotropes are needed alongside the heart failure treatment. Diuretics alone would drop pressure further and worsen perfusion. Admit to intensive care, give noradrenaline or dobutamine as needed, and involve cardiology urgently.
cards.q: A patient with acute heart failure has a blood pressure of 85/50 and signs of shock. Should you still give furosemide alone?

cards.a: Check the ECG, chest X-ray, electrolytes, kidney function, troponin, BNP and blood gas, and look for triggers: ischaemia, arrhythmia, infection, anaemia, thyroid disease, missed medicines and high salt intake. BNP is raised in heart failure but can also be raised in kidney failure and pulmonary embolism, so interpret it with the clinical picture.
cards.q: Which tests and triggers should be checked in every patient with acute decompensated heart failure?

cards.a: Check for a pneumothorax, worsening pulmonary oedema, or a large pleural effusion. Non-invasive ventilation helps only if the mask fits, the patient can protect the airway and there is no pneumothorax. A chest X-ray and blood gas guide the next step, and intubation is needed if ventilation fails.
cards.q: A patient with pulmonary oedema on CPAP is not improving. What should you look for next?

cards.a: High-quality chest compressions, early defibrillation for shockable rhythms, adrenaline, and treating reversible causes. Interruptions in compressions reduce coronary perfusion, so keep pauses short and resume immediately after a shock. The goal is return of spontaneous circulation with the best chance of a good neurological outcome.
cards.q: What are the two most important factors for survival in cardiac arrest?

cards.a: Hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hydrogen ion excess (acidosis), hypo or hyperkalaemia, hypothermia, and tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis in the lungs (pulmonary embolism) and thrombosis in the heart (coronary). These are the reversible causes of arrest; finding and fixing them is as important as compressions and drugs.
cards.q: List the reversible causes of cardiac arrest that must be considered during resuscitation.

cards.a: Give adrenaline 1 mg every 3 to 5 minutes. Adrenaline improves coronary perfusion pressure, but it does not replace good compressions or defibrillation. In a shockable rhythm give it after the second shock; in a non-shockable rhythm give it as soon as intravenous access is obtained.
cards.q: A patient is in asystole. What is the drug and dose schedule during CPR?

cards.a: Asystole is a non-shockable rhythm, so do not defibrillate. Continue CPR, give adrenaline as soon as possible, and search for reversible causes, especially hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hyperkalaemia and hypothermia. Check the leads are connected and the gain is correct before declaring asystole.
cards.q: A patient is in asystole. Should you defibrillate?

cards.a: Do not stop at 20 minutes if there is a reversible cause, if the patient is hypothermic, or if there is ongoing good-quality CPR with signs of life. Hypothermic patients can survive prolonged arrest because the cold protects the brain. In general, a team decision weighs the duration, the rhythm, the cause and the quality of resuscitation.
cards.q: When is it reasonable to continue resuscitation beyond 20 minutes in cardiac arrest?

cards.a: The priority is high-quality compressions and early defibrillation; the airway can be managed with a bag-valve-mask initially. Intubation is important but should not interrupt compressions for more than a few seconds. A supraglottic airway is a reasonable alternative if intubation is difficult.
cards.q: During a cardiac arrest, should intubation be prioritised over chest compressions?

cards.a: Pulseless electrical activity means there is organised electrical activity on the monitor but no pulse. It is a non-shockable rhythm, so treat it like asystole: CPR, adrenaline, and an urgent search for reversible causes, especially hypovolaemia, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, pulmonary embolism and severe hyperkalaemia.
cards.q: What is pulseless electrical activity (PEA), and how is it treated?

cards.a: Give intravenous amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock, then 150 mg after the fifth if VF persists, alongside adrenaline. Amiodarone stabilises the heart rhythm and increases the chance that defibrillation will succeed. Lidocaine is an alternative if amiodarone is unavailable.
cards.q: A patient remains in refractory VF after three shocks. What drug should be given next?

cards.a: Yes, if the rhythm is shockable and the patient is in VF, defibrillate immediately even if the patient is hypothermic, but drugs may be less effective and shocks may not work until the patient is rewarmed. Continue CPR and rewarm actively; do not declare death until the patient is warm.
cards.q: A hypothermic patient is found in VF. Should you defibrillate?

cards.a: Hyperkalaemia causes a wide QRS, peaked T waves and eventually a sine-wave pattern and asystole. Give intravenous calcium to stabilise the heart, insulin with glucose and nebulised salbutamol to shift potassium into cells, and sodium bicarbonate if there is severe acidosis. Dialysis removes potassium definitively.
cards.q: A patient with kidney failure arrests with a wide QRS and peaked T waves. What is the likely cause and the emergency treatment?

cards.a: Give 10 mL of 10 percent calcium gluconate intravenously over 10 minutes. Calcium stabilises the cardiac membrane and protects against fatal arrhythmia within minutes, but it does not lower potassium. Follow it with insulin and glucose to shift potassium and arrange definitive removal.
cards.q: What is the first drug for hyperkalaemia causing ECG changes, and what does it do?

cards.a: Targeted temperature management: cool the patient to 32 to 36 degrees Celsius for at least 24 hours, then rewarm slowly. It reduces brain injury after return of circulation. The patient must be comatose after arrest to benefit, and shivering, infection and bleeding must be monitored during cooling.
cards.q: A patient remains comatose after return of spontaneous circulation following a cardiac arrest. What is the post-arrest temperature management?

cards.a: Do not stop sedation and cooling too early to assess prognosis, wait at least 72 hours after rewarming, and use clinical examination, EEG, imaging and biomarkers together. A single test can be misleading, and a poor result early does not guarantee a poor outcome. Discuss with the family and the intensive care team.
cards.q: How should neurological prognosis be assessed after cardiac arrest, and what is the common pitfall?

cards.a: Get a 12-lead ECG immediately to look for STEMI, because many arrests are caused by a blocked coronary artery. If there is ST elevation, urgent angiography is indicated. Also check electrolytes, blood gas and a chest X-ray, and admit to intensive care for monitoring and targeted temperature management.
cards.q: A patient has return of spontaneous circulation after an out-of-hospital arrest. What is the first investigation?

cards.a: A coronary angiogram is indicated if there is ST elevation, haemodynamic instability or an ischaemic cause is suspected. If the ECG shows no ST elevation but the cause is unclear, discuss with cardiology; angiography may still be needed, but the timing depends on the patient's stability and other causes.
cards.q: After return of spontaneous circulation, which patients need urgent coronary angiography?

cards.a: Continue CPR for 2 minutes, then recheck the rhythm. Stopping too early wastes the benefit of the shock and reduces coronary perfusion. The only pause should be a brief rhythm check; compressions resume immediately if there is still no pulse.
cards.q: After a shock is delivered in VF, what is the next step?

cards.a: No. Once the patient has return of spontaneous circulation, continue monitoring, oxygen to keep saturation 94 to 98 percent, and blood pressure support to keep mean arterial pressure above 65. Over-oxygenation and over-ventilation can worsen brain injury, so titrate oxygen carefully.
cards.q: After return of spontaneous circulation, should high-flow oxygen be continued indefinitely?

cards.a: Cardiac tamponade from blood or fluid compressing the heart. The classic triad is hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure and muffled heart sounds, plus a narrow pulse pressure and pulsus paradoxus. Get an urgent bedside echo, give fluids and vasopressors as a bridge, and remove the fluid by pericardiocentesis or surgery.
cards.q: A patient after a penetrating chest injury has hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure and muffled heart sounds. What is the diagnosis and the key triad?

cards.a: Pulsus paradoxus is an exaggerated fall in systolic blood pressure of more than 10 mmHg during inspiration. In tamponade the stiff pericardium limits filling, so inspiration pulls blood into the right heart and reduces left heart filling, dropping blood pressure. It is a useful bedside clue but is not specific to tamponade.
cards.q: What is pulsus paradoxus, and why does it occur in tamponade?

cards.a: Bedside echocardiography is the fastest and most accurate test, showing fluid around the heart and collapse of the right atrium or ventricle during diastole. It can be done at the bedside in an unstable patient and guides pericardiocentesis. Do not send an unstable patient for a CT scan first.
cards.q: What is the best bedside test for suspected cardiac tamponade in an unstable patient?

cards.a: Remove the fluid by pericardiocentesis under echo guidance, or surgery if the fluid is blood or the cause is trauma or dissection. Fluids and vasopressors buy time but do not fix the compression. If the patient is in shock, do not delay drainage for more tests.
cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for cardiac tamponade?

cards.a: Yes, if the tamponade is caused by aortic dissection, pericardiocentesis can worsen bleeding and is usually avoided when surgery is immediately available. The definitive treatment is surgical repair of the dissection, with fluids and vasopressors as a bridge. This is why the cause of tamponade must be identified before drainage.
cards.q: A patient with tamponade is found to have an aortic dissection. Should pericardiocentesis still be done?

cards.a: Hypovolaemia can mask tamponade because the jugular veins are flat when volume is low. Give fluids first to restore filling pressure, and the signs of tamponade will become apparent. Do not exclude tamponade just because the neck veins look flat in a bleeding patient.
cards.q: Why might the classic signs of tamponade be absent in a patient who is also hypovolaemic?

cards.a: Tamponade is fluid compressing the heart from outside, causing low output and a narrow pulse pressure with muffled sounds. Constrictive pericarditis is a stiff, scarred pericardium that limits filling over months, causing chronic right heart failure, a raised jugular pressure with a prominent Y descent, and a pericardial knock. Echo and the time course distinguish them.
cards.q: What is the difference between cardiac tamponade and constrictive pericarditis?

cards.a: Tuberculous or malignant pericarditis, or uraemic pericarditis in kidney failure. These cause slow accumulation of fluid, so the pericardium stretches and the patient may tolerate a large effusion before tamponade develops. The treatment is drainage plus treatment of the underlying cause.
cards.q: A patient with a large pericardial effusion has no tamponade signs. What causes are most likely, and why is the patient stable?

cards.a: Acute limb ischaemia. The six Ps are pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis and poikilothermia (cold). The most urgent are paraesthesia and paralysis, which mean nerve and muscle are dying. Give oxygen, analgesia, heparin immediately, and call vascular surgery urgently.
cards.q: A patient has sudden severe leg pain, a pale cold foot, absent pulses, numbness and weakness. What is the diagnosis and which signs are most urgent?

cards.a: Heparin prevents the clot from extending while definitive treatment is arranged, and it protects the collateral circulation. Give it immediately once the diagnosis is suspected and bleeding is excluded, even before imaging if the limb is threatened. Do not delay anticoagulation for a full work-up.
cards.q: Why is heparin given immediately in acute limb ischaemia, even before imaging?

cards.a: Surgical embolectomy or bypass, often with a Fogarty catheter to remove the clot. Endovascular thrombolysis is an alternative if the limb is viable and there is time, but surgery is faster when the limb is threatened. The choice depends on the duration, the cause and the patient's fitness.
cards.q: A patient has acute limb ischaemia from an embolus with a threatened limb. What is the definitive treatment?

cards.a: Embolic occlusion is sudden, often in a patient with AF, with a clear onset and no prior claudication. Thrombotic occlusion develops on top of chronic atherosclerosis, so the patient usually has prior claudication and the onset is more gradual. Both need urgent vascular review, but an embolus is more likely to need embolectomy.
cards.q: How do you distinguish embolic from thrombotic acute limb ischaemia clinically?

cards.a: No. Pain relief alone does not restore blood flow, and the limb will die if revascularisation is delayed. Analgesia is important for comfort, but the priority is anticoagulation, vascular surgery review and restoring perfusion. The window for limb salvage is usually 6 hours.
cards.q: A patient with acute limb ischaemia has good pain relief with morphine. Is the limb now safe?

cards.a: Reperfusion injury: when blood flow returns, potassium, acid and myoglobin are released from the damaged muscle into the circulation, causing hyperkalaemia, acidosis and acute kidney injury. Check electrolytes, kidney function and creatine kinase after revascularisation, give fluids, and monitor for compartment syndrome.
cards.q: After revascularisation for acute limb ischaemia, what complication should be monitored for in the first 24 hours?

cards.a: A fasciotomy to relieve pressure in the muscle compartments. Swelling after reperfusion compresses the vessels and nerves, causing further ischaemia. The signs are severe pain, a tense calf, pain on passive stretch and paraesthesia. Do not wait for absent pulses, which are a late sign.
cards.q: A patient after limb revascularisation develops a tense, painful calf with pain on passive stretch. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Do not give thrombolysis if there is active bleeding, recent surgery or stroke, or a threatened limb needing immediate surgery. Thrombolysis takes hours to work and can cause major bleeding, so it is reserved for a viable limb with no contraindication. Surgery is preferred when the limb is immediately threatened.
cards.q: When should thrombolysis be avoided in acute limb ischaemia?

cards.a: A large anterior STEMI with cardiogenic shock. The pump has failed, so the first priority is urgent revascularisation and circulatory support, not just pain relief. Call cardiology and critical care immediately, give oxygen, aspirin and anticoagulation, and prepare for vasopressors or mechanical support.
cards.q: A patient with chest pain, ST elevation in V2 to V5, a blood pressure of 80/50 and pulmonary oedema is in the emergency department. What is the most urgent priority?

cards.a: Check the blood pressure in both arms, get an ECG and troponin, and consider CT angiography if dissection is suspected. A tearing pain radiating to the back with a pulse deficit points to dissection, not ACS, and giving heparin for ACS could be fatal. Do not anchor on the first diagnosis.
cards.q: A patient with severe chest pain has a blood pressure difference between arms. What should you check before giving heparin for ACS?

cards.a: A beta blocker, because it lowers heart rate and oxygen demand and reduces arrhythmia risk. A calcium channel blocker such as diltiazem is an alternative if a beta blocker is contraindicated. Do not give a beta blocker if there is acute heart failure, shock or severe bronchospasm.
cards.q: A patient with NSTEMI has ongoing chest pain and a heart rate of 110. Which drug helps reduce myocardial oxygen demand?

cards.a: Yes, if the patient is unstable with hypotension, altered mental status or shock, synchronised cardioversion is the treatment regardless of the arrhythmia type. Stable patients can be treated with drugs, but instability always overrides the drug-first approach. Prepare sedation if time allows, but do not delay cardioversion in a collapsing patient.
cards.q: A patient with SVT is hypotensive and confused. Should you still try vagal manoeuvres first?

cards.a: Give intravenous magnesium, correct potassium, stop QT-prolonging drugs, and consider overdrive pacing or isoproterenol. Amiodarone prolongs the QT and can worsen torsades, so it must be avoided. This distinction is a common Step 3 trap.
cards.q: What is the treatment for torsades de pointes, and which common antiarrhythmic must be avoided?

cards.a: Admit to intensive care, monitor continuously, and treat the cause. A patient with syncope from VT, a prolonged QT, or a structural heart disease is high risk and needs admission even if they feel well now. Discharge is only safe after cardiology review and a plan for defibrillator assessment if indicated.
cards.q: A patient has syncope from sustained VT but is now stable. Should they be discharged from the emergency department?
A patient with chest pain after cocaine use has ST elevation and hypertension. What is the first treatment, and which drug should be avoided?
cards.a: Give benzodiazepines first, plus aspirin and nitrates if blood pressure allows, and oxygen if needed. Benzodiazepines reduce the cocaine-driven sympathetic surge, heart rate and blood pressure. Avoid beta blockers in acute cocaine-associated chest pain, because unopposed alpha vasoconstriction can worsen coronary spasm. Urgent cardiology review and monitoring are needed.

Give IV thrombolysis with alteplase or tenecteplase if no contraindications, because the benefit is greatest early and the window is up to 4.5 hours from last known well. Do not delay for MRI or extra labs beyond glucose and CT.
cards.q: A patient arrives 2 hours after sudden left-sided weakness and slurred speech. CT head shows no bleed. What is the next best step in management?

cards.a: Up to 4.5 hours from last known well time, not from when symptoms were first noticed by someone else. After 4.5 hours IV thrombolysis is not given, but thrombectomy may still be an option.
cards.q: What is the time window for IV thrombolysis in acute ischaemic stroke?

cards.a: Up to 24 hours from last known well in selected patients with a large vessel occlusion and salvageable brain tissue on imaging. This is why a large vessel occlusion should not be ruled out just because thrombolysis time has passed.
cards.q: What is the time window for mechanical thrombectomy in large vessel occlusion stroke?

cards.a: Lower blood pressure to below 185 over 110 before giving thrombolysis, usually with IV labetalol or nicardipine, because high pressure greatly raises the risk of bleeding into the brain after thrombolysis.
cards.q: A stroke patient has a blood pressure of 195 over 115 and is a candidate for thrombolysis. What should be done first?

cards.a: To exclude haemorrhage quickly, because thrombolysis in a haemorrhagic stroke would worsen bleeding and can be fatal. CT also excludes a large established infarct or tumour mimicking stroke.
cards.q: Why is a non-contrast CT head done first in suspected acute stroke?

cards.a: Give glucose and recheck, because severe hypoglycaemia can mimic stroke exactly and is rapidly reversible. Do not give thrombolysis until hypoglycaemia is corrected and symptoms persist.
cards.q: A patient with acute ischaemic stroke has a blood glucose of 38 mg per dL and confusion with weakness. What is the first step?

cards.a: Active internal bleeding, recent intracranial haemorrhage, recent major surgery or head trauma, or a known intracranial tumour or aneurysm, because thrombolysis dissolves clot everywhere and can cause catastrophic bleeding.
cards.q: Which finding is an absolute contraindication to IV thrombolysis in acute stroke?

cards.a: No, because an INR above 1.7 is a contraindication to IV thrombolysis. The bleeding risk outweighs benefit, and thrombectomy should be considered instead if there is a large vessel occlusion.
cards.q: A patient had a stroke 3 hours ago and is on warfarin with an INR of 2.1. Can IV thrombolysis be given?

cards.a: Do not give IV thrombolysis, because a direct oral anticoagulant taken within the last 48 hours is a contraindication unless specific reversal and lab testing allow it. Consider thrombectomy if there is a large vessel occlusion.
cards.q: A patient with acute stroke took apixaban 4 hours ago. What is the next step regarding thrombolysis?

cards.a: Below 100,000 per microlitre, because severe thrombocytopenia raises the risk of haemorrhage after thrombolysis. Check a platelet count before giving it when bleeding risk is suspected.
cards.q: What platelet count is too low for IV thrombolysis in acute stroke?

cards.a: Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage. Stop the infusion immediately, get an urgent non-contrast CT head, check coagulation and fibrinogen, and involve neurosurgery and critical care, because ongoing bleeding can cause herniation.
cards.q: A patient receives thrombolysis and then develops severe headache, vomiting and a falling level of consciousness. What is the most likely complication and next step?

cards.a: Below 180 over 105, because higher pressure after thrombolysis increases the risk of bleeding into the infarcted brain. Monitor closely and treat with IV antihypertensives if needed.
cards.q: After thrombolysis, what blood pressure target is maintained for the first 24 hours?

cards.a: Because combining them with thrombolysis greatly increases bleeding risk without added benefit in the first day. Start antiplatelet therapy after 24 hours and after a repeat CT excludes haemorrhage.
cards.q: Why are aspirin, heparin and other antithrombotics avoided for 24 hours after thrombolysis?

cards.a: Usually after 4 to 14 days depending on infarct size and bleeding risk, not immediately, because early anticoagulation after a fresh infarct raises the risk of haemorrhagic transformation. Small infarcts are anticoagulated earlier than large ones.
cards.q: A patient with acute ischaemic stroke has atrial fibrillation. When should anticoagulation be started?

cards.a: CT angiography of the head and neck, because it identifies a large vessel occlusion that may need thrombectomy. Do not delay thrombolysis while waiting for it if the patient is eligible.
cards.q: What vessel imaging is needed urgently in a patient with severe stroke symptoms and suspected large vessel occlusion?

cards.a: Left middle cerebral artery, because it supplies the dominant hemisphere language area and the motor cortex for the right side. Gaze deviates toward the side of the lesion in a cortical stroke.
cards.q: A patient has sudden right-sided weakness, aphasia and gaze deviation to the left. Which artery is most likely occluded?

cards.a: Lateral medullary syndrome from posterior inferior cerebellar artery occlusion, because the lateral medulla contains vestibular, cerebellar, cranial nerve and spinothalamic pathways. This is a posterior circulation stroke, not a peripheral vertigo cause.
cards.q: A patient has sudden vertigo, vomiting, ataxia and dysarthria with crossed face and body sensory loss. Which stroke syndrome is this?

cards.a: Yes, if the deficit is thought to be due to stroke and not just the post-seizure state, because a seizure at onset is not an absolute contraindication. Careful assessment is needed to avoid treating a Todd paresis as a stroke.
cards.q: A patient with acute ischaemic stroke is eligible for thrombolysis but has a seizure at onset. Can thrombolysis still be given?

cards.a: Control blood pressure, aiming for a systolic of 130 to 150 in most cases, and reverse any anticoagulation, because ongoing bleeding and haematoma expansion worsen outcome. Avoid lowering pressure too fast or too low, which can reduce brain perfusion.
cards.q: A patient with sudden severe headache, vomiting and a blood pressure of 220 over 130 has a large bleed on CT. What is the first management priority?

cards.a: Reverse warfarin urgently with 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus vitamin K, because stopping warfarin alone is too slow and the haematoma can expand within hours.
cards.q: A patient on warfarin has an intracerebral haemorrhage with an INR of 3.5. What is the next best step?

cards.a: Idarucizumab, because it specifically binds and reverses dabigatran. For factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban or rivaroxaban, andexanet alfa or prothrombin complex concentrate is used.
cards.q: A patient on dabigatran has an intracerebral haemorrhage. What reversal agent is used?

cards.a: Because platelet transfusion in this setting has been shown to worsen outcome and increase death, unless the patient needs urgent neurosurgery. Stop the antiplatelet drug but do not transfuse platelets routinely.
cards.q: Why are platelets not routinely transfused in a patient with intracerebral haemorrhage on aspirin alone?

cards.a: Urgent neurosurgical evacuation, because a cerebellar haematoma can compress the brainstem and block cerebrospinal fluid flow, causing rapid deterioration and death. Medical treatment alone is not enough when the brainstem is compressed.
cards.q: A patient with a large cerebellar haemorrhage develops drowsiness and a dilated pupil. What is the next step?

cards.a: Those with a large haematoma, falling consciousness, intraventricular haemorrhage, hydrocephalus or brainstem compression, because they need close neurological monitoring, airway protection and rapid neurosurgical input.
cards.q: Which patients with intracerebral haemorrhage need admission to intensive care?

cards.a: Treat the seizure with a benzodiazepine and load levetiracetam, because seizures after haemorrhage can raise intracranial pressure and worsen bleeding. Prophylactic anti-seizure drugs are not given routinely if there was no seizure.
cards.q: A patient with intracerebral haemorrhage has a seizure in the emergency department. What should be done?

cards.a: Hypertensive small vessel disease affecting deep structures such as the basal ganglia, thalamus and pons, because chronic high pressure weakens small penetrating arteries. Lobar bleeds in older adults more often suggest amyloid angiopathy.
cards.q: What is the most common cause of spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage in an older adult with hypertension?

cards.a: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy, because amyloid deposition weakens cortical vessels and causes lobar bleeds in older adults, often recurrent and sometimes with microbleeds on MRI.
cards.q: A patient with a lobar haemorrhage has no hypertension and is 78 years old. What cause should be considered?

cards.a: No, lower it moderately to a systolic of 130 to 150, because dropping it too far can reduce blood flow to the injured brain and worsen ischaemia around the haematoma.
cards.q: A patient with intracerebral haemorrhage is hypertensive but has no signs of raised pressure. Should blood pressure be lowered aggressively to normal immediately?

cards.a: A seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, or repeated seizures without return to baseline between them, because after 5 minutes a seizure is unlikely to stop on its own and brain injury risk rises sharply.
cards.q: What is status epilepticus?

cards.a: A benzodiazepine, usually IV lorazepam or diazepam, because it is the fastest way to stop the seizure. Give it immediately and do not wait for labs or imaging.
cards.q: What is the first drug for a patient actively convulsing in the emergency department?

cards.a: Load a second-line agent such as IV levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate, because benzodiazepine-resistant seizures need a longer-acting anti-seizure drug. Admit to intensive care and prepare for intubation if it continues.
cards.q: A seizure continues after two doses of lorazepam. What is the next best step?

cards.a: Start a continuous infusion such as midazolam or propofol with intubation and continuous EEG monitoring, because refractory status epilepticus needs anaesthetic suppression of seizure activity and airway protection.
cards.q: A patient remains in status epilepticus after benzodiazepine and levetiracetam. What is the next step?

cards.a: Because seizures can continue silently without visible convulsions once the patient is paralysed or sedated, and only EEG can detect them. Treatment is guided by EEG, not by movements alone.
cards.q: Why is continuous EEG used in a patient who is intubated for status epilepticus?

cards.a: Usually not after a single unprovoked seizure with normal workup, because the recurrence risk is lower and daily drug side effects may outweigh benefit. Start treatment after two unprovoked seizures, or if there is a high recurrence risk such as an epileptiform EEG or structural lesion.
cards.q: A patient has a first unprovoked seizure with a normal examination, normal labs and normal imaging. Should a long-term anti-seizure drug be started?

cards.a: Missed doses, sleep deprivation, alcohol withdrawal, infection or a new interacting drug, because these lower the seizure threshold. Correct the trigger and reinforce adherence before changing the drug.
cards.q: A patient with epilepsy misses doses and has a breakthrough seizure. What is the most common precipitant to ask about?

cards.a: Valproate causes major birth defects and neurodevelopmental problems, so it should be avoided in pregnancy if possible. Switch to a safer agent such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam before conception under specialist guidance, and give folic acid.
cards.q: A pregnant patient with epilepsy is on valproate. What is the major concern?

cards.a: Chronic phenytoin toxicity and side effects, because phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism and folate deficiency. Check a level, review adherence and consider switching agents.
cards.q: A patient on phenytoin develops gum swelling, coarse facial features and a low folate level. What is the explanation?

cards.a: A postictal state, which is expected after a generalised seizure. Observe, protect the airway, check glucose and electrolytes, and look for a trigger, rather than assuming ongoing seizure unless confusion persists or seizures recur.
cards.q: A patient has a tonic-clonic seizure and is now confused and drowsy for 30 minutes afterwards. What is this called and what should be done?

cards.a: Temporal lobe, because temporal lobe seizures often cause automatisms, staring and postictal confusion. MRI may show mesial temporal sclerosis.
cards.q: A patient has focal seizures with lip smacking and staring, then confusion. Which lobe is most likely involved?

cards.a: Because rapid infusion can cause severe hypotension and cardiac arrhythmia. Give fosphenytoin instead, which is safer and can be infused faster, or infuse phenytoin slowly with cardiac monitoring.
cards.q: Why should phenytoin not be given as a rapid IV push in status epilepticus?

cards.a: Correct hyponatraemia carefully and look for its cause, because severe hyponatraemia can cause seizures and correcting it too fast can cause osmotic demyelination. Treat the seizure with a benzodiazepine while correcting sodium slowly.
cards.q: A patient with a seizure has a low sodium of 118 mmol per L. What is the management priority?

cards.a: Secure the airway with intubation, because prolonged seizures impair breathing and aspiration risk is high. Do not delay airway management while giving anti-seizure drugs.
cards.q: A patient in status epilepticus is hypoxic and has a falling oxygen saturation. What is the next step?

cards.a: Subarachnoid haemorrhage, usually from a ruptured aneurysm, because thunderclap headache with meningism is the classic presentation. This is a neurosurgical emergency.
cards.q: A patient has sudden severe headache described as the worst headache of life, vomiting and neck stiffness. What is the most likely diagnosis?

cards.a: Do a lumbar puncture looking for xanthochromia, because CT sensitivity falls with time and a small bleed can be missed. A normal CT does not exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage.
cards.q: A patient with suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage has a normal non-contrast CT head done 8 hours after onset. What is the next step?

cards.a: Because CT first excludes a large bleed, mass or hydrocephalus that would make lumbar puncture dangerous. Lumbar puncture is done only after CT is normal and there is no contraindication.
cards.q: Why is lumbar puncture not done before CT in suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage?

cards.a: Subarachnoid haemorrhage, because blood that has been in the subarachnoid space breaks down to bilirubin causing xanthochromia. A traumatic tap clears between tubes and does not cause xanthochromia.
cards.q: A lumbar puncture shows uniformly bloody cerebrospinal fluid that does not clear between tubes and xanthochromia is present. What does this mean?

cards.a: Cerebral vasospasm, because it typically peaks 4 to 14 days after the bleed and causes delayed cerebral ischaemia. Treat with nimodipine and maintain normal blood volume and pressure.
cards.q: A patient with subarachnoid haemorrhage develops worsening headache and confusion on day 7. What is the most likely cause?

cards.a: Oral nimodipine for 21 days, because it reduces delayed cerebral ischaemia and improves outcome even though it does not always prevent angiographic vasospasm. Start it as soon as the diagnosis is made.
cards.q: What drug is given to prevent vasospasm after aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage?

cards.a: Acute hydrocephalus from blood blocking cerebrospinal fluid flow. Treat with an external ventricular drain, because relieving pressure is urgent and medical treatment alone will not clear the blockage.
cards.q: A patient with subarachnoid haemorrhage becomes drowsy with a dilated ventricle on CT. What is the cause and treatment?

cards.a: Secure the aneurysm early, within 24 to 72 hours, by surgical clipping or endovascular coiling, because rebleeding is most likely in the first hours and days and is often fatal. The choice depends on aneurysm location and patient factors.
cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for a ruptured cerebral aneurysm?

cards.a: Cerebral salt wasting or syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, both common after subarachnoid haemorrhage. Distinguish them by volume status, because cerebral salt wasting needs salt and fluid replacement while inappropriate antidiuretic hormone needs fluid restriction.
cards.q: A patient with subarachnoid haemorrhage has a low sodium and is clinically euvolaemic. What is the likely cause?

cards.a: Because very low pressure can reduce cerebral perfusion and worsen vasospasm risk, while very high pressure raises rebleed risk. Keep systolic below about 160 and avoid large swings until the aneurysm is secured.
cards.q: Why is blood pressure not lowered aggressively in acute subarachnoid haemorrhage before the aneurysm is secured?

cards.a: Treat the seizure and give short-term levetiracetam prophylaxis, because early seizures are common after subarachnoid haemorrhage and can cause rebleeding. Long-term prophylaxis is not routine if no further seizures occur.
cards.q: A patient with subarachnoid haemorrhage has a seizure at presentation. What should be done?

cards.a: A warning leak from the aneurysm, because a small bleed days before a major rupture is a classic history. It should prompt urgent imaging even if the patient felt better in between.
cards.q: A patient has a sentinel headache a week ago, then a thunderclap headache today. What does the earlier headache suggest?

cards.a: Reverse anticoagulation urgently, because ongoing anticoagulation worsens bleeding and rebleed risk. Involve neurosurgery immediately and do not delay imaging.
cards.q: A patient with suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage is on anticoagulation. What is the next step?

cards.a: Assess for contraindications to lumbar puncture, including focal neurology, seizures, papilloedema or reduced consciousness, and get a CT head if any are present, because lumbar puncture with raised pressure can cause herniation.
cards.q: A patient has fever, headache, neck stiffness and confusion. What is the first step before lumbar puncture?

cards.a: Give antibiotics immediately, do not delay for CT or lumbar puncture, because delay increases death and disability. Give dexamethasone before or with the first antibiotic dose, then do CT and lumbar puncture as soon as safe.
cards.q: A patient has suspected bacterial meningitis. When should antibiotics be given relative to CT and lumbar puncture?

cards.a: Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin, with ampicillin added if the patient is over 50, pregnant or immunocompromised to cover Listeria, because Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis are the most common causes and Listeria risk rises in those groups.
cards.q: What empiric antibiotics are given to an adult with suspected bacterial meningitis?

cards.a: Because it reduces inflammation and hearing loss and improves outcome in pneumococcal meningitis when given before or with the first antibiotic. It should not delay antibiotics.
cards.q: Why is dexamethasone given in bacterial meningitis?

cards.a: Bacterial meningitis, because neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose and high protein is typical. Viral meningitis usually has lymphocytes, normal glucose and only mildly raised protein.
cards.q: Cerebrospinal fluid shows high protein, low glucose, high white cells with neutrophils and high opening pressure. What diagnosis does this support?

cards.a: Viral meningitis, most often enterovirus, because a lymphocytic picture with normal glucose is typical. Management is supportive, with aciclovir added until herpes encephalitis is excluded.
cards.q: Cerebrospinal fluid shows lymphocytes, normal glucose and mildly raised protein. What diagnosis does this support?

cards.a: Herpes simplex encephalitis. Start IV aciclovir immediately without waiting for PCR, because delay worsens brain injury and death. Herpes simplex is the most common cause of sporadic encephalitis.
cards.q: A patient has fever, confusion, seizures and temporal lobe changes on MRI. What is the most likely diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Because herpes encephalitis progresses rapidly and early aciclovir saves brain tissue and life, while waiting for PCR can cause irreversible damage. Aciclovir is relatively safe compared with the risk of untreated herpes.
cards.q: Why is aciclovir started empirically in a patient with suspected encephalitis even before test results return?

cards.a: Give IV ceftriaxone immediately, resuscitate with fluids, admit to intensive care and give prophylaxis to close contacts, because meningococcal disease can progress to septic shock and death within hours.
cards.q: A patient with meningococcal meningitis has a purpuric rash and shock. What is the immediate management?

cards.a: Close contacts such as household members, intimate partners and healthcare workers exposed to respiratory secretions, because they are at risk of invasive disease. Give rifampicin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone as prophylaxis.
cards.q: Who needs antibiotic prophylaxis after exposure to meningococcal meningitis?

cards.a: Tuberculous meningitis, because a chronic lymphocytic picture with very low glucose and high protein is typical. Start anti-tuberculous treatment promptly and involve infectious diseases, as delay is dangerous.
cards.q: A patient has chronic headache, low-grade fever and cerebrospinal fluid with lymphocytes, very high protein and very low glucose. What diagnosis should be considered?

cards.a: Induction with amphotericin B plus flucytosine, because cryptococcal meningitis in HIV needs fungicidal combination therapy. Manage raised pressure with repeated lumbar punctures if needed.
cards.q: A patient with HIV and headache has cerebrospinal fluid with a positive cryptococcal antigen. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Get a CT head before lumbar puncture, because focal signs and seizures suggest a mass, abscess or raised pressure that makes lumbar puncture unsafe. Give antibiotics first and do not delay them for the scan.
cards.q: A patient with suspected meningitis has a focal neurological deficit and a seizure before lumbar puncture. What should be done first?

cards.a: Cerebrospinal fluid PCR for herpes simplex virus, because it is highly sensitive and specific. A negative early PCR does not exclude it if clinical suspicion is high, so continue aciclovir and repeat testing.
cards.q: What is the most important test to confirm herpes simplex encephalitis?

cards.a: Sensorineural hearing loss from inflammation damaging the cochlea and auditory nerve, a common complication of pneumococcal meningitis. Dexamethasone given early reduces this risk.
cards.q: A patient with bacterial meningitis develops hearing loss after treatment. What is the explanation?

cards.a: Early meningitis, partially treated meningitis, or a non-meningitis cause such as subarachnoid haemorrhage or viral illness, because a normal fluid early does not always exclude meningitis. Reassess and repeat testing if symptoms persist.
cards.q: A patient has fever, headache and neck stiffness but cerebrospinal fluid is normal. What else should be considered?

cards.a: Assess airway, breathing and circulation and protect the airway, because a Glasgow Coma Scale of 8 or less means the patient cannot protect their own airway. Intubate if needed and check glucose immediately.
cards.q: A patient is found unresponsive with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 8. What is the first management step?

cards.a: Opioid overdose. Give naloxone, because pinpoint pupils with respiratory depression is classic for opioids and naloxone reverses it rapidly. Also check for other causes and monitor for recurrence.
cards.q: A comatose patient has pinpoint pupils, slow breathing and a low respiratory rate. What is the likely cause and treatment?

cards.a: Give IV dextrose immediately, because severe hypoglycaemia is a rapidly reversible cause of coma. Recheck glucose and look for the cause, such as insulin overdose or liver failure.
cards.q: A comatose patient has a glucose of 28 mg per dL. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Bedside glucose, because hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia are common, reversible and quickly tested. Also check oxygen, electrolytes, renal and liver function, and review all drugs.
cards.q: What is the most useful initial test in a patient with unexplained altered mental status?

cards.a: Delirium, because acute fluctuating confusion with inattention in an older or post-operative patient is typical. Look for infection, drugs, pain, dehydration and metabolic causes, and treat the underlying trigger.
cards.q: A patient is confused, agitated and has a fluctuating level of consciousness after surgery. What is the most likely diagnosis?

cards.a: Delirium is acute, fluctuating and affects attention, while dementia is chronic, progressive and affects memory first with preserved attention early. A sudden change from baseline suggests delirium, even in a patient with dementia.
cards.q: How is delirium distinguished from dementia?

cards.a: Hepatic encephalopathy, because liver failure causes ammonia accumulation and a flapping tremor. Treat with lactulose to reduce ammonia and look for a precipitant such as infection or bleeding.
cards.q: A patient with altered mental status has a high ammonia level and asterixis. What is the likely cause?

cards.a: Osmotic demyelination syndrome, which can cause locked-in syndrome and permanent disability. Correct sodium slowly, no more than 8 to 10 mmol per L in 24 hours, unless there are severe symptoms such as seizures.
cards.q: A patient with confusion has a sodium of 112 mmol per L that fell rapidly. What is the risk of correcting it too fast?

cards.a: Raised intracranial pressure with herniation, because unequal pupils and abnormal posturing indicate brainstem compression. This needs urgent airway protection, hyperosmolar therapy and neurosurgery.
cards.q: A patient is unresponsive with unequal pupils and a extensor posturing after head injury. What does this suggest?

cards.a: Sedatives, opioids, anticholinergics, antihistamines and benzodiazepines, because these commonly cause confusion, especially in older adults. Stop or reduce the offending drug if possible.
cards.q: What drugs should be reviewed first in a patient with new confusion?

cards.a: Hypercapnic encephalopathy from respiratory failure, because high carbon dioxide causes drowsiness and confusion. Treat the underlying lung disease and ventilatory failure, not just the confusion.
cards.q: A patient with altered mental status has a normal CT head but a very high carbon dioxide level. What is the explanation?

cards.a: When there is a large haematoma with midline shift, falling consciousness or brainstem compression, because the blood must be evacuated to relieve pressure. Small haematomas without mass effect can be observed with close monitoring.
cards.q: A patient is confused after a fall and has a subdural haematoma on CT. When is surgery needed?

cards.a: Get an urgent non-contrast CT head, because subarachnoid haemorrhage is the most dangerous cause and must be excluded first. If CT is normal, do a lumbar puncture.
cards.q: What is the first step when a patient presents with a thunderclap headache?

cards.a: Giant cell arteritis. Start high-dose steroids immediately, because delay can cause permanent blindness in the other eye. Check ESR and CRP and arrange temporal artery biopsy, but do not wait for it to start steroids.
cards.q: A patient has a new headache with jaw pain, scalp tenderness and visual loss. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Meningitis, because fever with headache and neck stiffness needs urgent assessment even without a rash. Give antibiotics promptly if bacterial meningitis is suspected.
cards.q: A patient has headache, fever and a stiff neck but no rash. What should not be missed?

cards.a: Raised intracranial pressure, possibly from a tumour or mass, because morning headache with vomiting and papilloedema is classic. Get urgent imaging and do not do a lumbar puncture before imaging.
cards.q: A patient has a headache that is worse in the morning, with vomiting and papilloedema. What does this suggest?

cards.a: Post-dural puncture headache from cerebrospinal fluid leak, because the positional pattern is diagnostic. Treat with hydration, caffeine and bed rest, and an epidural blood patch if severe or persistent.
cards.q: A patient has a headache after a lumbar puncture that is worse when standing and better lying down. What is the cause?

cards.a: A posterior communicating artery aneurysm compressing the third cranial nerve, because a painful third nerve palsy with pupil involvement is a neurosurgical emergency. Get urgent vascular imaging.
cards.q: A patient has sudden headache, double vision and a drooping eyelid with a dilated pupil. What is the concern?

cards.a: Migraine with aura, because recurrent episodic headache with visual aura and photophobia in a young adult with normal examination is typical. Red flags are absent, so no urgent imaging is needed.
cards.q: A patient has recurrent headaches with nausea, light sensitivity and an aura, with a normal examination between attacks. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Cauda equina syndrome, because compression of the nerve roots below the spinal cord causes saddle anaesthesia, bladder and bowel dysfunction and leg weakness. This is a surgical emergency.
cards.q: A patient has back pain, saddle numbness, bladder retention and leg weakness. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Urgent surgical decompression, ideally within 24 to 48 hours, because delay increases the risk of permanent bladder, bowel and leg dysfunction. Get an urgent MRI of the lumbosacral spine.
cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for cauda equina syndrome?

cards.a: Spinal epidural abscess, because fever with back pain and neurology after a procedure is classic. Get an urgent MRI and start antibiotics, with surgery if there is cord compression.
cards.q: A patient has severe back pain, fever and a raised CRP after a recent spinal procedure. What should be suspected?

cards.a: Spinal cord compression or injury, because a sensory level with bilateral weakness and bladder involvement localises to the cord. Get urgent MRI and involve neurosurgery or orthospine immediately.
cards.q: A patient has bilateral leg weakness, a sensory level at the chest and urinary retention after trauma. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Because evidence shows little benefit and a higher risk of infection and other complications. Management focuses on stabilisation, decompression when indicated and supportive care.
cards.q: Why is high-dose methylprednisolone not routinely given in acute traumatic spinal cord injury now?

cards.a: Give high-dose dexamethasone, because steroids reduce oedema around the cord and preserve function while definitive treatment is arranged. Do not delay steroids or imaging.
cards.q: A patient with spinal cord compression has a known cancer with metastases to the spine. What is the first step besides imaging?

cards.a: Central cord syndrome, because the central cervical cord contains fibres for the arms more than the legs. It often follows hyperextension injury in older adults with cervical spondylosis.
cards.q: A patient has neck pain, weakness in the arms more than the legs, and bladder dysfunction after a fall. What syndrome is this?

cards.a: Brown-Sequard syndrome from a hemisection of the cord, because pain and temperature cross within a few levels while motor and proprioception stay on the same side. It is often due to trauma or a tumour.
cards.q: A patient has loss of pain and temperature on one side of the body and loss of power and proprioception on the other side below a level. What syndrome is this?

cards.a: Neurogenic shock from loss of sympathetic tone, because a high cord injury interrupts sympathetic outflow. Treat with fluids and vasopressors, and distinguish it from haemorrhagic shock.
cards.q: A patient with a spinal cord injury has low blood pressure and a slow heart rate. What is the cause?

cards.a: Yes, because early cauda equina can present without bladder involvement. Any new leg weakness, saddle numbness or bladder change with back pain needs urgent MRI.
cards.q: A patient has acute back pain and leg weakness but no bladder symptoms. Should cauda equina still be considered?

cards.a: Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing, because the brainstem responds to rising pressure by raising blood pressure to maintain perfusion. It is a late and ominous sign of herniation.
cards.q: What is the Cushing reflex in raised intracranial pressure?

cards.a: Treat for herniation with hyperosmolar therapy such as mannitol or hypertonic saline, hyperventilate briefly if needed, elevate the head and get urgent neurosurgery, because the brain is herniating and time is critical.
cards.q: A patient with a head injury has a falling Glasgow Coma Scale, a dilated pupil and a rising blood pressure. What is the next step?

cards.a: Because it improves venous drainage from the brain and lowers pressure without reducing arterial perfusion. Keep the neck midline and avoid tight neck ties that obstruct venous return.
cards.q: Why is the head of the bed raised to 30 degrees in a patient with raised intracranial pressure?

cards.a: Normal carbon dioxide, around 35 to 40 mmHg, because low carbon dioxide constricts vessels and can reduce brain blood flow, while high carbon dioxide dilates vessels and raises pressure. Prolonged hyperventilation is harmful.
cards.q: What is the target for carbon dioxide in a patient with raised intracranial pressure who is ventilated?

cards.a: Serum osmolality, sodium, renal function and fluid balance, because mannitol can cause dehydration, kidney injury and electrolyte shifts. Do not give it if osmolality is already very high.
cards.q: A patient with raised intracranial pressure is given mannitol. What must be monitored?

cards.a: Intubate and ventilate, because the patient cannot protect the airway and hypoxia or hypercapnia will worsen brain injury. Avoid hypotension and hypoxia, which are the main secondary insults.
cards.q: A patient has a severe head injury and a Glasgow Coma Scale of 7. What is the airway management?

cards.a: Hypotension and hypoxia, because even one episode of low blood pressure or low oxygen greatly worsens outcome. Maintain systolic pressure above 110 and oxygen saturation above 94 percent.
cards.q: What is the most important factor to avoid in the first hours after a severe brain injury?
